title: The Lov\'asz Number Is Not Alone: A Continuum Of R\'enyi Points In The Entanglement-assisted Spectrum Of Graphs
authors: Seth Douglas Nidhal Mghirbi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20775v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Li and Zuiddam's entanglement-assisted asymptotic spectrum of graphs consists of the normalized graph parameters that are additive under disjoint unions, multiplicative under strong products and monotone under entanglement-assisted cohomomorphisms; the entanglement-assisted Shannon capacity is their pointwise minimum. To our knowledge, the Lov\'asz number [MATH] was its only known element. We find a continuum of others. Three quantities of Duan and Winter, [MATH], the minimal Holevo capacity [MATH] and the logarithm of the no-signalling simulation cost [MATH], are the smallest information radii of classical-quantum channels compatible with a graph, measured with Petz-R\'enyi divergences of orders [MATH], [MATH] and [MATH]. At order zero this is due to Schrijver (as credited by Dalai) and to Duan and Winter; at order one it is the min-max formula for the Holevo capacity. Interpolating in the order gives a family [MATH], [MATH], and we prove that every member lies in the spectrum. The main step, multiplicativity under strong products for channels that need not factor, follows from an exact nesting identity for compressions. Sandwiched R\'enyi radii of order [MATH] give the same family, at [MATH]. On the five-cycle the family takes every value in [MATH]. A Hilbert-Schmidt inequality for the pentagon gives [MATH], proving a conjecture of Duan and Winter. We also settle the two open links of their inequality chain: the graph-level no-signalling simulation rate always equals its single-letter value [MATH], and a 32-vertex graph from the Mermin-Peres magic square has [MATH], certified in exact rational arithmetic. Finally, [MATH] never exceeds the projective rank of the complement; a rank inequality for the same square makes this strict on a 1440-vertex graph.
tldr: The paper uncovers a continuum of Rényi-type points in the entanglement-assisted asymptotic spectrum of graphs, generalizing the Lovász number and connecting to channel capacities.
motivation: The entanglement-assisted asymptotic spectrum of graphs previously had only the Lovász number as a known element, leaving the entanglement-assisted Shannon capacity poorly characterized.
method: The authors use minimal information radii of classical-quantum channels with Petz-Rényi divergences of varying orders, proving multiplicativity under strong products via an exact nesting identity for compressions.
result: They prove a continuum of Rényi points lies in the spectrum, compute the family on the five-cycle, prove a Duan-Winter conjecture, and settle two open links in their inequality chain including a no-signalling simulation rate result.
conclusion: This work significantly advances the mathematical theory of entanglement-assisted graph spectra and links graph parameters to quantum channel capacities and no-signalling simulation costs.

The entanglement-assisted Shannon capacity is the pointwise minimum of this spectrum. Previously, the Lovász number ϑ was the only known element. The authors construct a continuum of new elements by interpolating between three quantities of Duan and Winter: log₂ϑ, the minimal Holevo capacity C_min, and the logarithm of the no-signalling simulation cost Σ. These are identified as the smallest information radii of classical-quantum channels compatible with a graph, measured with Petz-Rényi divergences of orders 0, 1, and 2, respectively. By varying the order α ∈ [0,2], they define a family ϑ_α and prove that every member lies in the spectrum. The key technical step is proving multiplicativity under strong products for channels that need not factor, which follows from an exact nesting identity for compressions. They also show that sandwiched Rényi radii of order β ∈ [1/2,∞] yield the same family via α = 2 - 1/β.

On the five-cycle C₅, the family ϑ_α takes every value in [√5, 5/2]. A Hilbert-Schmidt inequality for the pentagon yields C_min(C₅) = log₂(5/2), proving a conjecture of Duan and Winter. Finally, they prove that Σ never exceeds the projective rank of the complement, and a rank inequality for the same square makes this strict on a 1440-vertex graph.

The paper thus significantly expands the known asymptotic spectrum of graphs, provides new tools for computing entanglement-assisted capacities, and resolves several open problems in the area. The results are of interest to quantum information theorists, graph theorists, and researchers in quantum Shannon theory.

title: Classification Of Quantum States Through Conserved Operators
authors: Federico Petrovich, R. Rossignoli, M. Cerezo
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20988v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Determining whether quantum states can be interconverted by a prescribed set of transformations is a fundamental problem in quantum information. Here we develop a general classification framework based on conserved operators (COs), i.e., not necessarily hermitian matrices having the state of interest as an eigenstate. We first show that COs belonging to the algebra generating the allowed transformations can be obtained from the kernel of a quantum covariance matrix. Their number determines the dimension of the accessible orbit, while their algebraic structure and eigenvalues provide further constraints on state convertibility. We establish general bounds on the number of COs and prove that highest-weight states, like separable states in the case of [MATH] qudits, attain the maximum. We also show how these operators generate parent Hamiltonians having the characterized state as an exact ground state. We then also consider positive zero-eigenvalue COs, which encode forbidden directions of reduced density matrices and incorporate rank-based constraints into the same framework. Applying this approach to multiqubit SLOCC, we obtain complementary classifications from algebraic and rank COs. While for [MATH] qubits both lead to the usual classes, for [MATH] qubits they distinguish 17 and 20 types separately, and 29 when combined. The combined classification yields 287 fixed types and [MATH] continuous families for [MATH] qubits, and 4926 fixed types and 147 continuous families for [MATH] qubits, providing, to our knowledge, the most refined exhaustive classification of SLOCC-convertibility classes based on such data.
tldr: Develops a general classification framework based on conserved operators to characterize quantum state convertibility and SLOCC entanglement classes.
motivation: Determining whether quantum states can be interconverted under prescribed transformations is a fundamental problem in quantum information, and existing SLOCC classifications are often incomplete or lack exhaustive refinement.
method: Conserved operators are obtained from the kernel of a quantum covariance matrix, with their number, algebraic structure, and eigenvalues providing constraints on state convertibility; positive zero-eigenvalue conserved operators encode rank-based constraints from reduced density matrices, and the framework is applied to multiqubit SLOCC.
result: For three qubits, algebraic and rank conserved operators distinguish 17 and 20 types separately, and 29 when combined; for four qubits, the combined classification yields 287 fixed types and continuous families plus 4926 fixed types and 147 continuous families.
conclusion: The approach provides the most refined exhaustive classification of SLOCC-convertibility classes based on such data, and links conserved operators to parent Hamiltonians for which the classified state is an exact ground state.

title: Quantum Partial Information Decompositions, An Operational Order On Ensembles, And Direct Quantifications Of Objective Information
authors: Alexander Nico-Katz
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20694v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The partial information decomposition (PID) framework is an extension of classical information theory that enables a systematic analysis of the structure of information in multipartite systems. We advance a simple extension of this framework enabling the construction of multipartite quantum PIDs (QPIDs); generalizing recent, exclusively bipartite, extensions. We construct two QPIDs of the Holevo quantity. First a naive QPID based on the classical minimum mutual information. Second a sophisticated QPID enabled by our development of an operational partial order on quantum ensembles in terms of ensemble (inter-)convertability. Finally, as a concrete example of how QPIDs can be applied, we investigate objectivity scenarios; using our Holevo QPIDs to directly quantify objective information in extended graph states. These findings ultimately establish a foundation upon which generic multipartite QPIDs can be systematically constructed, introduce an operational partial order on ensembles, advance QPIDs as interesting objects of study in their own right, and demonstrate their immediate applicability to problems in quantum information.
tldr: Introduces multipartite quantum partial information decompositions (QPIDs) of the Holevo quantity, including an operational partial order on quantum ensembles, and applies them to quantify objective information in extended graph states.
motivation: Classical partial information decomposition (PID) lacks a general quantum multipartite extension, as existing quantum PIDs are restricted to bipartite systems. A systematic framework is needed to analyze the structure of information in multipartite quantum systems.
method: The paper extends the PID framework to quantum multipartite settings by constructing two QPIDs of the Holevo quantity: a naive QPID based on the classical minimum mutual information, and a sophisticated QPID enabled by an operational partial order on quantum ensembles defined via ensemble interconvertibility.
result: It develops an operational partial order on quantum ensembles, constructs two distinct QPIDs, and demonstrates their utility by directly quantifying objective information in extended graph states.
conclusion: The work establishes a foundation for generic multipartite QPIDs, introduces an operational partial order on ensembles, and shows immediate applicability to problems in quantum information, particularly objectivity scenarios.

title: Infinite Magic And The Emergence Of The Continuum
authors: Leo Shaposhnik, Lorenzo Leone, Lennart Bittel, Dimitris Saraidaris, Alexander Jahn, Jens Eisert
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20790v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Which features of a quantum state are needed for a relativistic quantum field theory to emerge from a lattice system? We address this question by establishing a quantitative relationship between the type classification of hyperfinite von Neumann algebras and the quantum-information-theoretic resource of nonstabilizerness, also called magic. Our results establish two complementary parts of this relationship. First, we prove that any stabilizer system on a lattice defines a canonical GNS Hilbert space in which local von Neumann algebras do not contain type III factors in their central decomposition. As an explicit example, we prove that for stabilizer systems with short-range order, the local algebras are isomorphic to tensor products of hyperfinite factors of type I or type II. This demonstrates that the absence of magic is accompanied by the absence of type III factors in the local algebras, therefore prohibiting the appearance of a quantum field theory. Second, for the hyperfinite factors of Araki, Woods and Powers, we prove a quantitative equivalence: The limiting factor is of type III if and only if the locally optimized min-relative entropy of magic diverges. This divergence is necessary to generate the continuous spectrum associated to a type III factor. Thus, in this setting, the emergence of a type III factor requires not merely the presence of magic, but an infinite amount of it. These results provide a rigorous setting supporting the proposal that infinite magic is a necessary structural ingredient for the emergence of a relativistic continuum from lattice systems.
tldr: The paper proves a quantitative link between nonstabilizerness (magic) and the emergence of type III von Neumann algebras, showing that infinite magic is necessary for a relativistic continuum to arise from lattice systems.
motivation: It addresses which quantum-information features of lattice states are required for a relativistic quantum field theory to emerge, focusing on the role of magic as a resource.
method: It combines algebraic quantum field theory, the type classification of hyperfinite von Neumann algebras, and quantum resource theory, using the locally optimized min-relative entropy of magic as a diagnostic.
result: Stabilizer systems yield local algebras without type III factors, while for Araki-Woods-Powers factors a type III limit occurs if and only if the min-relative entropy of magic diverges.
conclusion: The work provides a rigorous setting supporting the proposal that infinite magic is a necessary structural ingredient for the emergence of a relativistic continuum from lattice systems.

This implies that without magic, type III factors—characteristic of QFTs—cannot appear. Second, for the hyperfinite factors of Araki, Woods, and Powers, they demonstrate that the limiting factor is type III if and only if the locally optimized min-relative entropy of magic diverges. This divergence is required to produce the continuous spectrum of a type III factor, indicating that an infinite amount of magic is necessary for the emergence of a relativistic continuum from lattice systems.

For the converse direction, they focus on the hyperfinite factors of Araki, Woods, and Powers, which are inductive limits of matrix algebras with specific embeddings. deep_read.results_analysis: The key results are twofold. First, for stabilizer systems, the local algebras are either type I or type II, with no type III factors. title: Entanglement Of Superpositions In Zero-energy Subspace: Insights From Stabilizer Theory

abstract: ArXiv:2610.20846v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Exact zero-energy eigenstates built from entangled dimers have recently been found in a large class of spin Hamiltonians. title: Mechanical Trisqueezing In Circuit Quantum Acoustodynamics With Snail Devices
authors: Yi-Zhou Bu, Matteo Fadel, Kai Xu, Heng Fan
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20670v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Continuous-variable quantum information processing with mechanical oscillators requires a uni- versal gate set, including a genuine non-Gaussian evolution. While circuit quantum acoustodynamics (cQAD) experiments have realized bilinear and quartic (four-wave mixing) operations by coupling mechanical modes to transmon qubits, the intrinsic Kerr nonlinearity of these devices precludes access to odd-order effective Hamiltonians such as trisqueezing. Here we propose a cQAD architec- ture in which a mechanical mode, hosted in a high-overtone bulk acoustic-wave resonator (HBAR), is coupled to a superconducting nonlinear asymmetric inductive element (SNAIL). By combining the cubic nonlinearity of the SNAIL with parametric flux driving, we engineer a three-wave mixing interaction that generates trisqueezed mechanical states, producing the characteristic triangular, star-shaped Wigner function with negative regions indicative of non-Gaussianity. We derive the effective trisqueezing Hamiltonian from the full circuit model, identify the drive frequencies and flux modulation required to isolate the desired interaction from competing terms, and quantify the achievable coupling strengths for parameters compatible with current fabrication capabilities. Our results establish a hardware-efficient route to non-Gaussian resource generation in mechanical quantum systems, extending the toolbox of cQAD toward universal continuous-variable quantum computation and enhanced quantum-limited sensing.

title: Quantum Prepare-and-measure Scenarios: Concepts And Methods
authors: A. de Oliveira Junior, Santiago Zamora, Jonatan Bohr Brask, Rafael Chaves, Armin Tavakoli
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20725v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Prepare-and-measure scenarios are among the simplest and most widely used settings for quantum communication. A sender prepares a physical system in one of several possible states, which a receiver then measures. Despite this simple structure, these scenarios offer a rich framework for exploring the differences between classical and quantum communication, revealing quantum advantages, and developing protocols for quantum cryptography and device certification. In this tutorial, we give a ground-up introduction to prepare-and-measure scenarios and the methods used to study them. We introduce different frameworks for constraining and characterising communication, with an emphasis on semi-device-independent approaches to quantum information. We also cover modern convex-optimisation techniques for characterising the correlations achievable in these scenarios and illustrate how these tools can be applied in practice. Our aim is to give newcomers the conceptual and technical foundations needed to approach the current literature and apply prepare-and-measure methods in their own research. We conclude with a discussion of open problems and directions for future work.

title: A Rydberg Atom Array Coupled To A High-cooperativity Optical Cavity
authors: Tai Xiang, Yue-Hui Lu, Tsai-Chen Lee, Jacquelyn Ho, Michael Lan, Zhenjie Yan, Harry Levine, Nathaniel B. Vilas, Dan M. Stamper-Kurn
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20889v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Integrating Rydberg-state control of atom-atom interactions with cavity control of atom-light interactions enables the combination of local entangling operations with photon-mediated long-range coupling, measurement, and communication. Such integration is challenging because electric fields generated by charges on cavity optics and by cavity-stabilizing actuators may disturb Rydberg-state coherence. Here, we couple a Rydberg tweezer array to a high-cooperativity optical cavity, suppressing the electric fields produced by cavity length actuation so that the residual field variation of about [MATH] rms does not limit Rydberg coherence. We demonstrate two capabilities that neither system provides alone. First, we use Purcell-enhanced fluorescence to read out atoms directly in the ground-Rydberg basis within [MATH], well within the Rydberg-state lifetime, with ground- and Rydberg-state detection infidelities of [MATH] and [MATH], respectively, and with low atom loss. Second, we use Rydberg-Rydberg interactions to control collective light-atom scattering into the cavity mode. Specifically, we drive blockaded Rabi oscillations between a state with two ground-state atoms, which scatter collectively with a superradiant or subradiant rate controlled by the atomic positions, and an entangled state with a single Rydberg excitation, which scatters like a single atom. These capabilities open routes toward networked Rydberg processors, mid-circuit measurements in analog quantum simulators, and many-body quantum optics with entangled emitters coupled collectively to light.

title: A Constructive Solution To The $n$-representability Problem
authors: A. Eugene Deprince III Nicholas C. Rubin
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20737v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a solution to the fermionic quantum marginal problem by constructing the complete family of two-body witnesses at each level of a weighted sum-of-squares hierarchy. Our construction combines positive-semidefinite Gram matrices with explicit linear nullspace constraints that exactly cancel all higher-body contributions, replacing the search for individual representability conditions with a systematic algebraic procedure. Beyond the completeness proof, we demonstrate the construction numerically by solving the associated semidefinite program and recovering the exact ground-state energy of a Richardson Hamiltonian in the three-fermion sector. We further prove that higher-degree particle-number multipliers are unnecessary when the full sum-of-squares generating algebra is used. These results establish a unified constructive framework for verifying the physicality of a candidate two-particle reduced density matrix through a complete characterization of all two-body witnesses.

result: They achieve a complete characterization of all two-body witnesses and recover the exact ground-state energy of a Richardson Hamiltonian in the three-fermion sector.

title: Syndrome-Resolved Decoding Of Qubit Readout Errors
authors: Han Zheng, Vladimir Pe\v{s}i\'c, Nikolay Gusarov, Andrea Lizzit, Taketo Imaizumi, Chulwoo Ahn, Marco Nicolas Mueller, Raymond Mencia, Edoardo Charbon, Vladimir E. Manucharyan
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20810v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Readout errors in superconducting qubits include incorrect state assignment, bit flips within the computational subspace, and leakage to non-computational states. These errors require different mitigation strategies, yet conventional measurement fidelity and repeatability metrics do not resolve their individual contributions. Previous repeated-readout studies have shown that temporal correlations reveal additional information about readout errors. Here we introduce the Readout Error Decoder (RED), which converts repeated thresholded binary records into a channel-resolved error budget. Controlled error injections validate the channel-specific response of the decoder. We demonstrate RED on both fluxonium and transmon qubits and across distinct leakage-lifetime regimes. RED identifies the error channels limiting readout performance without requiring dedicated discrimination of non-computational states, providing a basis for targeted readout optimization across different qubit modalities.

motivation: Conventional readout fidelity and repeatability metrics conflate distinct error channels such as misassignment, bit flips, and leakage, limiting targeted readout optimization.
method: RED converts repeated binary readout records into a channel-resolved error budget, validated through controlled error injections and demonstrated on fluxonium and transmon qubits across different leakage-lifetime regimes.
result: RED identifies the error channels limiting readout performance without requiring dedicated discrimination of non-computational states, and its channel-specific response matches injected errors.
conclusion: The decoder provides a practical basis for targeted readout optimization across different superconducting qubit modalities.

title: Practical Wavelength Selection For Quantum-augmented Networks Over Shared Optical Fiber
authors: Nitin Jha, Prateek Paudel, Abhishek Parakh
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20987v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In a quantum augmented network, sharing optical fiber with classical traffic requires quantum wavelength selection to balance logical fidelity, block acceptance, and classical data reception. Here we develop a wavelength-selection framework for an error-corrected three-stage quantum communication protocol. Under a thermal-background model with independent errors, an ideal one-photon receiver, and ideal recovery, we derive an accepted qubit channel and a key-independent lower bound on logical entanglement fidelity. Combining this bound with block acceptance gives an entanglement-fidelity yield bound, which we maximize over evaluated wavelengths subject to fidelity and classical link-budget requirements. For the Steane [[7,1,3]] code at 5 km per traversal and -10 dBm per classical channel, the largest fidelity certificate occurs near 1537 nm, whereas the largest yield bound occurs near 1551 nm. Along the 1.25 Gb/s classical link budget with 0.2% base error, the optimized yield bound falls below 10^-6 near 10 km per traversal, while fidelity remains certified at 0.99 or higher at longer spans. These results distinguish fidelity and yield constraints and identify certified operating regions for quantum-augmented networks sharing optical fiber.

title: Alternating Squeezing And Photon Subtraction For Optical Cat-State Generation
authors: Johanna Conrad, Fabian Steinlechner, Ren\'{e} Sondenheimer
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20728v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Schr\"{o}dinger cat states are important non-Gaussian resources for quantum information processing and quantum-enhanced metrology. Although photon subtraction from squeezed vacuum states has proven useful for generating such states in the optical domain, scaling to large amplitudes while maintaining high fidelity and heralding probability remains challenging. To address these obstacles, we analyze alternating squeezing and photon-number-subtraction operations. Rather than optimizing for a single heralding outcome, we formulate cat-state generation as a fidelity-constrained multibranch problem, jointly optimizing the total probability of all photon-number outcomes satisfying a prescribed fidelity threshold at one common experimental setting. Already for plain photon subtraction, this provides a more operational measure of the usable generation probability and can favor parameter configurations that differ from single-branch optima. Considering experimental constraints on available squeezing and photon-number-resolving capability, we demonstrate improvements in fidelity and success probability compared with plain photon subtraction, without necessarily increasing the required squeezing resources. Without restrictions on photon-number resolution, we find that the optimal architecture of the alternating scheme reduces to one of two single-subtraction endpoint configurations, depending on the available squeezing resources. When photon-number resolution is additionally limited, genuinely alternating branches can become advantageous. We derive analytical expressions for the conditional states, cat-state fidelities, and heralding probabilities, enabling efficient multibranch optimization and a systematic analysis of resource trade-offs, sensitivity to experimental parameter deviations, and heralding loss. Together, these results identify the architecture best suited to a given resource budget.

title: Fisher Information Analysis Of A Langevin System With Thermal And Athermal Noise
authors: Welles A. M. Morgado Eduardo S. Nascimento

We apply this method to a system of Langevin equations analogous to the Brownian Gyrator, in which the coupling parameter [MATH] and the athermal noise strength [MATH] are treated as unknown quantities. Using the FI, we discuss the estimation of the coupling parameter between the degrees of freedom and the quantity [MATH] associated with the external noise effects. We find that the diagonal components of the FI exhibit nontrivial behavior, whereas the off-diagonal components display a monotonic dependence on the parameters of interest. This distinction may contribute to an accurate estimation of [MATH] and [MATH].

title: Perfect And Peak State Transfer On Ibm Quantum Hardware
authors: Krystal Guo Priscilla Awuah
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20855v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We run continuous-time quantum walks with perfect and peak state transfer on a present-day superconducting quantum processor, IBM Quantum's [MATH]-qubit Heron device ibm_kingston, deliberately without error correction or error mitigation. Perfect state transfer and its relaxations have been studied extensively in algebraic graph theory, where one can prove exactly which graphs move a quantum state from one vertex to another with probability one (or with the largest probability the graph allows, in the case of peak state transfer), and at what time. Our experiments cover perfect state transfer on the hypercubes [MATH] and [MATH], and on the Hamming-weighted paths [MATH], the equitable-partition quotients of the hypercubes [MATH], for [MATH] up to [MATH]; peak state transfer on the [MATH] family for [MATH] up to [MATH]; and, for comparison, moving the state along a path of qubits by a sequence of SWAP gates.
tldr: The paper experimentally demonstrates perfect and peak state transfer via continuous-time quantum walks on IBM's superconducting Heron processor without error correction.
motivation: Quantum walks are a fundamental tool for quantum simulation and algorithm design, and demonstrating state transfer on real hardware is a step toward practical quantum information processing. However, this work does not implement error correction and is limited to small-scale state transfer, so its immediate relevance to error-corrected quantum computing is low.

title: On The Subadditivity Of Mutual f-Information
authors: Amin Gohari Hamidreza Abin
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21231v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We address an open problem raised by Polyanskiy and Wu in their textbook concerning the subadditivity of mutual \(f\)-information. We study two notions of generalized mutual information: mutual \(f\)-information, defined by \(_f(X;Y)=D_f(p_{XY}\|p_Xp_Y)\), and variational \((G,f)\)-information, obtained by minimizing an average of transformed \(f\)-divergences. For the first notion, we derive a sufficient condition on \(g(x)=x^2f''(x)\) that guarantees subadditivity under conditionally independent observations. This condition yields explicit families beyond the previously known examples generated by \(x\log x\) and \((x-1)\log x\). Our proof relies on the concavity of a generalized variance functional. For the variational notion, we extend existing sufficient conditions beyond the transforms \(G(x)\in\{x,\log(1+x),-\log(1-x)\}\). Using a comparison inequality for \(G^{-1}(G(A)+G(B))\), we obtain differential criteria for concave and convex transforms. Explicit constructions illustrate the resulting classes of subadditive information measures.
tldr: The paper derives sufficient conditions for the subadditivity of mutual f-information and variational (G,f)-information, extending known subadditive families beyond KL divergence.
motivation: It addresses an open problem raised by Polyanskiy and Wu on the subadditivity of mutual f-information, a generalized information measure.
method: The authors analyze f-divergence-based mutual information, derive a sufficient condition on g(x)=x^2 f''(x) using concavity of a generalized variance functional, and use a comparison inequality for G^{-1}(G(A)+G(B)) to extend variational (G,f)-information.
result: They obtain explicit sufficient conditions and new families of subadditive information measures, going beyond the previously known cases generated by x log x and (x-1) log x, and extend the admissible transforms beyond G(x) in {x, log(1+x), -log(1-x)}.
conclusion: The work characterizes broad classes of subadditive generalized information measures, contributing to classical information theory rather than directly to quantum information.

title: An Exact Computer-assisted Lower Bound For Fisher-information Convexity Along The Two-dimensional Heat Flow
authors: Xiaoyan Huo Fayez Abu-Ajamieh
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20653v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the sharp constant in the differential inequality \[ I(t)I''(t)\geq c\,[I'(t)]^2 \] for Fisher information along the probability-normalized heat flow on [MATH]. The unrestricted log-convexity value [MATH] is false in two dimensions, whereas the known square-root convexity theorem gives the universal value [MATH]. We construct an exact, machine-verifiable sum-of-squares certificate proving the stronger universal bound \[ c\geq {250000}=0.926764. \] Together with an independent exact Fourier/Gaussian-envelope construction, this gives \[ 0.926764\leq c_*<0.94176665012062, \] where [MATH] is the sharp constant for positive-time Gaussian convolutions of arbitrary probability measures on [MATH]. We formulate the proof in explicit two-dimensional index notation. The lower bound follows from an exact rational polynomial identity involving a strictly positive denominator, a weighted total derivative, and eleven positive rational Gram matrices. All [MATH] recorded leading principal minors are strictly positive and the complete polynomial identity has zero residual. No symmetry, log-concavity, finite-variance, or finite-entropy assumption is imposed on the initial measure. The sharp value remains open.
tldr: The paper provides an exact sum-of-squares certificate for a lower bound on the sharp constant in the Fisher-information convexity inequality along the two-dimensional heat flow, improving the universal bound to c ≥ 0.926764.
motivation: The sharp constant in the differential inequality I(t)I''(t) ≥ c [I'(t)]^2 for Fisher information along the heat flow is unknown; log-convexity (c=1) fails in 2D, and only the square-root convexity bound c=3/4 was previously known.
method: A machine-verifiable sum-of-squares proof using an exact rational polynomial identity with a strictly positive denominator, a weighted total derivative, and eleven positive rational Gram matrices; complemented by an independent Fourier/Gaussian-envelope construction.
result: Proves the lower bound c ≥ 0.926764 and establishes an upper bound c* < 0.94176665012062 for the sharp constant, narrowing the gap without imposing symmetry, log-concavity, finite-variance, or finite-entropy assumptions.
conclusion: The exact sharp constant remains open, but the work provides a rigorous computer-assisted lower bound that significantly improves the known universal value.

title: Benchmarking Post-Quantum Key Encapsulation In S3-Compatible Object Storage Under Client Concurrency
authors: Revanth Reddy Lingala, K. Gangadhara Rao, Padigela Srujan, Saarthak Manocha, Vainavi Venkat
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21457v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Data encrypted today with classical public-key algorithms could be decrypted once large quantum computers exist. Cloud object stores keep data for years, so the client-side encryption that protects it must move to post-quantum algorithms such as ML-KEM, which adds a key-encapsulation step and a larger ciphertext to every stored object. So far, the cost of ML-KEM has been measured for the algorithm on its own and for securing network connections, but not for encrypting each object in a storage system that serves many clients at once. It has therefore been unclear whether ML-KEM slows such a system, under which conditions, and why. We address this problem by measuring per-object ML-KEM against classical key exchange on an S3-compatible object store, with two client implementations, two processor types and up to 500 concurrent workers, using pre-registered experiments and statistical equivalence tests. ML-KEM reduced throughput only when the client's processor was at or near full load, with one unexplained exception, and then by 4.0 to 4.9% in our main client. Controlled experiments on one processor type traced most of that loss to the way the software library was called, and a second, native client showed that the size of the loss depends on the implementation. The lasting cost is storage: 1,056 more bytes per object than with classical key exchange. The results cover two clients, one single-node store and one cloud provider.
tldr: The paper benchmarks per-object ML-KEM key encapsulation against classical key exchange in an S3-compatible object store under client concurrency, finding minimal throughput loss except near full CPU load and a storage overhead of 1,056 bytes per object.
motivation: Cloud data encrypted with classical public-key algorithms is vulnerable to future quantum computers, so post-quantum migration is needed, but the cost of per-object ML-KEM in a multi-client object storage system was previously unclear.
method: The authors measured per-object ML-KEM against classical key exchange on an S3-compatible object store using two client implementations, two processor types, and up to 500 concurrent workers, with pre-registered experiments and statistical equivalence tests.
result: ML-KEM reduced throughput only when the client processor was at or near full load, by 4.0–4.9% in the main client with one unexplained exception; controlled experiments traced most of the loss to how the software library was called, and the lasting cost was 1,056 more bytes of storage per object than classical key exchange.
conclusion: ML-KEM imposes acceptable throughput overhead for S3-compatible object storage except under CPU saturation, and the exact loss depends on implementation; the persistent cost is additional storage per object.

title: Iterative Bounded Distance Decoding With 2-Bit Reliability Marker For Product-Like Codes
authors: Xiaowei Wu, Min Qiu, Yueying Zhan, Lei Yang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21279v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a novel soft-aided hard-decision decoding scheme for product codes based on two-bit quantized reliability markers. In particular, one bit is used for a two-level tolerance miscorrection check to validate the bounded distance decoding (BDD) result, while the other identifies bits to be randomly flipped upon BDD failure and miscorrection. List decoding is incorporated to further facilitate the error performance. Density evolution is performed for the design of the quantization thresholds. Compared to iterative BDD, the proposed scheme requires only moderate increases in memory and computational overhead. Simulation results verify that our scheme outperforms several unquantized soft-aided decoders, while maintaining small memory costs and low BDD attempts.
tldr: The paper proposes a soft-aided hard-decision decoding scheme for product-like codes using two-bit quantized reliability markers, combining bounded distance decoding, list decoding, and density evolution.
motivation: To improve the error-correction performance of product codes while maintaining low memory and computational overhead compared to existing soft-aided decoders.
method: One reliability bit is used for a tolerance miscorrection check of bounded distance decoding (BDD) results, and the other identifies bits to randomly flip upon BDD failure or miscorrection; list decoding is incorporated and density evolution designs the quantization thresholds.
result: Simulations show the scheme outperforms several unquantized soft-aided decoders while requiring only moderate increases in memory and computational overhead and keeping BDD attempts low.
conclusion: The proposed 2-bit reliability marker approach offers an effective performance-complexity trade-off for decoding product-like codes.

title: Sparse-QITE: Discovering Compact Generators For Quantum Imaginary-Time Evolution Via Regularization Methods
authors: Rafael G\'omez-Lurbe, Luca Ion, Alberto Acevedo, Andreu Angl\'es-Castillo
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20791v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum imaginary-time evolution (QITE) provides a systematic route to ground-state preparation, but its cost grows rapidly with the locality [MATH] of the unitary approximation, for which the local Pauli basis scales as [MATH]. We introduce Sparse-QITE, a regularized formulation that promotes compact generators, reducing the number of quantum operations and yielding circuits with fewer gates and lower depth. We derive rigorous bounds on the sparsification error and benchmark the method in one-dimensional transverse-field Ising and antiferromagnetic Heisenberg models. Sparse-QITE exhibits a controllable sparsity--accuracy trade-off while retaining strong compression even in the high-accuracy regime. In scalability experiments with respect to [MATH], the active support grows much more slowly than in standard QITE and, in several regimes, approximately saturates over the domain sizes studied. After circuit construction and transpilation, some of the largest-domain cases require only about [MATH] of the standard-QITE gate count while maintaining high accuracy. We further introduce adaptive and active-discovery variants: the former selects the regularization strength dynamically during the evolution, while the latter reduces the number of Pauli expectation values that need to be evaluated and, consequently, the measurement requirements. These results establish sparsity-promoting regularization as a route toward more resource-efficient QITE. More broadly, these results suggest that sparsity-promoting regularization may also benefit variational quantum algorithms.
tldr: Sparse-QITE applies sparsity-promoting regularization to quantum imaginary-time evolution, producing compact generators and reducing gate count and circuit depth for ground-state preparation.
motivation: Standard quantum imaginary-time evolution (QITE) suffers from rapidly growing Pauli basis size and circuit cost as locality increases, limiting its practical use.
method: The authors introduce a regularized QITE formulation that promotes sparse Pauli coefficients, derive rigorous sparsification-error bounds, and benchmark it on 1D transverse-field Ising and antiferromagnetic Heisenberg models, including adaptive and active-discovery variants.
result: Sparse-QITE achieves a controllable sparsity–accuracy trade-off, yields active support that grows much more slowly than standard QITE, and in some large-domain cases requires only about a fraction of the standard-QITE gate count after transpilation while maintaining high accuracy.
conclusion: Sparsity-promoting regularization provides a route to more resource-efficient QITE and may also benefit variational quantum algorithms, though it remains a quantum-simulation algorithmic technique rather than a direct contribution to the researcher's core interests.

title: Critical Ising Model On The Periodic Cubic Lattice $(\mathbb{Z}/L\mathbb{Z})^{3}$
authors: Shenglan Yuan
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21326v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the critical behaviour of the nearest-neighbour Ising model on the three-dimensional periodic cubic lattice [MATH], and we present a companion set of Monte Carlo simulations. After recalling the rigorous results on the continuity of the spontaneous magnetization in [MATH] and the triviality of the scaling limit in [MATH], we compile modern high-precision estimates of the 3D Ising critical exponents and verify the scaling relations that connect them. We then describe numerical measurements of the Binder cumulant, the magnetic susceptibility, the specific heat, the two-point correlation function, and the finite-size scaling of the magnetization. We discuss the systematic uncertainties that affect the extraction of the exponent ratios [MATH] and [MATH], and we emphasize that an exponential fit of the correlation function is not appropriate at the critical point, where the decay is algebraic.
tldr: A numerical and review study of the critical behavior of the nearest-neighbour Ising model on a three-dimensional periodic cubic lattice, including high-precision critical exponents and Monte Carlo measurements.
motivation: The 3D Ising model is a paradigmatic model of classical critical phenomena, and precise characterization of its exponents and scaling relations remains important for statistical mechanics and field theory.
method: The paper recalls rigorous results on spontaneous magnetization continuity and triviality of the scaling limit, compiles modern high-precision estimates of 3D Ising critical exponents, and performs companion Monte Carlo simulations measuring the Binder cumulant, susceptibility, specific heat, two-point correlations, and finite-size scaling of magnetization.
result: The compiled exponents are verified against scaling relations, and systematic uncertainties in extracting exponent ratios are discussed, with the caveat that exponential fits of the correlation function are inappropriate at criticality where decay is algebraic.
conclusion: The work consolidates current knowledge of 3D Ising criticality and provides benchmark Monte Carlo data, but contains no quantum information or quantum thermodynamics content.

title: Agent-assisted Experimental Strategy Transfer Across Quantum Processors
authors: Shi-Yao Hou, Zipeng Wu, Chao Zhang, Guanru Feng, Keren Li, Jingen Xiang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21047v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Progress in quantum hardware requires a growing volume of experiments across diverse devices, straining the capacity of human experts. Automation remains challenging because device differences and drift can render workflows developed on one processor unsuitable for another. Here we present an agent-assisted experimental strategy for conducting experiments across three-qubit nuclear magnetic resonance processors. Developed on one processor and applied sequentially to four others, the strategy uses an agent to assess experimental evidence, select subsequent measurements and adapt procedures, with operators providing instrument preparation and physical intervention. Using three-qubit Grover state preparation as a common task, each deployment combined device-specific calibration, control-pulse optimization and measurement. The experimental strategy was refined through sequential deployment, and all four processors ultimately produced outputs dominated by their respective marked states. The marked-state populations of the reconstructed dominant eigenstates ranged from \(0.910\) to \(0.959\), with relative deviations below \(3.8\%\) from the ideal value of 0.945. These results demonstrate that an agent-assisted experimental strategy can be reused and refined across processors to realize a common quantum task, providing a basis for scaling experimental practice beyond individual devices.
tldr: An agent-assisted experimental strategy, developed on one three-qubit NMR processor, was successfully transferred and refined across four other processors to perform Grover state preparation.
motivation: Quantum hardware progress requires many experiments across diverse devices, straining human experts, and device differences make workflows hard to reuse.
method: An agent assesses experimental evidence, selects measurements, and adapts procedures, while operators handle instrument preparation and physical intervention; each deployment includes device-specific calibration, control-pulse optimization, and measurement.
result: All four processors produced outputs dominated by their marked states, with marked-state populations of the reconstructed dominant eigenstates ranging from 0.910 to 0.959, and relative deviations below 3.8% from the ideal 0.945.
conclusion: Agent-assisted experimental strategies can be reused and refined across quantum processors, providing a basis for scaling experimental practice beyond individual devices.

title: On The Structure Of Polynomial Ideal Codes And Additive Reed--Solomon Codes
authors: Rub\'en Rodr\'iguez-Ballesteros Umberto Mart\'inez-Pe\~{n}as
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21509v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study structural properties of polynomial ideal (PI) codes and additive Reed--Solomon (aRS) codes in the folded Hamming metric (equivalently, the Hamming metric over a larger alphabet). We first determine the maximum possible length of PI codes, prove that the dual of every PI code is a generalized PI code, and deduce that PI codes are dually QMDS together with an explicit formula for their weight distribution. We then show that PI codes defined by irreducible polynomials correspond to aRS codes with pairwise nonconjugate evaluation points. For these aRS codes, the previous results on PI codes apply (duality, QMDS property and weight distribution). We show that, asymptotically, aRS codes with nonconjugate evaluation points achieve the same length as PI codes. We also compute the permutation group of such aRS codes. We also extend the family of PI codes to consider arbitrary polynomial modules (not necessarily pairwise coprime), and study when these and general aRS codes satisfy the QMDS and dually QMDS properties.
tldr: A structural study of polynomial ideal codes and additive Reed–Solomon codes in the folded Hamming metric, establishing length bounds, duality, QMDS properties, and weight distributions.
motivation: Polynomial ideal codes and additive Reed–Solomon codes generalize classical Reed–Solomon and evaluation codes, and understanding their structure in the folded Hamming metric is of interest to coding theorists.
method: The authors derive maximum code lengths, prove that duals of PI codes are generalized PI codes, connect PI codes over irreducible polynomials to aRS codes with nonconjugate evaluation points, and compute permutation groups and weight distributions.
result: PI codes are shown to be dually QMDS with explicit weight distributions, their duals are generalized PI codes, and aRS codes with nonconjugate evaluation points asymptotically match PI codes in length; the framework is extended to arbitrary polynomial modules.
conclusion: The work clarifies the structural and duality properties of PI and aRS codes, extending them to general polynomial modules and characterizing when QMDS and dual QMDS conditions hold.

title: Representation-split Carleman Lattice Boltzmann With Near-unit Step Success Probability On Quantum Computers
authors: Sauro Succi Hua-Dong Yao
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20620v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Carleman lattice Boltzmann method replaces the quadratic collision of the lattice Boltzmann equation by a linear map on a lifted state. Existing block encodings of this map succeed with probability [MATH] to [MATH] per step, so that the probability of a multi-step evolution decays exponentially with the number of steps. This study develops multi-relaxation-time Carleman lattice Boltzmann, a representation split in which the Carleman-lifted collision is performed in a moment basis on the amplitude-encoded state, while streaming remains a permutation in population space. The level-2 hierarchy closes under collision but not under streaming, which generates the work of pressure, advection and stress on the momentum flux. The state therefore remains the full pair array, and the moment representation is an orthogonal change of basis of the population one, with identical dynamics and truncation error. The operator to be block encoded changes with the basis, and with it the success probability of a quantum step. In the weighted Hermite basis with the amplitude encoding [MATH], the relaxation is a diagonal operator of norm one, and the level-2 collision stage becomes this diagonal plus a sparse coupling from products of conserved moments. A structured block encoding of this form raises the single-step success probability on the D2Q9 lattice from [MATH] for the best population encoding to 0.98. With the pair sector in relative coordinates and scaled, one step requires [MATH] Toffoli gates and is verified by statevector simulation. The encoding and readout overhead of a [MATH]-step run is then polynomial in [MATH] and [MATH] rather than accumulating a factor [MATH]. For resolved flows, the remaining exponential loss in coherent multi-step Carleman lattice Boltzmann evolution is set by the non-equilibrium norm relaxed by dissipation rather than by the block encoding.
tldr: This paper develops a representation-split Carleman lattice Boltzmann method on quantum computers, achieving near-unit single-step success probability via structured block encoding.
motivation: Existing block encodings of Carleman lattice Boltzmann collision maps have low per-step success probability, causing exponential decay in multi-step evolutions.
method: The collision is performed in a weighted Hermite moment basis on an amplitude-encoded state while streaming remains a permutation in population space, yielding a diagonal-plus-sparse block encoding with a moment-basis orthogonal change.
result: The single-step success probability on the D2Q9 lattice is raised from the best population-encoding value to 0.98, with one step requiring a certain number of Toffoli gates verified by statevector simulation.
conclusion: The encoding and readout overhead for a multi-step run becomes polynomial, and the remaining exponential loss is set by non-equilibrium dissipation rather than block encoding.

title: Equality Of The Jellium And The Uniform Electron Gas Energies
authors: Mih\'aly A. Csirik
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20910v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Jellium, a system of electrons in a uniform neutralizing background, and the uniform electron gas (UEG), a system of electrons with constant density and no background, are two standard models of the electron gas. We prove that the ground-state energy per unit volume of Jellium, as defined by Lieb and Narnhofer, coincides with the UEG energy defined by Lewin, Lieb and Seiringer, i.e. \[ e^\hbar_{\rm Jel}(\rho_0)=e^\hbar_{\rm UEG}(\rho_0). \] This equality was previously established in the classical case by Lewin, Lieb and Seiringer and independently by Cotar and Petrache.
tldr: The paper rigorously proves that the ground-state energy per unit volume of Jellium (electrons in a uniform neutralizing background, à la Lieb–Narnhofer) equals that of the uniform electron gas (constant density, no background, à la Lewin–Lieb–Seiringer).
motivation: Jellium and the uniform electron gas are two standard but inequivalent-looking models of the electron gas, and establishing whether their ground-state energies coincide was an open question already resolved classically.
method: A rigorous mathematical-physics analysis comparing the variational definitions of the two models' ground-state energies, extending the techniques used in the classical proof to the quantum setting.
result: The equality e^ℏ_Jel(ρ0) = e^ℏ_UEG(ρ0) is established, mirroring the earlier classical result of Lewin–Lieb–Seiringer and, independently, Cotar–Petrache.
conclusion: The two definitions of the electron gas are physically equivalent at the level of ground-state energy density, unifying two canonical models of condensed-matter and electronic-structure theory.

title: Reducing Qubo Complexity In Drone Delivery Through Classical Feasibility Preprocessing
authors: Silvie Ill\'esov\'a, Vojt\v{e}ch Nov\'ak, Martin Beseda
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21003v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Drone-delivery planning combines routing decisions with operational constraints such as payload capacity and limited onboard energy, resulting in combinatorial optimization problems that can become costly to encode directly in binary form. This work investigates a hybrid quantum--classical approach in which candidate drone missions are generated and evaluated classically before constructing a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) model for mission selection. Payload- and energy-infeasible missions are removed during preprocessing, while the reduced QUBO is solved using exact enumeration, simulated annealing (SA), and the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA), with mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) used as a classical reference. Experiments on controlled synthetic delivery instances evaluate solution quality, the effect of preprocessing, and computational scaling. Exact QUBO optimization reproduces the MILP optimum on the evaluated small instances, while SA achieves [MATH] feasibility with a median optimality gap of [MATH]. Combined payload-and-energy preprocessing reduces the mean number of QUBO variables by [MATH] and quadratic interactions by [MATH], while reducing mean SA runtime by [MATH]. In contrast, the evaluated shallow statevector-based QAOA configuration achieves lower feasibility and is restricted to small QUBO instances. These results indicate that, in the considered setting, the main practical benefit of the hybrid architecture comes from classical feasibility preprocessing that reduces the binary search space before QUBO-based optimization.
tldr: The paper applies classical feasibility preprocessing to reduce QUBO complexity for drone-delivery mission selection, solving the reduced problem with exact enumeration, simulated annealing, and QAOA.
motivation: Drone-delivery planning combines routing and operational constraints, leading to combinatorial optimization problems that are costly to encode directly as QUBOs.
method: Candidate missions are generated and evaluated classically, payload- and energy-infeasible ones are removed, then a reduced QUBO is constructed and solved using exact enumeration, SA, and QAOA, with MILP as a classical reference.
result: Preprocessing cut QUBO variables and interactions substantially and reduced SA runtime; exact QUBO matched MILP on small instances, SA achieved good feasibility, while shallow QAOA showed lower feasibility and was limited to small instances.
conclusion: The main practical benefit in this setting comes from classical feasibility preprocessing that shrinks the binary search space before QUBO-based optimization.

title: Thermodynamically Consistent Machine Learning For Fracture Prediction In Heterogeneous Materials
authors: Muhamad Alim, Xiaolong He, Mei-Na Tsao, Chi-Hua Yu, J. S. Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20614v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Understanding fracture behavior is critical for assessing the structural integrity and longevity. Highly time-consuming physics-based fracture simulations motivate the development of machine-learning-based fracture evolution prediction with surrogate models. However, most existing machine-learning models for fracture prediction operate as black boxes and require large training datasets to generalize reliably. In this work, Thermodynamically Consistent Latent Dynamics Identification (tLaSDI) for parametric systems is introduced to predict fracture patterns and evolution in heterogeneous materials. The model learns the thermodynamic state variable in a lower-dimensional latent space using parametric GENERIC Formalism-Informed Neural Networks (pGFINNs) that enforce key thermodynamic principles, such as total energy conservation and entropy generation. This model embeds physics into the neural network architecture using a hard-constraint method that inherently complies with the underlying thermodynamic principles. The proposed tLaSDI-pGFINNs is further enhanced by a Geometry-Conditioned Autoencoder in learning the geometry configuration for effective geometry-guided learning. The energy and entropy evolution histories demonstrate that the model preserves the thermodynamic constraints on unseen testing samples. The results further show that tLaSDI-pGFINNs can more accurately capture both fracture patterns and the subsequent fracture evolution than the purely data-driven Autoencoder Long Short-Term Memory (AE-LSTM) model.
tldr: Introduces tLaSDI-pGFINNs, a thermodynamically consistent latent dynamics model for predicting fracture patterns and evolution in heterogeneous materials.
motivation: Physics-based fracture simulations are highly time-consuming, while existing machine-learning surrogates act as black boxes and require large training datasets for reliable generalization.
method: The model learns a lower-dimensional latent thermodynamic state using parametric GENERIC formalism-informed neural networks that enforce total energy conservation and entropy generation, enhanced by a geometry-conditioned autoencoder.
result: The approach preserves thermodynamic constraints on unseen testing samples and more accurately captures fracture patterns and subsequent evolution than a purely data-driven AE-LSTM baseline.
conclusion: Thermodynamically consistent latent dynamics offers a promising physics-informed surrogate for fracture prediction in heterogeneous materials, though it does not connect to quantum information or quantum thermodynamics.

title: A Tutorial On Quantum Scattering Theory And Coupled-channel Calculations Of Bimolecular Collisions
authors: Christiane P. Koch Karl P. Horn
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20882v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Collisions between atoms and molecules govern how energy is exchanged and redistributed in the gas phase, underpinning phenomena from spectral line broadening and interstellar molecular excitation to the cooling and trapping of molecules. A quantitative account of these collisions requires connecting the theoretical description of the interaction between the collision partners to measurable quantities such as cross sections. However, scattering theory as presented in quantum mechanics textbooks does not readily translate into numerical methods. Here, we formulate the scattering problem in Dirac notation, as customary in present-day quantum mechanics courses, and show how to build a practical numerical framework from it. We derive the "coupled channel" representation of the scattering problem with correct asymptotic behaviour and introduce Numerov's method to obtain time-independent wavefunctions, from which we calculate cross sections, the observables measured in scattering experiments. Starting from single channel scattering, we build up to the realistic collision of a ground-state atom with a diatomic molecule.
tldr: A tutorial presenting quantum scattering theory and coupled-channel calculations for bimolecular collisions in Dirac notation with numerical methods.
motivation: The paper aims to bridge textbook quantum scattering theory and practical numerical computation for atom-molecule collisions, which govern energy exchange in gas-phase and cold-molecule settings.
method: It formulates the scattering problem in Dirac notation, derives the coupled-channel representation with correct asymptotic behavior, and uses Numerov's method to obtain time-independent wavefunctions and cross sections.
result: The tutorial develops a step-by-step computational framework from single-channel scattering to realistic collisions between a ground-state atom and a diatomic molecule.
conclusion: The work provides a pedagogical and practical guide for calculating scattering observables, but it is not directly connected to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Singular Wave Functions And Quantum Collapse In Inverse-power Potentials
authors: Boris Malomed Hidetsugu Sakaguchi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21044v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum collapse (QC) occurs under the action of the inverse-power potential U(r)=-U_{0}/(2r^{n}) in the framework of the Schroedinger equation. The corresponding stationary wave functions feature an infinite number of spatial oscillations at [MATH]. The ground state (GS) is missing in the presence of the QC, but the available bound states at finite energies may be physically relevant, as they are normalizable. This work aims to produce singular stationary wave functions. The analytical findings represent an asymptotic form of the stationary wave functions at [MATH], which fill a continuous spectrum, and some exact solutions for the wave functions, obtained under appropriate conditions. As a regularized version, we also consider the potential truncated at a finite difference from the center. The regularized wave functions feature a finite number of spatial oscillations, the missing GS reappears, and the spectrum of the bound states is discrete.
tldr: The paper analyzes singular stationary wave functions and quantum collapse in inverse-power potentials within the Schrodinger equation.
motivation: Inverse-power potentials can induce quantum collapse, which removes the ground state and leads to infinitely oscillating wave functions; understanding these singular solutions and their regularization is a mathematical physics problem.
method: Analytical derivation of asymptotic and exact stationary wave functions, complemented by a regularized version where the potential is truncated at a finite distance from the center.
result: The singular bound states form a continuous spectrum, while the regularized potential yields a discrete spectrum, a finite number of spatial oscillations, and restores the missing ground state.
conclusion: The work provides a detailed mathematical characterization of quantum collapse in inverse-power potentials, but it does not address quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Free Fermion Frustration-free Models Have Zero Hall Conductance
authors: Sven Bachmann, Zhiqian Du, Martin Fraas
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21172v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give a new proof that translation-invariant free Fermion frustration-free models have zero Hall conductance. Our proof is analytic in nature and it uses the bulk-edge correspondence. The central argument, which holds beyond the translation-invariant situation, is that in frustration-free models, edge modes cannot merge into the ground state band. We give an example of a gapped frustration-free model that is nonetheless gapless on the half-plane.
tldr: The paper provides a new analytic proof that translation-invariant free fermion frustration-free models have zero Hall conductance, using bulk-edge correspondence and showing edge modes cannot merge into the ground state band.
motivation: Hall conductance quantization and bulk-edge correspondence are central in topological condensed matter physics; the authors aim to clarify constraints on frustration-free free fermion models.
method: The proof is analytic and relies on the bulk-edge correspondence, with a general argument that in frustration-free models edge modes cannot merge into the ground state band, extending beyond translation invariance.
result: They prove zero Hall conductance for translation-invariant free fermion frustration-free models and construct a gapped frustration-free model that is nevertheless gapless on the half-plane.
conclusion: The findings constrain the topological response of frustration-free free fermion systems and highlight subtle edge physics, though they are not directly connected to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: It Takes Two Moments: Rigidity And Limits Of Continuous Encoders For Over-the-Air Computation
authors: Saeed Razavikia
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21536v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study over-the-air computation of functions, such as empirical variance, formed by combining two separately postprocessed sums of locally transformed observations. We consider continuous encoders subject to pointwise peak-power constraints over a single use of a complex multiple-access channel. With four or more transmitters, we identify conditions under which exact noiseless recovery forces every continuous encoder collection into a common affine structure that preserves both sums, reducing infinite-dimensional encoder design to selecting a finite set of coefficients. To quantify resilience against channel noise, we introduce a robustness score that measures the separation of noiseless received aggregates relative to variations in the desired function value. Within this characterized encoder family, we formulate robustness maximization as an exact convex semi-infinite program, eliminating rank constraints without a relaxation gap, and construct a decoder that attains the minimum uniform noise-amplification constant. For several function classes, including empirical variance, we derive closed-form robustness-optimal encoders and scores. Under mild regularity conditions, we also establish sharp limits on the Gaussian mean squared error at high signal-to-noise ratios and show how using the input distribution reduces average error at the expense of uniform robustness.
tldr: This paper studies continuous encoder design for over-the-air computation of functions such as empirical variance under peak-power constraints, characterizing rigid affine encoder structures and optimizing robustness against channel noise.
motivation: Over-the-air computation aims to efficiently compute functions of distributed data via wireless multiple-access channels, but practical encoder design is challenged by power constraints, noise, and the need for robust function recovery.
method: The authors analyze continuous encoders under pointwise peak-power constraints for a complex multiple-access channel, prove structural rigidity for four or more transmitters, and formulate robustness maximization as an exact convex semi-infinite program.
result: They derive closed-form robustness-optimal encoders and scores for several function classes, construct a decoder minimizing uniform noise amplification, and establish sharp high-SNR limits on Gaussian mean squared error.
conclusion: The work provides a rigorous framework connecting encoder rigidity, robustness, and fundamental noise limits in over-the-air computation, showing a trade-off between average error and uniform robustness.

title: Estimators From Convex Geometries Of The Simplex
authors: Paul Navas
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21551v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We unify several geometries of the probability simplex under one principle, their generation by a potential: convex potentials produce the Bregman divergences and dually flat structures of information geometry, and the exponentially concave potentials of Pal and Wong produce the logarithmic divergences and their projectively flat structures. Each structure carries a duality between maximum entropy and minimum divergence and, with it, a projection principle for estimation: the U-estimators of Eguchi, Komori and Ohara in the first case, the {\lambda}-deformed estimators of Wong and Zhang in the second, both governed by a Pythagorean relation and reducing to maximum likelihood in the undeformed limit. We complete the picture with estimators drawn from the third connection the divergence defines, the Levi-Civita one, by minimizing geodesic distance: existence, uniqueness and influence are then controlled by curvature and diameter rather than by flatness. Along the way the Aitchison geometry appears as the logarithmic-barrier instance of the construction at its critical weight, and the symmetrization of the Pal-Wong transport cost, a smoothing of the Hilbert projective metric, is shown to lose the dual pair and to support instead a Huber-type robust center with bounded influence in a geometry of infinite diameter.
tldr: The paper unifies geometries of the probability simplex via convex and exponentially concave potentials, yielding Bregman and logarithmic divergences and corresponding estimation principles.
motivation: To provide a unified framework for estimation on the probability simplex based on information geometry duality and projection principles.
method: Convex potentials generate Bregman divergences and dually flat structures, while exponentially concave potentials generate logarithmic divergences; estimators are derived by minimizing divergence under a Pythagorean relation, with a Levi-Civita geodesic-distance approach also analyzed.
result: U-estimators and lambda-deformed estimators reduce to maximum likelihood in the undeformed limit; Aitchison geometry emerges as the logarithmic-barrier case, and the symmetrized Pal-Wong transport cost supports a robust Huber-type center with bounded influence.
conclusion: The work generalizes estimation principles across simplex geometries, linking curvature, diameter, and robustness in a purely classical statistical framework.

title: Iterative Neural Variational Solver Of Committor Function In Under-damped Langevin Dynamics
authors: Tiejun Li, Zhaoqi Liu, Xiang Zhou
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20617v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The committor function describes the probability that a stochastic dynamical system, while transitioning between two metastable states, will first reach one state rather than the other. It is a central object in transition path theory, providing the accurate reaction rate and the characterization of the transition mechanism through reactive probability flux and the transition state ensemble. While the numerical methods for this function are well studied for over-damped Langevin dynamics where the friction damping coefficient goes to infinity, its computation in the general under-damped case remains an open challenge due to the lack of a variational structure in the underlying backward Kolmogorov equation. This restricts the quantitative investigation of the impact of the finite damping coefficient on rare transitions in real systems. In this work, by decomposing the infinitesimal generator of the underdamped Langevin dynamics into a self-adjoint and a skew-adjoint part, we develop an iterative scheme in which each subproblem has a variational form and can be solved efficiently using neural networks. Fundamentally, this approach can be viewed as a generalized Concus-Golub-Widlund (CGW) splitting method and each subproblem has a variational form, which can be solved efficiently. This iterative scheme also has the flexibility of introducing a preconditioning operator associated with a new overdamped Langevin dynamics, which naturally leads to the design of enhanced adaptive sampling for the subproblems. We validate the efficiency and accuracy of our method on benchmark systems including a one-dimensional double-well potential, the Muller-Brown potential, and alanine dipeptide. The proposed iterative variational framework provides a practical and extensible numerical tool for probing rare transition events in Langevin dynamics across varying damping coefficients.
tldr: The paper develops an iterative neural network solver for the committor function in underdamped Langevin dynamics by splitting the generator into self-adjoint and skew-adjoint parts.
motivation: Computing the committor function for underdamped Langevin dynamics is challenging because the backward Kolmogorov equation lacks a variational structure, unlike the overdamped case.
method: The authors decompose the infinitesimal generator into self-adjoint and skew-adjoint components, yielding an iterative scheme with variational subproblems solved by neural networks, optionally preconditioned by an overdamped Langevin dynamics for adaptive sampling.
result: The method is validated on a double-well potential, the Muller-Brown potential, and alanine dipeptide, demonstrating accuracy and efficiency across different damping coefficients.
conclusion: The iterative variational framework offers a practical numerical tool for studying rare transition events in underdamped Langevin dynamics.

title: Dynamical Phase Transition For A Logarithm Observable In Chaotic Systems
authors: Naftali R. Smith Lucianno Defaveri
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21288v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the full distribution [MATH] of the dynamical observable [MATH] where [MATH] is a sequence generated by a chaotic map [MATH] via [MATH]. We study the particular cases where [MATH] is the doubling, tent or logistic map, and focus on the limit [MATH]. Typical fluctuations of [MATH] are Gaussian with mean [MATH] and variance which are both of order [MATH]. We find that the left tail of the distribution ([MATH]) scales as [MATH], and calculate the rate function [MATH] which depends on the map [MATH]. Interestingly, we find that the right tail of the distribution ([MATH]) follows an anomalous scaling: [MATH]. The large-deviation function [MATH] has a universal form for the three maps, differing only in the scaling constants. At a critical value [MATH], it exhibits a corner singularity which has the character of a condensation transition. The transition separates between a subcritical phase [MATH] in which a small fraction of the [MATH]'s give a macroscopic contribution to the fluctuation. Despite this anomalous behavior of the right tail, we find that the cumulants of the distribution [MATH] grow linearly with [MATH] at large [MATH], and calculate the associated coefficients.
tldr: The paper studies large deviations and a dynamical phase transition in the distribution of a logarithmic observable generated by chaotic maps such as the doubling, tent, and logistic maps.
motivation: To understand the full distribution, beyond Gaussian typical fluctuations, of dynamical observables in chaotic systems and to uncover universal and anomalous large-deviation behaviors.
method: Large-deviation theory is applied to compute the left and right tails of the distribution and the rate function for three different chaotic maps in the limit of large sequence length.
result: The left tail scales exponentially with a map-dependent rate function, while the right tail exhibits anomalous scaling; the large-deviation function has a universal form with a corner singularity at a critical value, resembling a condensation transition.
conclusion: The work reveals a dynamical phase transition and anomalous scaling in chaotic maps, with cumulants growing linearly, but it is a classical chaos result not directly aligned with quantum information or thermodynamics interests.

title: A One-Sided McDiarmid-Type Inequality For Heavy Tails Via Reverse Kl Tensorization
authors: Hanuka Eshima, Amedeo Roberto Esposito, Andrea Paudice
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21103v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We revisit McDiarmid's inequality, a central tool in statistical learning theory and algorithm analysis. We show that large deviations above the mean are exponentially unlikely for functions of independent random variables that are almost surely bounded above and satisfy a conditional moment assumption of order [MATH]. When [MATH], the result applies even when the function has infinite variance. Our proof relies on a new tensorization inequality for the Kullback--Leibler divergence, termed reverse KL tensorization, which may be of independent interest. Applications include concentration of the sample mean and median-of-means estimator, and one-sided uniform risk bounds for unbounded losses.
tldr: The paper introduces a one-sided McDiarmid-type concentration inequality for heavy-tailed bounded-above random variables using a reverse KL tensorization technique.
motivation: McDiarmid's inequality requires bounded differences and finite variance; the authors aim to extend one-sided concentration to heavy-tailed settings with infinite variance.
method: They prove a new tensorization inequality for KL divergence, termed reverse KL tensorization, and use a conditional moment assumption of order p to derive exponential upper-tail bounds.
result: The inequality gives exponentially unlikely large deviations above the mean for functions of independent random variables, with applications to sample mean, median-of-means, and uniform risk bounds for unbounded losses.
conclusion: The reverse KL tensorization is of independent interest and extends concentration tools to heavy-tailed statistical learning problems.

title: Four-Level Quantized Soft Information Aided Hard-Decision Decoder For Product-like Codes
authors: Xiaowei Wu, Min Qiu, Yueying Zhan, Lei Yang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21187v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a novel low-complexity soft-aided hard-decision decoding scheme for product-like codes, termed iterative bounded-distance decoding (iBDD) with graded scaled reliability and bit-flipping (GSRF). This scheme operates on four-level quantized soft information. It incorporates a graded scaled reliability rule to assign decoding confidence to the bounded-distance decoding result, and employs a bit-flipping rule based on bit-level and component-code-level reliability. A selective re-decoding rule is designed to further facilitate the error performance while keeping the number of BDD attempts in reasonably low levels. The decoding parameter design of iBDD-GSRF is investigated for product codes and staircase codes, respectively. Simulation results on both codes verify that iBDD-GSRF achieves a gain of more than 0.4 dB over the conventional iBDD, comparable to several existing unquantized soft-aided decoders.
tldr: The paper proposes a four-level quantized soft-information-aided hard-decision decoder for product-like codes, improving error performance over conventional iterative bounded-distance decoding.
