motivation: Product-like codes such as product codes and staircase codes require efficient decoding, and soft-aided hard-decision decoding can trade complexity for performance. The work aims to design a low-complexity scheme that exploits quantized soft information without the cost of full soft decoding.
method: The authors introduce iterative bounded-distance decoding with graded scaled reliability and bit-flipping (iBDD-GSRF), using four-level quantized soft information, a graded scaled reliability rule to assign confidence to BDD results, a bit-flipping rule based on bit-level and component-code-level reliability, and a selective re-decoding rule to limit BDD attempts.
result: Simulations on product codes and staircase codes show that iBDD-GSRF achieves more than 0.4 dB gain over conventional iBDD, with performance comparable to several existing unquantized soft-aided decoders.
conclusion: The proposed iBDD-GSRF offers a favorable complexity-performance trade-off for decoding product-like codes, making it attractive for practical high-throughput communication systems.

title: The Sharp Scale Inequality For The Schatten Trace Class
authors: Yong Jiao, Sijie Luo, Lian Wu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21445v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we establish the metric cotype [MATH] inequality for the Schatten trace class [MATH] at the optimal order of the scaling parameter. More precisely, for every integer [MATH], every even integer [MATH], and every mapping [MATH], the following holds &\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n}_{x}\left\|f\left(x+{2}e_{j}\right)-f(x)\right\|_{1}^{2}\right)^{1/2}\\ \leq&\left(3\,m+6\right)\left(_{x,\varepsilon}\left\|f(x+\varepsilon)-f(x)\right\|_{1}^{2}\right)^{1/2}, where [MATH] and [MATH] are independently uniform on [MATH] and [MATH], respectively. The order [MATH] is necessary for any fixed metric cotype constant. This settles the optimal scaling problem for the Schatten trace class posed by Mendel and Naor \cite[Section 8]{MN} (see also \cite[Question 3]{GMN}).
tldr: The paper establishes the sharp metric cotype inequality for the Schatten trace class S_1 at the optimal scaling order, settling a problem of Mendel and Naor.
motivation: Metric cotype inequalities are central in the nonlinear geometry of Banach spaces, and the optimal scaling for the Schatten trace class was left open by Mendel and Naor and later highlighted by Giladi–Naor–Mendel.
method: The authors prove an explicit inequality bounding the L^2 norm of finite differences along e_j by a multiple of the average over ±1 steps, for maps into S_1, and show that the obtained scaling order is necessary for any fixed metric cotype constant.
result: For every n, even m, and map f, they obtain the inequality with constant 3m+6, and prove that the order m cannot be improved.
conclusion: This resolves the optimal scaling problem for the Schatten trace class and provides a sharp metric cotype inequality in the noncommutative setting.

title: Can Autonomous Vehicles Keep Their Cool? A Survey Of Thermal Side-Channel And Perception Attacks
authors: Ce Zhou Harsh Aaryan
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21034v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autonomous vehicles (AVs) couple safety-critical perception to thermally constrained compute. Interfaces built for night perception and package thermal reliability were never engineered as confidentiality boundaries, and closing one such path leaves the other intact. Physical adversaries can spoof thermal infrared (IR) sensors used for night driving, while unprivileged software co-tenants can fingerprint perception workloads from thermal, dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS), and thermal event interrupt (TEI) telemetry required for package safety. These paths differ in mechanism and privilege; both exploit interfaces that AV stacks cannot disable without compromising Safety of the Intended Functionality (SOTIF). Classical microarchitectural and cyber-physical systems (CPS) surveys address cache timing, adversarial machine learning, and camera or LiDAR spoofing; no prior survey jointly frames physical thermal IR attacks and unprivileged silicon thermal telemetry as one residual-risk class. This survey systematizes thirteen representative works into thermal perception integrity, telemetry leakage, and model-information extraction, comparing them by privilege, timescale, co-tenancy, deployability, and AV relevance. We distinguish attack family from adversary class and map defenses to residual risk while thermal management remains operational. A commodity proxy supports the software co-tenant branch only; physical IR evidence comes from cited literature. We identify open problems in on-target automotive evaluation, fusion trust under IR spoofing, chiplet thermal coupling, capability-based telemetry, and standards-ready threat analysis, aiming to motivate co-design across sensors, operating systems, silicon, and automotive standards.
tldr: This survey systematizes thermal side-channel and perception attacks on autonomous vehicles, jointly framing physical thermal infrared spoofing and unprivileged silicon thermal telemetry leakage as a residual-risk class.
motivation: Autonomous vehicles couple safety-critical perception with thermally constrained compute, and interfaces for night perception and package thermal reliability were not designed as confidentiality boundaries.
method: The authors review thirteen representative works, categorize them into thermal perception integrity, telemetry leakage, and model-information extraction, and compare privilege, timescale, co-tenancy, deployability, and AV relevance.
result: They distinguish attack families from adversary classes, map defenses to residual risk under operational thermal management, and note that software co-tenant evidence comes from a commodity proxy while physical IR evidence is drawn from cited literature.
conclusion: The survey identifies open problems in automotive evaluation, fusion trust under IR spoofing, chiplet thermal coupling, capability-based telemetry, and standards-ready threat analysis to motivate cross-layer co-design.

title: On The Complexity Of Symmetric Boolean Functions In Multiparty Private Simultaneous Messages
authors: Marshall Ball, Peter Crawford-Kahrl, Vladimir Podolskii, Morgan Prior
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21216v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multiparty Private Simultaneous Messages (PSM), also known as Decomposable Randomized Encoding (DRE) or information-theoretic garbling, is a model for non-interactive secure computation. Each party encodes its input using shared randomness and sends a message to an evaluator who does not know that randomness. The evaluator must recover the function output without learning anything else about the inputs. Perfect privacy requires identical transcript distributions on inputs with the same output. We also study the weaker notion of support privacy, which requires only that these distributions have the same support. We study the communication complexity of symmetric Boolean functions when each of the [MATH] parties holds one input bit. Lower bounds. We prove a superlinear lower bound for support-private PSM protocols computing [MATH]. Our technique gives [MATH] lower bounds for [MATH] and [MATH] (with even [MATH]), and an [MATH] lower bound for [MATH] when [MATH] for a fixed constant [MATH]. Upper bounds. We construct perfectly private PSM protocols of total communication [MATH] for every symmetric Boolean function, improving on the known quadratic bound. For [MATH], known branching-program constructions yield an upper bound of [MATH]. For [MATH] and [MATH] with prime [MATH], the lower bounds are tight up to constant factors in the stated regimes. Under support privacy, we obtain [MATH] communication for every symmetric Boolean function. Earlier lower-bound techniques of Ball et al. (ITCS 2020) yield only trivial linear bounds for symmetric Boolean functions. Concurrent and independent work by Holmgren and Wu proves a [MATH] lower bound for [MATH] using the same combinatorial core. Both works used AI assistance.
tldr: The paper studies communication complexity of symmetric Boolean functions in multiparty private simultaneous messages (information-theoretic garbling), deriving new lower and upper bounds.
motivation: PSM/DRE enables non-interactive secure computation with perfect or support privacy, and symmetric Boolean functions are a natural benchmark for communication complexity.
method: It uses combinatorial lower-bound techniques for support-private and perfectly private PSM protocols, together with explicit protocol constructions based on branching programs and related encodings.
result: The authors prove superlinear and quadratic lower bounds for several symmetric functions and construct perfectly private protocols with improved near-linear total communication, with tightness up to constants in some regimes.
conclusion: The work advances classical communication complexity for information-theoretic secure computation but has no direct connection to the user's quantum information, information thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems interests.

title: Reaction Attack On Ckks Deployments With Asymptotically Optimal Query Complexity
authors: Song Bian, Hyeongmin Choe, Jiseung Kim, Changmin Lee
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21127v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a protocol-level reaction leakage in CKKS deployments where public coefficient-to-slot (C2S) evaluation keys are combined with a client's 1-bit validity response. Under this deployment surface, a malicious evaluator can recover a ternary secret key using asymptotically optimal [MATH] reaction queries, where [MATH] is the entropy of the secret key. The attack does not break RLWE or CKKS IND-CPA security. Instead, it exploits the interaction between client-side validity reactions and public homomorphic linear transformations. A shift of a public encryption key yields a ciphertext whose plaintext is a function of the secret key; the public [MATH] layer then repacks this information to construct a ciphertext whose validity depends strictly on whether a targeted secret coefficient matches a guessed value. Furthermore, each submitted query is independently randomized with a fresh encryption of zero, so that each resulting malicious ciphertext appears entirely distinct, thereby allowing the attack to simply evade trivial detection mechanisms on the client side. We implemented the full end-to-end attack in Lattigo v6.2.0 and recovered the full secret key across four parameter sets drawn from standard CKKS presets. For uniform ternary secrets, the attack uses [MATH] queries and is within a factor [MATH] of the oracle-only entropy lower bound. For sparse ternary secrets, a tailored variant further reduces the number of queries in practice. Our results show that observable validity reactions form a practical key-recovery channel in CKKS deployments exposing this surface, even when the underlying cryptographic assumptions remain intact.
tldr: A protocol-level reaction attack recovers CKKS secret keys using validity responses and public coefficient-to-slot keys with asymptotically optimal query complexity.
motivation: CKKS deployments may expose public linear transformation keys and client validity reactions, creating a practical side-channel that does not break underlying cryptographic assumptions.
method: The attack shifts public encryption keys to construct ciphertexts whose validity depends on a targeted secret coefficient, randomizes each query with a fresh encryption of zero, and uses the public C2S layer to repack information.
result: Implemented in Lattigo v6.2.0, the attack recovered full secret keys across four standard CKKS parameter sets using O(H) queries for uniform ternary secrets and fewer in practice for sparse secrets.
conclusion: Observable validity reactions form a practical key-recovery channel in CKKS deployments that expose this surface, even when RLWE and IND-CPA security remain intact.

title: Thermochemically Constrained Multiscale Laplace Neural Operator To Learn Stiff Chemical Kinetics With Conditional Diffusion Model Sampling
authors: Dong Yang, Xiongbo Duan, Min Zhang, Yuqiang Li
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20643v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Stiff chemical kinetics is a major computational bottleneck in reacting-flow simulations, while data-driven solvers remain sensitive to training-state coverage and chemical dynamics. This work combines conditional diffusion sampling with a thermochemically constrained multiscale Laplace neural operator (TC-MLNO) for chemistry ODE integration. The diffusion model learns the equivalence-ratio-conditioned joint distribution of temperature and species from low-dimensional flame data, augmenting the state space without independent perturbations. TC-MLNO represents transient, non-periodic responses through pole-residue Laplace layers and assigns fast, medium, and slow species to separate branches. Thermochemical constraints are imposed through losses for mass and elemental conservation and heat release rate. The framework is evaluated in 1D premixed flames, a 2D developing jet, and a 3D turbulent burner flame. With equal-sized datasets, diffusion sampling reduces the 95th-percentile distance to the base flame manifold by up to 37.5% and the a posteriori full-species macro-average error by up to 92.7% versus random sampling, especially for minor species and radicals. TC-LNO yields smaller errors than the DeepONet baseline for 84.9% of retained modes and reduces the 95th-percentile error for the most attenuated modes from 0.372 to 0.081. In multidimensional flames, TC-MLNO better preserves reaction-zone locations, heat-release structures, and chemically sensitive species than DeepONet. Errors of representative radical and nitrogen-containing species in the 3D flame decrease by 88.0%-88.9%. Compared with direct CVODE integration, TC-MLNO reduces mean chemistry and total solution times by 90.1% and 62.6%, respectively. These results show that distribution-aware sampling and Laplace neural operator learning provide an accurate and efficient alternative for stiff chemical ODE integration.
tldr: A thermochemically constrained multiscale Laplace neural operator combined with conditional diffusion sampling accelerates stiff chemical kinetics integration in reacting-flow simulations.
motivation: Stiff chemical kinetics is a major bottleneck in reacting-flow simulations, and data-driven solvers are often limited by training-state coverage and sensitivity to chemical dynamics.
method: The authors combine a conditional diffusion model that learns the equivalence-ratio-conditioned joint distribution of temperature and species with a multiscale Laplace neural operator (TC-MLNO) that represents transient responses via pole-residue Laplace layers and enforces thermochemical constraints through conservation losses.
result: The framework reduces errors versus random sampling and DeepONet baselines, improves preservation of reaction zones and heat-release structures, and achieves 90.1% and 62.6% reductions in mean chemistry and total solution times compared to CVODE.
conclusion: Distribution-aware sampling and Laplace neural operator learning provide an accurate and efficient alternative for stiff chemical ODE integration in multidimensional flames.

title: An Implicit Multiscale Solver For Steady Kinetic Equations Based On Wave-particle Decomposition
authors: Kun Xu Chang Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20660v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Steady kinetic computations require accurate transport on meshes that do not resolve the mean free path and efficient removal of slowly decaying macroscopic errors. We develop a closed wave-particle decomposition (WPD) and a residual-based implicit solver for this problem. The wave accumulates only the Maxwellian along a local characteristic horizon and is determined by the conservative variables; the particle carries the kinetic complement and collision remainder. Under moment compatibility, the closed system is equivalent to the kinetic equation. For the Bhatnagar-Gross-Krook and Shakhov models, a hydrodynamic expansion gives the wave and particle contributions to the Euler and Navier-Stokes fluxes. The implicit iteration couples macroscopic prediction to microscopic correction through a discrete endpoint term and synchronizes the conservative moments after each accepted correction. Its stationary states satisfy the target discrete kinetic equation independently of the iteration controls. Formal analysis gives the smooth fixed-mesh fluid limit. Linear model analysis relates convergence to the horizon-to-relaxation ratio, incomplete macroscopic solves and explicit collision remainders. One- and two-dimensional computations of a normal shock, internal flows and hypersonic external flows test these properties across rarefied and continuum regimes. The results show kinetic fidelity and substantial reductions in iteration counts and wall time relative to the conventional iterative scheme near the continuum limit. Collision-model comparisons and parameter studies support the predicted convergence mechanisms.
tldr: The paper develops an implicit multiscale solver for steady kinetic equations using a wave-particle decomposition, targeting rarefied and continuum flow regimes.
motivation: Steady kinetic computations require accurate transport on meshes that do not resolve the mean free path and efficient removal of slowly decaying macroscopic errors.
method: It introduces a closed wave-particle decomposition and a residual-based implicit solver, where the wave part captures the Maxwellian along a local characteristic horizon and the particle part carries the kinetic complement, with coupling through a discrete endpoint term.
result: For BGK and Shakhov models, hydrodynamic expansion gives Euler and Navier-Stokes fluxes; numerical tests on shock and flow problems show kinetic fidelity and reduced iteration counts and wall time near the continuum limit.
conclusion: The proposed implicit solver provides a multiscale framework for steady kinetic equations with improved efficiency and convergence properties, supported by formal analysis and collision-model comparisons.

title: The Blume-Capel Model As A $\phi^6$ Field Theory: A Monte Carlo And Flow Model Study
authors: Ejaaz Merali, Ryan Larson, Ehsan Khatami, Richard T. Scalettar
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20982v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We report Monte Carlo simulations of a continuous spin variant of the Blume-Capel model. We compute the phase diagrams in the crystal-field-temperature plane, as a function of the softness of the spins. We show that normalizing flows, a class of generative models capable of direct sampling without autocorrelation, are effective samplers across the phase diagram, including in the first-order transition region and in the vicinity of the tricritical point. Finite-size scaling analyses of flow samples locate the first- and second-order transitions as well as the tricritical point with accuracy comparable to canonical and extended-ensemble Monte Carlo.
tldr: Monte Carlo and normalizing flow simulations map the phase diagram of a continuous-spin Blume-Capel model, including first-order transitions and the tricritical point.
motivation: The Blume-Capel model is a canonical system for studying phase transitions, and normalizing flows offer a promising autocorrelation-free sampling method for statistical physics.
method: The authors simulate a continuous-spin variant of the Blume-Capel model using canonical and extended-ensemble Monte Carlo as well as normalizing flows.
result: Normalizing flows effectively sample across the phase diagram, including the first-order transition region and near the tricritical point, and finite-size scaling of flow samples locates transitions with accuracy comparable to Monte Carlo.
conclusion: Normalizing flows are viable tools for studying phase diagrams and critical phenomena in classical spin models.

title: A Panoramic Network Overview Of Shortcut Impact On Power Grids
authors: Yunju Choi, Daekyung Lee, Heetae Kim
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21157v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Synchronization of coupled oscillators on complex networks underlies critical functions in natural and engineered systems, including power-grid operation. While synchronization stability on fixed network topologies has been studied extensively, less is known about how an added transmission link affects stability depending on where it is placed relative to generation and consumption. We address this question using simplified ring-network power-grid models in which producer and consumer nodes are spatially organized into clusters. Long-range transmission links, which we refer to as shortcuts, are added between non-adjacent nodes, and synchronization stability is quantified by basin stability in second-order coupled-oscillator dynamics. We compare shortcut placements across four scenarios varying network size, power allocation, power-injection heterogeneity, and producer--consumer arrangement. When producers and consumers form two spatially separated clusters, center-to-center shortcuts do not reduce the mean basin stability in the configurations examined and increase it by up to 75\% relative to the shortcut-less baseline. Peripheral shortcuts instead reduce mean basin stability by up to 28\% in some configurations despite the added connection, producing Braess-like degradation. In alternating multi-block networks, however, no single shortcut placement provides the same substantial enhancement, indicating that the center-to-center advantage does not directly generalize to more complex spatial arrangements. Representative time-domain simulations further show faster decay of frequency deviations for center-to-center than for peripheral shortcuts. These results demonstrate that the effect of added connectivity depends critically on where the new link is placed relative to the spatial organization of generation and consumption.
tldr: This paper studies how adding long-range transmission links (shortcuts) affects synchronization stability in simplified ring-network power-grid models, finding that center-to-center shortcuts can enhance basin stability while peripheral shortcuts can degrade it.
motivation: Synchronization of coupled oscillators is critical for power-grid operation, but how the placement of added transmission links affects stability relative to generation and consumption is not well understood.
method: The authors use second-order coupled-oscillator dynamics on ring-network power-grid models with producer and consumer nodes clustered spatially, adding shortcuts between non-adjacent nodes and quantifying synchronization stability via basin stability across four scenarios varying network size, power allocation, heterogeneity, and arrangement.
result: Center-to-center shortcuts increase mean basin stability by up to 75% relative to the shortcut-less baseline when producers and consumers form separated clusters, whereas peripheral shortcuts reduce it by up to 28% in some configurations, and the advantage does not generalize to alternating multi-block networks.
conclusion: The effect of added connectivity on power-grid synchronization depends critically on the spatial placement of the new link relative to generation and consumption, with center-to-center shortcuts generally beneficial in clustered configurations but not universally.

title: Poisson Statistics For One-dimensional Anderson--Bernoulli Schr\"odinger Operators
authors: Yi Han
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21268v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove Poisson local eigenvalue statistics for one-dimensional Schr\"odinger operators with nondegenerate Bernoulli potentials at any fixed nonzero coupling. After unfolding by the integrated density of states (IDS), the local eigenvalue process converges to a Poisson point process of unit intensity at every energy in the interior of the almost-sure spectrum. The theorem also holds for bounded nonconstant iid potentials, provided the IDS is continuous and strictly increasing near the reference energy. If the IDS also has a finite positive derivative at that energy, the usual linear normalization gives the same limit. The proof uses a phase coordinate with exact IDS drift to obtain a uniform exponential crossing law and joint Poisson counts in disjoint energy windows.
tldr: The paper proves Poisson local eigenvalue statistics for one-dimensional Anderson-Bernoulli Schrödinger operators at fixed nonzero coupling.
motivation: Understanding spectral statistics of random Schrödinger operators with Bernoulli potentials is a fundamental problem in mathematical physics and disordered systems.
method: The proof uses a phase coordinate with exact integrated density of states (IDS) drift to obtain a uniform exponential crossing law and joint Poisson counts in disjoint energy windows.
result: After unfolding by the IDS, the local eigenvalue process converges to a Poisson point process of unit intensity at every energy in the interior of the almost-sure spectrum, and the theorem extends to bounded nonconstant iid potentials under continuity and strict monotonicity conditions on the IDS.
conclusion: The work establishes Poisson local eigenvalue statistics for one-dimensional Anderson-Bernoulli models and certain iid potentials, contributing to the mathematical theory of random Schrödinger operators.

title: Factor-Assisted Density Estimation: When Ambient Dimension Enables Oracle Rates
authors: David Dunson Sunrit Chakraborty
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20944v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study density estimation in the high-dimensional factor model, whose fixed-dimensional latent factors have an unknown smooth density. We propose factor-assisted density estimation (FADE), a non-iterative procedure that applies kernel density estimation to spectral estimates of the latent scores. The score proxies are dependent and do not follow the latent density, so standard kernel-density arguments do not apply. A refined rowwise expansion separates error into a conditionally centered Gaussian perturbation and a uniformly controlled remainder. We show that FADE achieves the oracle rate in sufficiently high ambient dimension and prove a minimax lower bound separating ordinary nonparametric difficulty from a Gaussian deconvolution obstruction. Together, the upper and lower bounds establish rate optimality of FADE in specified high-dimensional regimes. We also derive [MATH] upper and lower bounds for the induced observation density, distinguishing latent-distribution uncertainty from the cost of estimating a growing number of parameters. These results formalize a blessing of ambient dimension: sufficiently many observed coordinates can make a simple spectral reduction statistically lossless even for the nonparametric task of recovering an unobserved low-dimensional density.
tldr: The paper proposes factor-assisted density estimation (FADE), a non-iterative spectral method for density estimation in high-dimensional factor models that achieves oracle rates when the ambient dimension is sufficiently large.
motivation: High-dimensional density estimation is statistically difficult, but factor models assume a low-dimensional latent structure with an unknown smooth density, motivating a method that can exploit many observed coordinates.
method: FADE applies kernel density estimation to spectral estimates of latent scores, with a refined rowwise expansion separating a conditionally centered Gaussian perturbation from a uniformly controlled remainder.
result: The authors show that FADE achieves the oracle rate in high ambient dimension and prove a minimax lower bound separating ordinary nonparametric difficulty from a Gaussian deconvolution obstruction.
conclusion: These results formalize a blessing of ambient dimension: sufficiently many observed coordinates can make a simple spectral reduction statistically lossless even for nonparametric recovery of an unobserved low-dimensional density.

title: Lwm-tf: A Wireless Foundation Model On 5g Nr Time-Frequency Resource Grids
authors: Namhyun Kim, Sadjad Alikhani, Ahmed Alkhateeb
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21013v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Received OFDM grids preserve both pilot and payload observations, yet wireless foundation models are rarely pre-trained on them. We introduce LWM-TF, a 9.58M-parameter factorized masked autoencoder pre-trained on complex 5G NR uplink grids taken after the FFT and before channel estimation. Each block attends first across OFDM symbols and then across resource blocks and receive antennas, and the mask follows the same two axes. Because the payload phase is unpredictable, the model reconstructs the normalized log-power of each masked token and predicts its scale separately; ablations show that the two terms are complementary and that this target outperforms complex-signal reconstruction. The encoder is pre-trained on 850,496 physical uplink shared channel (PUSCH) slots from a 10^6-slot dataset simulated with the NR transmit chain under various channel conditions. With the encoder frozen, linear probes classify modulation, predict CRC success, and detect UE mobility. On a separately generated test set, 16 labeled slots per class give 0.85 modulation accuracy, 0.82 CRC area under the ROC curve (AUROC), and 0.73 mobility AUROC, ahead of a supervised CNN on every paired draw. With 10,000 labels the probes reach 0.94, 0.96, and 0.92, well above engineered receiver statistics, and detect mobility where the CNN stays at chance. Without any impairment labels, distances in the frozen feature space flag unseen waveform impairments with 0.78 macro AUROC, against 0.68 for receiver statistics. A single pre-trained encoder thus provides receiver features that transfer across tasks, most strongly when labels are scarce.
tldr: LWM-TF is a 9.58M-parameter factorized masked autoencoder pre-trained on raw 5G NR uplink OFDM time-frequency grids to produce transferable receiver features for tasks like modulation classification, CRC prediction, and mobility detection.
motivation: Wireless foundation models are rarely pre-trained directly on received OFDM grids that retain both pilot and payload observations, despite the richness of these post-FFT pre-channel-estimation signals.
method: A factorized masked autoencoder attends first across OFDM symbols then across resource blocks and receive antennas, with masking along the same two axes, and reconstructs normalized log-power plus a separately predicted scale rather than the complex signal; the encoder is pre-trained on 850,496 PUSCH slots from a 10^6-slot simulated dataset.
result: Frozen-encoder linear probes achieve 0.85 modulation accuracy, 0.82 CRC AUROC, and 0.73 mobility AUROC with only 16 labels per class, rising to 0.94/0.96/0.92 with 10,000 labels and beating a supervised CNN and engineered receiver statistics; impairment detection reaches 0.78 macro AUROC without impairment labels.
conclusion: A single pre-trained masked-autoencoder encoder provides receiver features that transfer across tasks and are especially strong in low-label regimes, suggesting a path toward general-purpose wireless foundation models.

title: Measure Theory In Convergence Spaces Part Ii: Abstract Integration In Net Convergence Structures
authors: Alexandre Reggiolli Teixeira
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21014v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The construction of a coherent and general integration procedure is the central question of this second part of our study of measure theory in convergence spaces. We define, and establish convergence theorems for such process of integration, called the net Riemann integration, in convergence groups and commutative monoids, preserving the prescribed convergence throughout. The underlying interchange theorem admits noncommutative groups and requires right completeness only at the cardinality of the error family. Under intrinsic stability assumptions, countable error control therefore needs only sequential completeness, even for arbitrary integration nets, from which we also stablish a general version of Henstock's lemma. The resulting uniform theorems reaches incomplete ranges in which no complete subspace contains a tail of the approximating integrals. In the ordered locally solid convergence theory side, countability of the inner direction replaces countable accessibility of the approximants, and local existence arguments yield monotone and dominated convergence and, under additional controller assumptions, a further extension through increasing integrable barriers with pointwise coverage and uniformly vanishing excess primitives. This constructs the limiting integral without a common integrable envelope and gives uniform control of primitive variation. We finish with two appendices on new and general results of abstract metrization of net convergences and related topics.
tldr: The paper develops a general theory of net Riemann integration in convergence spaces, groups, and commutative monoids, proving abstract convergence theorems.
motivation: The central question is how to construct a coherent and general integration procedure within the framework of measure theory in convergence spaces.
method: It defines net Riemann integration preserving prescribed convergence, establishes interchange theorems requiring only right completeness at the error family cardinality, and uses ordered locally solid convergence theory with local existence arguments.
result: The work yields convergence theorems, a general Henstock's lemma, and monotone and dominated convergence results, including an extension through increasing integrable barriers and uniform control of primitive variation.
conclusion: It constructs limiting integrals without a common integrable envelope and provides uniform control of primitive variation, with appendices on abstract metrization of net convergences.

title: Adaptive Randomized Neural Networks For PDEs: Structure-Aware Feature Redistribution And Residual-Driven Block Enrichment
authors: Fei Wang You Yang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21077v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Randomized neural networks retain an output-linear least-squares solve, but globally sampled random features may fail to capture the spatial and scale structure of PDE solutions. We propose SFRBE--RaNN, a two-stage adaptive trial-space construction. SFR redistributes a fixed feature budget according to regional indicator masses and adapts regional weight scales through low-dimensional residual-based optimization. RBE constructs nonredundant enrichments by screening multiple activation families, removing represented response directions, and selecting the smallest admissible prefix. For solution-dependent operators, candidates are screened with a frozen operator and accepted only after nonlinear residual verification. For fixed linear problems, we establish an exact discrete residual-reduction identity and a conditional solution-error estimate. Building on this identity, we combine safeguarded SFR with RBE capture factors to derive a finite-horizon error bound involving baseline best approximation and empirical consistency, together with a conditional random-search success-probability bound. Numerical experiments on localized, multiscale, and nonlinear space--time problems demonstrate the method's effectiveness.
tldr: A two-stage adaptive randomized neural network method (SFRBE-RaNN) for solving PDEs that redistributes random features by regional indicator mass and enriches residual-driven basis directions.
motivation: Globally sampled random features in randomized neural networks often fail to capture the spatial and scale structure of PDE solutions, limiting accuracy on localized, multiscale, and nonlinear problems.
method: SFR redistributes a fixed feature budget using regional indicator masses and adapts regional weight scales via low-dimensional residual optimization, while RBE screens activation families, removes represented response directions, and selects the smallest admissible enrichment prefix.
result: For fixed linear problems an exact discrete residual-reduction identity and conditional solution-error estimate are derived, yielding a finite-horizon error bound and a random-search success-probability bound; numerical experiments confirm effectiveness on localized, multiscale, and nonlinear space-time problems.
conclusion: Structure-aware feature redistribution and residual-driven block enrichment improve randomized neural network solvers for PDEs, but the work lies in numerical analysis and scientific machine learning rather than quantum information science.

title: Quantum Color Newton Rings
authors: Honghuai Fang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21102v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study integral Newton rings attached to symmetric quantum colors. We show that their boundary values at a deleted node are exactly the elements of Habiro's cyclotomic completion, and we describe their quantum neighborhoods at [MATH] uniformly in the rank. The symmetric-color [MATH] invariants of a knot are the values of an element of such a ring. In its expansion at [MATH], the coefficient of [MATH] has denominator dividing the [MATH]th power of the Alexander polynomial, with integral numerator, and this exponent is sharp. For [MATH] and [MATH] at [MATH], the period matrices of the rank-two coefficient recurrences have spectral modules of exact order three in the Picard group of an affine elliptic curve.
tldr: The paper studies integral Newton rings associated with symmetric quantum colors and their connection to Habiro's cyclotomic completion and knot invariants.
motivation: The work aims to understand the arithmetic and structural properties of quantum color invariants and their generating rings, particularly through cyclotomic completions and recurrence relations.
method: The authors analyze boundary values at deleted nodes, describe quantum neighborhoods uniformly in rank, and examine expansion coefficients of symmetric-color knot invariants in terms of the Alexander polynomial.
result: They show that the denominator of a specific coefficient divides a power of the Alexander polynomial, establish sharpness of the exponent, and find spectral modules of exact order three in the Picard group of an affine elliptic curve for rank-two recurrences.
conclusion: The paper advances the mathematical theory of quantum knot invariants and their arithmetic properties, but it lies outside the physical and information-theoretic quantum research directions considered.

title: Persistence In Probability For Stochastic Delay Equations With Multiplicative Noise
authors: John Ioannis Stavroulakis Mark van Den Bosch
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21599v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the stochastic delay equation dX(t)=[-\gamma X(t)+r f(X(t-\tau))]\,dt+\sigma X(t)\,dW(t), where [MATH], [MATH], and with [MATH] either globally Lipschitz or globally bounded and locally Lipschitz, with [MATH] and [MATH] for all [MATH]. Under the condition r\liminf_{x\to 0^{+}}{x}>\gamma+{2}\sigma^2, independent of the time delay [MATH] we obtain that every solution [MATH] with nonnegative initial history and [MATH] is bounded away from zero in probability. This result then confirms a recent conjecture of van den Bosch, van Gaans, and Verduyn Lunel, and yields a non-trivial invariant measure for, e.g., the Mackey--Glass or Nicholson's blowflies equation with multiplicative noise. To get to this result, we apply a transformation to the solution process, essentially rewriting the equation using a stochastic integrating factor. A comparison with a linear equation gives contraction estimates for negative conditional moments and hence boundedness away from zero in probability. The same argument yields persistence whenever the linear comparison equation has a positive first Lyapunov exponent.
tldr: The paper proves persistence in probability for a class of stochastic delay differential equations with multiplicative noise, confirming a recent conjecture and yielding nontrivial invariant measures for examples like Mackey-Glass and Nicholson's blowflies equations.
motivation: The authors aim to establish boundedness away from zero in probability for stochastic delay equations with multiplicative noise, independent of the delay, thereby resolving a conjecture of van den Bosch, van Gaans, and Verduyn Lunel.
method: They transform the solution using a stochastic integrating factor, compare with a linear equation to derive contraction estimates for negative conditional moments, and use these to prove persistence when the linear comparison equation has a positive first Lyapunov exponent.
result: Under the condition r liminf_{x→0+} f(x)/x > γ + 2σ^2, every nonnegative solution is bounded away from zero in probability for all delays, which implies a nontrivial invariant measure for the Mackey-Glass and Nicholson's blowflies equations with multiplicative noise.
conclusion: The work provides a general persistence criterion for stochastic delay equations with multiplicative noise, with implications for population dynamics models and invariant measures.

title: Foundations Of Hardware-Software Leakage Contracts
authors: Jan Reineke
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20754v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Microarchitectural attacks such as Spectre and Meltdown undermine security by exploiting software-visible side effects of microarchitectural optimizations like caches and speculative execution. To use modern hardware securely, programmers must take into account the security implications of these optimizations. Yet instruction set architectures (ISAs)---the conventional abstraction layer between hardware and software---are ill-suited for secure programming: by design, they abstract from microarchitectural details and therefore fail to reflect their security consequences. A new security abstraction is emerging to fill this void: hardware-software leakage contracts. To support the principled development of secure software on modern hardware such contracts characterize side-channel leakage at the ISA level. Thereby they enable programmers and compilers to generate code that is provably resistant to side-channel attacks---without having to explicitly reason about the microarchitecture. On the other hand, they provide a specification for hardware designers to ensure that microarchitectures do not introduce unintended and undocumented side channels. This paper introduces the foundations of this emerging topic, discussing recent contributions and unresolved challenges along the way.
tldr: This paper introduces foundations for hardware-software leakage contracts, a security abstraction for specifying microarchitectural side-channel leakage at the ISA level.
motivation: Microarchitectural attacks like Spectre and Meltdown exploit software-visible side effects of caches and speculative execution, which conventional ISAs are ill-suited to address because they abstract away microarchitectural details.
method: The paper surveys and discusses recent contributions toward hardware-software leakage contracts, which characterize side-channel leakage at the ISA level and can serve as specifications for both secure programming and hardware design.
result: It outlines the emerging topic's foundations, highlights unresolved challenges, and explains how such contracts could enable provably side-channel-resistant code without explicit microarchitectural reasoning.
conclusion: Hardware-software leakage contracts offer a promising abstraction for secure programming and hardware design, but fundamental open problems remain.

title: Reconstruction Of Continuous Archimedean T-norms From Their Section Along An Increasing Curve
authors: Gabriel Bauza-Llompart, Raquel Fernandez-Peralta, Marc Munar
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20874v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The completion problem for continuous and Archimedean triangular norms (t-norms for short) consists in describing all the operators that take predefined values on a given subset of the unit square, and it reveals how much of a t-norm is determined by partial information. In this paper, we focus on the case where this subset is a parametric curve. We first formulate the problem in terms of the functional equation satisfied by an additive generator, and we then restrict our attention to curves of the form [MATH] with [MATH] continuous and increasing, which include the classical diagonal and horizontal section cases. We determine when the known values are compatible with a continuous and Archimedean t-norm, and we show that every completion is obtained by choosing the additive generator on a subinterval and reconstructing it elsewhere from the values on the curve. This description is recursive in general and becomes a closed formula under additional conditions, recovering the two classical results as particular cases. The completions are not unique, and we give examples with infinitely many t-norms sharing the same section along a curve. Finally, we combine our results with the reconstruction of a t-norm from its values above a level curve, which determines exactly the additive generator on that subinterval, so that the two pieces of information are complementary and together determine a unique completion.
tldr: The paper solves the completion problem for continuous Archimedean t-norms when the prescribed values lie on an increasing parametric curve.
motivation: The completion problem reveals how much of a triangular norm is determined by partial information, and extending it from classical diagonal and horizontal sections to general increasing curves provides a broader theoretical understanding.
method: The problem is formulated as a functional equation for the additive generator of a continuous Archimedean t-norm, and the generator is reconstructed recursively or via a closed formula from values on the curve.
result: The authors characterize compatibility of curve data with a continuous Archimedean t-norm, show completions are generally non-unique with examples of infinitely many t-norms sharing the same section, and recover the classical diagonal and horizontal section results as special cases.
conclusion: Combining section data with reconstruction from values above a level curve determines the additive generator on complementary subintervals, yielding a unique completion and clarifying the information content of such partial specifications.

title: From One Query To Many: A Critical Survey Of Privacy Accounting In Rag
authors: Zhiyuan Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21245v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) enables large language models to leverage external knowledge but introduces privacy risks when the retrieved corpus contains sensitive information. Differential privacy (DP) offers formal protection, yet interpreting and comparing privacy guarantees across existing DP-RAG methods remains challenging. In particular, a privacy budget reported for a single response does not directly characterize privacy loss over repeated queries, and even identical values of [MATH] may represent different guarantees depending on the protected data unit, accounting horizon, and observable outputs. This survey critically examines how privacy accounting evolves from single-query generation to multi-query RAG systems. We categorize existing approaches into query-time privatization, multi-query accounting, and one-time corpus privatization. We analyze their underlying assumptions and privacy--utility trade-offs. Rather than ranking methods by [MATH] alone, we propose a framework that interprets a DP-RAG guarantee along three dimensions: privacy granularity, accounting scope, and release boundaries. We conclude that an [MATH] is a claim only together with the three slots: the protected unit, the accounting scope, and the release boundary.
tldr: This survey analyzes privacy accounting for differential privacy in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), focusing on how guarantees change from single-query to multi-query settings.
motivation: RAG systems expose sensitive retrieved data and existing differential privacy guarantees are difficult to compare because reported privacy budgets depend on protected units, accounting scope, and release boundaries.
method: The paper categorizes DP-RAG approaches into query-time privatization, multi-query accounting, and one-time corpus privatization, then proposes a three-dimensional interpretation framework for privacy guarantees.
result: It shows that a single epsilon value is insufficient to characterize privacy loss across repeated queries and that comparing methods requires specifying privacy granularity, accounting scope, and release boundaries.
conclusion: The survey argues that DP-RAG guarantees should be interpreted as claims tied to the protected data unit, accounting horizon, and release boundary, rather than by epsilon alone.

title: Localized high-Q Resonances Enable Electrically Defined Beam Steering In Lithium Niobate Metasurfaces
authors: Jiyong Shim, Sahil Dagli, Hamish Carr Delgado, Remi Dado, Chih-Yi Chen, Feng Pan, Isabella He, Sajjad Abdollahramezani, Mark L. Brongersma, Jennifer A. Dionne
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21027v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: High-speed beam steering for LiDAR and optical communication requires independent, reconfigurable control of optical phase. We demonstrate a metasurface combining lithium niobate's Pockels effect with high-Q (Q > 1700) silicon guided-mode resonance nanoantennas whose localized resonances allow individual electro-optic control at a 1 [MATH]m pitch. Identical arrays steer light to 53.5[MATH] or 32.4[MATH], with the angle set by the bias pattern rather than antenna geometry. We measure 18.0% 0th-order modulation depth, 0.09% of incident power in the steered order, and a 940 MHz detected modulation bandwidth. Mode-overlap analysis shows how inter-element coupling limits usable Q, providing design rules for compact, high-speed beam steering.
tldr: The paper demonstrates an electrically reconfigurable lithium niobate metasurface that uses high-Q guided-mode resonances to steer light at a 1 μm pitch without changing antenna geometry.
motivation: High-speed beam steering for LiDAR and optical communication requires independent and reconfigurable control of optical phase, which is difficult to achieve with compact integrated devices.
method: The authors combine lithium niobate's Pockels effect with high-Q silicon guided-mode resonance nanoantennas and use mode-overlap analysis to evaluate inter-element coupling limits on usable Q.
result: Arrays with identical geometry steer light to 53.5° or 32.4° depending on bias pattern, achieving 18.0% 0th-order modulation depth, 0.09% of incident power in the steered order, and a 940 MHz modulation bandwidth.
conclusion: Localized high-Q resonances enable compact, electrically defined beam steering and provide design rules for high-speed metasurface devices, though the work is classical photonics and not directly connected to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Energy-Stable Parametric Operator Inference Across Regime Transitions: Application To Unconfined Buoyant Plumes In Stratified Ambients
authors: Abdollah Shafieezadeh Youngjun Kwon
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20626v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Buoyant plumes in stratified ambients arise in wildfire smoke transport, ventilation, and pollutant dispersion, where many-query prediction requires models that stay accurate and stable as the dynamics transition from free rise to internal-wave trapping. Operator Inference (OpInf) learns polynomial reduced models from snapshots, and the Boussinesq plume depends affinely on the squared buoyancy frequency [MATH]. However, this compatibility masks two stability gaps: a single affine operator family can distort the per-parameter dynamics into unstable spectra, and for quadratic OpInf models, finite-time blowup is governed by a cubic energy injection channel from the inferred quadratic operator. To address these gaps, we develop cyclic-skew regime-bridged OpInf (CR-OpInf). We derive an affine-inadequacy diagnostic that links the departure from a shared affine family to destabilizing spectral drift before integration. In place of the shared affine fit, we interpolate per-parameter operators with a Gaussian kernel. We also extend the cyclic-skew quadratic constraint to the buoyancy-source-forced parametric setting, closing the cubic energy channel and isolating this closure as the boundedness mechanism. We further introduce a regime-bridging basis split that resolves free rise and trapped intrusion structures while preserving the cyclic-skew structure under convex interpolation. Applied to an unconfined Boussinesq plume and a viscous Burgers problem spanning a smooth-to-shock transition, CR-OpInf remains bounded for five training horizons, avoids the divergence of affine and unconstrained variants, tracks the plume rise, and recovers stratification-dependent rise scaling at moderate horizons. To our knowledge, this is the first parametric OpInf study of an unconfined stratified plume.
tldr: The paper develops a parametric operator inference method (CR-OpInf) for stable reduced-order modeling of buoyant plumes across regime transitions.
motivation: Buoyant plumes in stratified ambients require accurate and stable reduced models for many-query prediction, but standard operator inference can produce unstable spectra and finite-time blowup.
method: CR-OpInf introduces an affine-inadequacy diagnostic, Gaussian kernel interpolation of per-parameter operators, a cyclic-skew quadratic constraint for buoyancy-source-forced systems, and a regime-bridging basis split.
result: Applied to an unconfined Boussinesq plume and a viscous Burgers problem, CR-OpInf remains bounded for five training horizons, avoids divergence of affine and unconstrained variants, and recovers stratification-dependent rise scaling.
conclusion: The work presents the first parametric operator inference study of an unconfined stratified plume, offering a stable reduced modeling framework for regime-transition dynamics.

title: Global-in-time Spectral Duhamel-Picard Method For Post-Exposure Bake Simulation And Physics-Informed Neural Operators For Euv Lithography
authors: Doyun Kim, Mircea Dusa, Werner Gilijns, Philippe Leray
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20655v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a global-in-time spectral Duhamel-Picard method with polynomial expansions for post-exposure bake (PEB) simulation. The coupled acid-quencher reaction-diffusion equations are reformulated as nonlinear Volterra integral equations using the Duhamel principle. Full trajectories are represented by finite polynomial expansions, with temporal coefficient fields determined over the bake interval by Anderson-accelerated Picard iteration, thereby avoiding sequential time marching. In 3-D PEB simulations, we employ Chebyshev and Legendre temporal bases while evaluating the Duhamel integrals using the corresponding Gaussian quadrature rules. We demonstrate that the proposed method simulates a large domain of [MATH] voxels on the order of one minute. The representation is further incorporated into a physics-informed neural operator (PINO) with a mixed-transform variant of a factorized Fourier neural operator, which is trained without precomputed solution trajectories. Together, the integral formulation and its PINO extension enable accelerated, time-marching-free prediction of concentration fields at arbitrary times within the bake interval.
tldr: The paper develops a global-in-time spectral Duhamel-Picard method and a physics-informed neural operator for fast, time-marching-free simulation of post-exposure bake reaction-diffusion equations in EUV lithography.
motivation: Post-exposure bake simulation of coupled acid-quencher reaction-diffusion equations is computationally expensive due to sequential time marching, motivating faster solvers and surrogate models for EUV lithography process modeling.
method: The coupled nonlinear reaction-diffusion PDEs are recast as Volterra integral equations via the Duhamel principle, with full trajectories expanded in Chebyshev/Legendre temporal polynomial bases and coefficients solved by Anderson-accelerated Picard iteration; the formulation is embedded in a physics-informed neural operator using a mixed-transform factorized Fourier neural operator.
result: The method simulates large 3-D PEB domains of ~10^9 voxels in about one minute, and the PINO extension predicts concentration fields at arbitrary bake times without requiring precomputed solution trajectories.
conclusion: The integral formulation and its neural-operator extension provide accelerated, time-marching-free prediction for lithography process simulation, though the work lies outside quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, and hybrid quantum systems.

title: Megabar Shocks On A Benchtop
authors: Yun Kai, Min Kim, Senpeng Lin, Zhen Sang, Jacob Gordon, Steven E. Kooi, Alexei Maznev, Thomas Pezeril, Cyril Williams, Tom Lockard, Damian Swift, Keith A. Nelson
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20749v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Techniques to generate megabar (100 GPa) pressure are critical for the study of materials under extreme conditions. However, kJ-class lasers are typically needed to generate such extreme pressures. Here, we present a method to reach megabar pressure on a benchtop using only tens of mJ a few millijoules of laser pulse energy. The core of our method is the utilization of multiple laser rings of different diameters and time delays to additively excite a focusing shock wave. Using high-speed imaging and a streak camera, we measured the shock trajectory and inferred pressure, temperature and density using hydrocode simulation. Our shock compression efficiency, informed by hydrocode, has achieved 23 GPa/mJ. If scaled up, our method may enable high-energy-density experiments on a benchtop.
tldr: A benchtop laser method generates megabar pressures by additively exciting a focusing shock wave with multiple delayed laser rings.
motivation: Generating megabar pressures normally requires kJ-class lasers, limiting access to high-energy-density experiments; this work aims to achieve such pressures on a benchtop.
method: Multiple laser rings of different diameters and time delays are used to additively drive a focusing shock wave, with shock trajectory measured by high-speed imaging and a streak camera and pressure/temperature/density inferred via hydrocode simulation.
result: The method reaches megabar pressure using only tens of millijoules of laser energy, achieving a shock compression efficiency of 23 GPa/mJ.
conclusion: Scaled up, this benchtop approach may enable broader high-energy-density experiments without large kJ-class laser facilities.

title: A Differentiable Pca-gpr Surrogate Framework For Full-transient Bayesian Inverse Uncertainty Quantification Of Black-box Nuclear Thermal-hydraulic Systems
authors: Zikang Yaoa, Eugene Yeea, Fue-Sang Lien
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20978v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Complex transient energy systems require uncertainty-quantified predictions, but Bayesian inverse uncertainty quantification (IUQ) is often impractical because posterior sampling with high-fidelity system codes requires many expensive full-transient simulations. This study develops a surrogate-assisted Bayesian IUQ framework that makes full-time-series calibration practical for the NACIE heavy-liquid-metal natural-circulation loop. The key innovation is to transform a black-box transient simulator into a differentiable probabilistic emulator by combining principal component analysis with Gaussian process regression (PCA--GPR). The surrogate reconstructs complete multichannel temperature and mass-flow histories from a compact latent representation, preserving dominant temporal and cross-channel correlations while enabling automatic differentiation of the log posterior. This allows both gradient-free ensemble slice sampling and gradient-informed sampling with the No-U-Turn Sampler and Microcanonical Langevin Monte Carlo. Five principal components capture more than 99\% of the output variance, and the surrogate achieves normalized root-mean-square errors below 2\%. Compared with direct Flownex SE evaluations, the surrogate reduces likelihood-evaluation cost by approximately 3000-fold while preserving posterior statistics and correlations. Posterior predictive analyses show reduced bias, narrower intervals, and improved agreement with measurements and independent validation.
tldr: The paper develops a differentiable PCA-GPR surrogate framework that makes full-transient Bayesian inverse uncertainty quantification tractable for black-box nuclear thermal-hydraulic system codes.
motivation: Bayesian inverse UQ for complex transient energy systems is impractical because posterior sampling requires thousands of expensive full-transient high-fidelity simulations.
method: The authors combine principal component analysis with Gaussian process regression to build a differentiable probabilistic emulator of a black-box simulator, then perform gradient-free ensemble slice sampling and gradient-informed NUTS and Microcanonical Langevin Monte Carlo sampling.
result: Five principal components capture over 99% of output variance, surrogate errors stay below 2% NRMSE, and likelihood evaluation cost drops roughly 3000-fold while preserving posterior statistics and correlations.
conclusion: The surrogate-assisted framework enables practical full-time-series calibration with reduced bias, narrower posterior intervals, and improved agreement with measurements and independent validation for the NACIE natural-circulation loop.

title: Co-designing A Layered Control Architecture
authors: Chris Verhoek, Charis Stamouli, George J. Pappas, Nikolai Matni
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20900v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Layered control architectures (LCAs) are ubiquitous in complex engineering systems. However, in practice they are largely designed ad hoc and mostly dictated by the experience of the designer. This is because there is currently no systematic and practically applicable theory available to holistically design LCAs. Hence, systematically reasoning about the optimality, stability, and feasibility of the LCA design is not possible. We set a first step toward such a theory by presenting a framework for co-designing a two-layer LCA for a linear time-invariant plant. The resulting co-design problem optimizes over architectural design variables (e.g., reduced order model dimension and sampling ratio between the layers) and tuning-based design variables (e.g., the numerical values of the feedback gain or the matrices of the reduced order model), all subject to constraints that ensure stability, feasibility, and compute properties of the closed-loop LCA. The proposed formulation allows to make informed tradeoffs along the Pareto front traced over different axes of optimality, e.g., speed, accuracy or computational effort. We demonstrate the effect of making various tradeoffs in a simple numerical example.
tldr: The paper proposes a framework for co-designing two-layer layered control architectures for linear time-invariant plants, jointly optimizing architectural and tuning variables subject to stability, feasibility, and compute constraints.
motivation: Layered control architectures are ubiquitous in complex engineering systems but are designed ad hoc based on designer experience, since no systematic theory exists for reasoning about their optimality, stability, and feasibility.
method: The authors formulate a co-design optimization problem over architectural variables (reduced-order model dimension, sampling ratio between layers) and tuning variables (feedback gains, reduced model matrices), constrained to guarantee closed-loop stability, feasibility, and computational properties.
result: The formulation enables informed tradeoffs along a Pareto front over axes such as speed, accuracy, and computational effort, illustrated with a simple numerical example.
conclusion: This constitutes a first step toward a systematic theory for holistic layered control architecture design, though it is limited to linear time-invariant plants and two-layer architectures.

title: $\lambda$-geodesic Convexity Of The Squared sliced-Wasserstein Distance
authors: Filippo Santambrogio Giacomo Cozzi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20972v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The squared Wasserstein distance with respect to a fixed target measure is not a convex function along Wasserstein geodesics over [MATH] when [MATH]. Still, in dimension [MATH], this function is [MATH]-geodesically convex. We prove that the square of the sliced-Wasserstein distance (which is a distance constructed averaging one-dimensional Wasserstein distances) is [MATH]-geodesically convex (possibly with [MATH]) on sets of measures satisfying upper bounds on their density, when the target measure satisfies some given geometric conditions. We also present some consequences of this result in the study of the sliced-Wasserstein flow.
tldr: The paper proves λ-geodesic convexity of the squared sliced-Wasserstein distance under density upper bounds and geometric conditions on the target measure, and applies this to the sliced-Wasserstein flow.
motivation: The squared Wasserstein distance is not convex along Wasserstein geodesics in general, but becomes λ-geodesically convex in one dimension. The authors seek an analogous convexity property for the sliced-Wasserstein distance.
method: They analyze the squared sliced-Wasserstein distance, which averages one-dimensional Wasserstein distances, and prove λ-geodesic convexity on sets of measures with upper-bounded densities when the target measure satisfies certain geometric conditions.
result: The main result establishes λ-geodesic convexity (possibly with λ=0) for the squared sliced-Wasserstein distance, and consequences for the sliced-Wasserstein flow are presented.
conclusion: The convexity result provides a foundation for studying optimization and flow problems involving the sliced-Wasserstein distance under density constraints.

title: Semisimplicity And Rigidity Of The Kontsevich--Zorich Cocycle For Products Of Strata
authors: Polina Baron
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21247v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the Kontsevich--Zorich cocycle, its fixed tensor constructions, and their finite direct sums over products of strata of Abelian differentials. The acting groups are closed subgroups [MATH] that, up to factor permutations and coordinatewise conjugation by rotations, are products of diagonal [MATH] blocks and a finite central group. For ergodic invariant probability measures, we prove Deligne-type semisimplicity: the bundles admit Hodge-compatible decompositions into [MATH]-invariant pieces [MATH], where [MATH] are division algebras, [MATH] carry pure variations of Hodge structure, and the multiplicity spaces [MATH] carry finite direct sums of pure Hodge structures. Every invariant subbundle arises from [MATH]-submodules of the [MATH]. If block marginal measures have smooth local supports and are locally equivalent to smooth volume, Hodge-orthogonal projections onto invariant subbundles are locally polynomial in period coordinates on the normalized support. The proof obtains a local product-of-quadrics model and joint polynomiality from polynomiality along stable and unstable leaves. On the cone obtained by scaling each diagonal block together, projection coefficients admit homogeneous degree-zero expressions with integral powers of reciprocal block areas. For the full product group [MATH], single-stratum measure classification supplies the support hypothesis, yielding rigidity for every ergodic invariant probability measure. Under the transported support hypothesis, arbitrary coordinatewise [MATH]-conjugates also admit polynomial equivariant projectors, though not necessarily Hodge-orthogonal. Genus-two examples show that nonrotational conjugation can destroy Deligne-torus invariance, and independent factor scalings can require square roots of area functions.
tldr: The paper proves Deligne-type semisimplicity and rigidity results for the Kontsevich–Zorich cocycle over products of strata of Abelian differentials.
motivation: The Kontsevich–Zorich cocycle is central to the dynamics of translation surfaces, and understanding its algebraic properties such as semisimplicity and rigidity is fundamental in Teichmüller dynamics.
method: The author studies fixed tensor constructions and finite direct sums of the cocycle, obtains a local product-of-quadrics model, and uses polynomiality along stable and unstable leaves to derive Hodge-compatible decompositions and polynomial equivariant projectors.
result: For ergodic invariant probability measures, the bundles admit Hodge-compatible decompositions into invariant pieces with pure variations of Hodge structure, and under smoothness and local equivalence hypotheses, projections onto invariant subbundles are locally polynomial in period coordinates.
conclusion: This work establishes rigidity and semisimplicity for the Kontsevich–Zorich cocycle in product settings, with genus-two examples showing limitations of the results under nonrotational conjugation.

title: Optimization Of A Perturbed Implicit Sweeping Process By Constrained Discontinuous Controls
authors: Yen Dang, Boris S. Mordukhovich, Dao Nguyen
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21384v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper studies optimal control problems governed by an implicit sweeping process with velocity-dependent constraint geometry, where the dynamics are described by a differential inclusion involving the normal cone to a moving convex polyhedral set. Such systems form a challenging class of nonsmooth differential inclusions due to the implicit coupling between the state, velocity, and constraint reaction. To address these difficulties, we use a method of discrete approximations together with tools of variational analysis and generalized differentiation. This approach allows us to derive necessary optimality conditions for local minimizer in discrete-time problems and subsequently pass to the limit to obtain optimality conditions for the original continuous-time system. The obtained results extend existing optimal control theory for sweeping processes to a class of implicit dynamical systems with state-and velocity-dependent constraints.
tldr: The paper derives necessary optimality conditions for optimal control problems governed by an implicit sweeping process with velocity-dependent polyhedral constraints.
motivation: Sweeping processes with implicit dynamics and state- and velocity-dependent constraints are challenging nonsmooth systems that extend beyond existing optimal control theory.
method: The authors use discrete approximations combined with variational analysis and generalized differentiation to treat the differential inclusion involving a normal cone to a moving convex polyhedral set.
result: They obtain necessary optimality conditions for local minimizers of discrete-time problems and then pass to the limit to establish optimality conditions for the original continuous-time system.
conclusion: The work extends optimal control theory for sweeping processes to a class of implicit dynamical systems with state- and velocity-dependent constraints.

title: Greedy Multiscale Kernel Algorithms
authors: Sara Avesani, Armin Iske, Michael Multerer, Tizian Wenzel
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21615v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multiscale kernel approximation and greedy kernel algorithms are two established tools for scattered data approximation. We combine them into greedy multiscale kernel algorithms, in which every level of a multiscale residual correction is constructed by a greedy kernel algorithm. For the multiscale [MATH]-greedy algorithm we prove convergence rates in the number of selected centres which coincide (up to an arbitrarily small loss in the exponent) with the rates of the single-scale [MATH]-greedy algorithm. The gain of the multiscale construction is in the stability, and we make this precise by a two-sided estimate for the condition number of kernel matrices with rescaled kernels. The lower bound shows that any single-scale method, and in particular the [MATH]-greedy algorithm, pays for its convergence rate with condition numbers growing at least like a power of the number of centres. In contrast, the multiscale scaling of the kernel keeps this lower bound fixed on every level without changing the rate. The upper bound identifies the separation of the centres at the scale of the kernel as the quantity to control. We give the operation counts of all the methods considered and compare the greedy multiscale algorithms numerically with single-scale greedy and classical multiscale methods, in terms of error, time and conditioning.
tldr: The paper introduces greedy multiscale kernel algorithms for scattered data approximation, proving convergence rates and improved stability compared to single-scale greedy methods.
motivation: Multiscale kernel approximation and greedy kernel algorithms are established but separate tools; combining them may yield better stability without sacrificing convergence rates.
method: The authors construct each level of a multiscale residual correction via a greedy kernel algorithm, specifically the multiscale P-greedy algorithm, and analyze convergence rates and condition numbers with rescaled kernels.
result: The multiscale P-greedy algorithm achieves convergence rates matching single-scale P-greedy up to an arbitrarily small loss in the exponent, while keeping condition numbers bounded across levels; a two-sided estimate for kernel matrix condition numbers is proved.
conclusion: Greedy multiscale kernel algorithms provide a stability advantage over single-scale methods without compromising convergence rates, as supported by operation counts and numerical comparisons.

title: Pantograph Difference Equations: Stability, Multistability, And Chaos
authors: Sachin Bhalekar Prashant M. Gade
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21635v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pantograph equations are functional differential equations with proportional delay, typically involving terms of the form [MATH], where [MATH]. These equations have been studied for several decades and have applications in areas ranging from number theory to electrodynamics. In this work, we investigate pantograph difference equations as discrete dynamical maps of the form \[ x_{i+1}=F(x_{i})+G(x_{h(i)}), \qquad i\geq 0, \] where [MATH]. In particular, we consider [MATH] and [MATH], with [MATH] and [MATH]. We distinguish between homogeneous pantograph difference equations, for which [MATH], and inhomogeneous pantograph difference equations, for which [MATH]. We first analyze linear pantograph difference equations and establish sufficient conditions for asymptotic stability and for nonconvergence to zero. For proportional delays, analytical stability and instability regions are combined with multi-horizon parameter scans to construct regime diagrams in the [MATH]-plane. We then investigate pantograph versions of the logistic and tent maps. In the homogeneous case, the dynamics evolves through step-like plateaus whose lengths increase at least exponentially, leading to slow convergence and finite-time multistability within computationally accessible time scales. In the inhomogeneous case, numerical experiments show finite-time exponential separation of nearby trajectories, consistent with chaotic dynamics.
tldr: This paper studies stability, multistability, and chaos in discrete pantograph difference equations with proportional delay.
motivation: Pantograph equations are functional differential equations with applications in number theory and electrodynamics, and the authors aim to extend their analysis to discrete dynamical maps.
method: They analyze linear pantograph difference equations for asymptotic stability and nonconvergence, construct regime diagrams via multi-horizon parameter scans, and numerically investigate pantograph versions of the logistic and tent maps.
result: They find sufficient conditions for stability and instability, exponentially increasing plateau lengths leading to slow convergence and finite-time multistability in the homogeneous case, and finite-time exponential separation of nearby trajectories consistent with chaos in the inhomogeneous case.
conclusion: The work characterizes rich dynamics in pantograph difference equations, but it is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Unmasking The Secret Code: Using Canaries To Show How Masked Context Controls Memorization In Sft
authors: Avi Schwarzschild, Om Thakkar, Sahra Ghalebikesabi, Congzheng Song, Vinnie Monaco
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20656v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Canaries, or synthetic training records containing known secrets, are widely used to assess whether language models reveal information from their training data. But how much do these measurements depend on the canaries themselves? We study this question through controlled fine-tuning experiments with language and vision-language models, spanning synthetic tasks and tasks where training improves useful performance. Whether a secret is provided in the training input strongly changes what the model learns; for example, models can reproduce a secret in the input yet fail to recall it when it is removed, even after extensive repetition during training. When training instead requires predicting the secret from the surrounding context, later recall can become reliable. Repetition alone is therefore insufficient to characterize memorization. We also find that changing when a canary appears, or which other canaries accompany it, can substantially change measured memorization without increasing that canary's repetition count. These results show that canary measurements depend on how secrets are presented during training and tested afterward. Audits should test whether their conclusions hold across these choices before extending them to other training records.
tldr: Controlled fine-tuning experiments show that whether a canary secret appears in the training input strongly determines whether language models memorize and later recall it, meaning canary-based memorization audits are highly sensitive to experimental design choices.
motivation: Canaries (synthetic records with known secrets) are widely used to probe whether language models leak training data, but it is unclear how much measured memorization depends on properties of the canaries themselves rather than the training procedure.
method: The authors run controlled fine-tuning experiments on language and vision-language models across synthetic and useful tasks, systematically varying whether secrets are given in the input, when canaries appear, which other canaries accompany them, and how repetition is counted.
result: Models can reproduce a secret present in the input yet fail to recall it once removed, even with heavy repetition; recall becomes reliable only when training requires predicting the secret from context, and changing canary timing or companions substantially alters measured memorization without changing repetition counts.
conclusion: Repetition alone is insufficient to characterize memorization, so audits should verify that conclusions are robust across choices of how secrets are presented during training and tested afterward before generalizing to other training records.

title: CascadeLedger: Counterfactual Auditing Of Information And Resource Integrity In Llm Cascades
authors: Miaobo Hu, Shuhao Hu, Xiaobo Guo, Xin Wang, Bokun Wang, Daren Zha, Jun Xiao
