abstract: ArXiv:2610.20668v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce CascadeLedger, a counterfactual execution-audit framework for budgeted language-model cascades. The protocol enforces call-before-read semantics, binds successful reads to service and cache identities, records availability and component-wise budget transitions, and freezes the event trace before any target or task scorer is joined. The central object is aggregate-equivalent trace validity: two executions can share a final answer, declared resource projection, and service histogram while differing in whether their routing decisions used only legitimately observable information. We complement single-trace invariants with counterfactual prefix non-interference (CPNI), which couples a visible prefix and policy randomness while changing only a declared hidden family. The counterfactual influence frontier (CIF) localizes the earliest violating prefix and a minimal hidden witness; projection-preserving adversarial mutation (PPAM) searches for invalid traces that remain acceptable to a non-counterfactual checker. Across frozen-cache, independently generated, and serving evaluations, the two-layer audit reports a clean false-positive rate of 0.0000, detects 0.9983 of serialized faults and 0.9982 of unlogged hidden-read faults, and changes 0.3403 of corrupted quality-resource conclusions after deterministic recomputation. The online recorder and offline CPNI audit have separate overhead measurements. Learned routing and semantic verification provide downstream compatibility studies under the same execution contract.
tldr: CascadeLedger is a counterfactual execution-audit framework for detecting information and resource integrity violations in budgeted LLM cascades.
motivation: Budgeted language-model cascades need auditing to verify that routing decisions rely only on legitimately observable information and that resource/cache transitions are correctly recorded.
method: The framework enforces call-before-read semantics, binds reads to service and cache identities, records budget transitions, freezes traces, and adds counterfactual prefix non-interference (CPNI), a counterfactual influence frontier (CIF), and projection-preserving adversarial mutation (PPAM).
result: It reports 0.0000 false positives, detects 0.9983 of serialized faults and 0.9982 of unlogged hidden-read faults, and changes 0.3403 of corrupted quality-resource conclusions after deterministic recomputation.
conclusion: CascadeLedger provides a two-layer audit for LLM cascades that localizes integrity violations and is compatible with learned routing and semantic verification under the same execution contract.

title: Privacy-Preserving Text Inference For Health-Misinformation Classification And Semantic Retrieval
authors: Jasleen Kaur, Chlo\'e Cachet, Koray Karabina, Jean Belo Klamti, Philippe Lamontagne
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20796v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Health-misinformation analysis presents a dual challenge: misleading claims can affect public well-being, while systems designed to detect them may expose sensitive user-submitted text. This motivates privacy-preserving inference for public-health applications in which user queries may contain confidential medical information and trained models and reference databases are maintained on organizational servers. We design a privacy-preserving text inference framework based on CKKS homomorphic encryption for health-misinformation classification and semantic retrieval. The classification pipeline fuses BioBERT embeddings, PCA-reduced MPNet embeddings, and SVD-reduced TF-IDF features, while the retrieval pipeline combines MPNet embeddings with ISCC-SCT semantic fingerprints through late fusion. We evaluate predictive performance and benchmark plaintext versus ciphertext-based execution. The hybrid classifier achieved an accuracy of 0.971 and a macro-F1 score of 0.950, with identical reported metrics under plaintext and ciphertext-based inference. The hybrid late-fusion similarity model achieved a Pearson correlation of 0.8691 with human sentence-pair similarity scores on STS-B. For ciphertext-based retrieval, we evaluated naive and optimized implementations. The optimized implementation uses CKKS single instruction, multiple data (SIMD) packing to compute and return multiple similarity scores together, reducing single-query latency over 7,128 indexed items from 222.028 to 5.168 seconds and communication overhead from 6.11 GB to 2.13 MB. These findings demonstrate the technical feasibility of privacy-preserving text inference for health-misinformation applications and characterize its predictive utility and efficiency trade-offs.
tldr: A privacy-preserving text inference framework using CKKS homomorphic encryption for health-misinformation classification and semantic retrieval, with benchmarked plaintext-versus-ciphertext performance.
motivation: Detecting health misinformation risks exposing sensitive user-submitted medical text, and models plus reference databases reside on organizational servers, motivating encrypted inference for public-health applications.
method: The pipeline fuses BioBERT embeddings, PCA-reduced MPNet embeddings, and SVD-reduced TF-IDF features for classification, while retrieval combines MPNet embeddings with ISCC-SCT semantic fingerprints via late fusion, all executed under CKKS homomorphic encryption with SIMD packing optimizations.
result: The hybrid classifier reached 0.971 accuracy and 0.950 macro-F1 with identical plaintext and ciphertext metrics; the optimized ciphertext retrieval used SIMD packing to cut single-query latency from 222.028 s to 5.168 s and communication from 6.11 GB to 2.13 MB over 7,128 indexed items.
conclusion: The work demonstrates technical feasibility of privacy-preserving text inference for health-misinformation applications and characterizes the predictive utility versus efficiency trade-offs.

title: Performance Characterization Of Pulsar's Software-defined Watermark Verifier
authors: Kaz Gunning Jason Anderson
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20827v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pulsar provides the world's most secure PNT service by incorporating a Combinatorial Watermark into its ranging service. Under conservative signal conditions, Pulsar's Combinatorial Watermark, where 21 ranging code chips are inverted among the 1023, provides 32-bit authentication security each second. In this work, we present our software-defined radio (SDR) implementation of the Pulsar watermark processor. We discuss various threat models, multiple receiver architectures, implications to the receiver, and results from using Pulsar's SDR processing watermarked signals daily from the Pulsar-0 mission. Our results demonstrate the feasible implementation of Pulsar's watermark verification process in commercial GNSS receivers. This is an important milestone in making Xona's Pulsar service available to customers later this year after deployment of our first four production satellites.
tldr: The paper presents an SDR implementation and performance characterization of Pulsar's software-defined watermark verifier for secure GNSS positioning, navigation, and timing (PNT).
motivation: Pulsar aims to provide secure PNT by embedding a combinatorial watermark into ranging signals, and commercial receiver feasibility must be demonstrated before service deployment.
method: The authors implement a software-defined radio watermark processor, analyze threat models and receiver architectures, and process watermarked signals daily from the Pulsar-0 mission.
result: The results show that Pulsar's watermark verification process can be feasibly implemented in commercial GNSS receivers, with 21 inverted chips among 1023 providing 32-bit authentication security each second under conservative conditions.
conclusion: This work marks an important milestone toward making Xona's Pulsar service available to customers following the deployment of production satellites.

title: On Knowledge Compilation Languages For QBFs
authors: Sravanthi Chede, Vaibhav Krishan, Anil Shukla
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20842v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this work, we design knowledge compilation languages for quantified Boolean formulas (QBFs), with a particular focus on model counting. We introduce various languages in increasing order of their power of representation, starting from a simple tree-based structure, and extending it to DAGs for a more efficient representation. We study the power and limitations of each language. We also show that QBF queries such as model counting and MaxQBF are easy to handle in all these languages. These languages naturally lead to various static proof systems for the #QBF problem, the model-counting version of the QBF problem. We compare these systems with one another and with a recently introduced line-based #QBF-system called Q-MICE (Chede, Chew, Krishan and Shukla, SAT `26). We show that a minor extension of the Q-MICE system efficiently simulates all these static proof systems, and is in fact exponentially stronger than each of them. We also initiate the implementation of a solver based on these languages. The solver compiles a representation of an input QBF in the proposed tree-like language, which is subsequently used for model counting. This is the first knowledge compilation based solver for #QBF which can handle QBFs with doubly exponential model counts as well. Experimentally, we compare its performance with the state-of-the-art #QBF-solver d4-QBF which works well for QBFs with small model counts.
tldr: The paper designs knowledge compilation languages for quantified Boolean formulas (QBFs) and applies them to model counting and proof systems, with a prototype solver for #QBF.
motivation: Model counting for QBFs (#QBF) is computationally hard, and efficient representation languages are needed to handle QBFs with large model counts.
method: The authors introduce tree-based and DAG-based knowledge compilation languages for QBFs, study their representation power, and use them to define static proof systems for #QBF.
result: They show that a minor extension of the Q-MICE proof system efficiently simulates all proposed static proof systems and is exponentially stronger; a prototype solver handles QBFs with doubly exponential model counts, outperforming d4-QBF on such cases.
conclusion: These knowledge compilation languages provide a foundation for proof systems and practical solving of #QBF, with the first solver capable of handling doubly exponential model counts.

title: Two Variables And Two-Dimensional Structures
authors: Bartosz Jan Bednarczyk, Daumantas Kojelis, Krzysztof Szyma\'nski
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20937v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the two-variable fragment FO^2 of first-order logic over two-dimensional structures. Formulae may employ two linear orders <=_1, <=_2, their successor relations S_1, S_2, and auxiliary predicates of any arity. Despite two decades of work, three cases of finite satisfiability in this setting were still open; we settle all three. First, finite satisfiability of FO^2 with one linear order and one successor relation, of the same or of a different order, is NExpTime-complete, even with arbitrary auxiliary predicates and constant symbols. This closes a gap left open by Manuel and Zeume (CSL 2013). As an application, a reduction based on swaps of adjacent elements shows that order-invariance and order-successor-invariance of FO^2 are coNExpTime-complete. This reproves the main result of Zeume and Harwath (LICS 2016) and settles their question on order-successor-invariance. Second, finite satisfiability of FO^2 with two linear orders is ExpSpace-hard, already without auxiliary non-unary predicates, matching the upper bound known since 2010. Our reduction combines Kieronski's encoding of alternating Turing machines with the classical fact that the pre-order and post-order traversals of a tree define its descendant relation. Third, with two linear orders and the successor of one of them, finite satisfiability is in ExpSpace even with arbitrary auxiliary predicates, improving the previous 2NExpTime bound and confirming a conjecture of Zeume and Harwath. Together with known results, our theorems show that in two dimensions, auxiliary (non-unary) predicates and constants come for free: with or without them, the complexities coincide. All our proofs are simple.
tldr: The paper settles three open cases of finite satisfiability for the two-variable fragment FO^2 of first-order logic over two-dimensional structures with linear orders and successor relations.
motivation: Despite two decades of work, three cases of finite satisfiability for FO^2 over two-dimensional structures remained open; the authors aim to close these gaps and unify the complexity landscape.
method: The proofs use reductions based on swaps of adjacent elements, Kieronski's encoding of alternating Turing machines, and the fact that pre-order and post-order traversals of a tree define its descendant relation.
result: Finite satisfiability of FO^2 with one linear order and one successor is NExpTime-complete; with two linear orders it is ExpSpace-hard (matching a known upper bound); with two linear orders plus one successor it is in ExpSpace, improving a 2NExpTime bound.
conclusion: In two dimensions, allowing auxiliary non-unary predicates and constants does not change complexity, and order-invariance notions are coNExpTime-complete.

title: Does Client Diversity Protect The Lightning Network? Evidence From The 2026 Core Lightning Shutdown
authors: Saurabh Kumar
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20952v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Client diversity is often cited as the Lightning Network's defence against a bug in any one implementation, yet LND runs 84% of public nodes and holds 84% of public channel capacity, a share that has barely moved since 2023. We test what diversity buys with a natural experiment. On 26 August 2026, amid security fixes in every implementation, Core Lightning (CLN) maintainers told operators who could not upgrade to disconnect their nodes. Using 805 daily gossip snapshots, 132,360 on-chain channel closes and a client classifier validated against self-identifying aliases and against the wallet that builds each node's funding transactions, we find that 22% of CLN nodes went dark overnight, ten times the usual rate, mostly Tor-reachable ones; a third were still dark five weeks later. The rest of the network barely noticed. Reachability among all node pairs fell by 7.8 percentage points, a loss exceeded in 4 of 94 ordinary two-day windows and half that of a Tor denial-of-service wave in July, while among CLN pairs it fell by 24.5 points, more than in any ordinary window. Calibrated failure scenarios explain the containment: the blast radius depends on whether a failure reaches the hubs, not on how many nodes run the failing software. Losing ACINQ's Eclair node alone costs the surviving network four times the reachability lost with all 619 routable CLN nodes, and minority clients' reliance on LND for connectivity is what their size implies; CLN nodes in fact peer with each other more than chance. Diversity statistics that count nodes mislead; the quantity to track is which software the hubs run.
tldr: A natural experiment from the 2026 Core Lightning shutdown shows that Lightning Network client diversity did not prevent large reachability losses within the affected implementation, and that hub software matters more than node counts.
motivation: Client diversity is often claimed to protect the Lightning Network from implementation-specific bugs, yet LND dominates public nodes and capacity, so the actual protective value of diversity is unclear.
method: Using 805 daily gossip snapshots, 132,360 on-chain channel closes, and a client classifier validated against self-identifying aliases and funding wallets, the study measures reachability changes during the August 2026 Core Lightning shutdown.
result: 22% of CLN nodes went dark overnight (ten times the usual rate), overall reachability fell 7.8 percentage points while CLN-pair reachability fell 24.5 points, and calibrated scenarios show losing one Eclair hub costs four times more reachability than losing all routable CLN nodes.
conclusion: Client diversity by node count is misleading; the real quantity to track is which software the network hubs run, because the blast radius of a failure depends on whether it reaches those hubs.

title: Precise Asymptotics For Dense High-Dimensional Huber Regression Under Heteroscedasticity
authors: Jing Zhou, Ramji Venkataramanan, Hui Zou
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20798v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study Huber regression in a heteroscedastic linear model in the proportional regime [MATH]. Our main result is an exact characterization of the asymptotic empirical distribution of the Huber estimator. This characterization is in terms of three scalar parameters which determine the first-order centre and the asymptotic variance of the Huber estimator. The result shows that with heteroscedastic noise, the first-order centre may contain an additional component along the variance index coefficient. We derive the displacement coefficients that determine this centre, as well as the exact asymptotic variance. The analysis uses the matrix approximate message passing (AMP) framework to jointly track the regression and variance index coefficients, extending the existing framework for homoscedastic M-estimators. We illustrate the implications of this characterization by constructing a test for centre displacement and examining its empirical size and power through simulations.
tldr: The paper provides an exact asymptotic characterization of the Huber estimator in a high-dimensional heteroscedastic linear model using matrix approximate message passing.
motivation: Huber regression is robust to outliers, but its high-dimensional behavior under heteroscedastic noise is not precisely understood, motivating an exact asymptotic analysis.
method: The authors extend the matrix AMP framework to jointly track regression coefficients and variance index coefficients, deriving scalar parameters that determine the asymptotic distribution of the Huber estimator.
result: They show that heteroscedastic noise introduces an additional displacement along the variance index coefficient, and they derive exact expressions for the first-order center and asymptotic variance.
conclusion: The characterization enables a test for center displacement, whose empirical size and power are examined via simulations.

title: On The Stability Of Basis Construction In Extended Krylov Subspace Methods
authors: Marcel Schweitzer Kathryn Lund
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21603v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Extended Krylov subspace methods (EKSMs) are a well known approach for approximating the action of a matrix function on a vector [MATH], and their block versions are often used for solving Lyapunov and Sylvester matrix equations. EKSMs produce Laurent approximations to the underlying operator, which are generally more accurate per iteration than polynomial KSMs, without requiring a pole selection procedure as rational KSMs do. At the same time, due to the expansion of the search space by not only [MATH] but also by its inverse, a number of implementation choices must be made that can affect the stability of the algorithm in floating-point arithmetic. We concentrate on two variants that often appear in the literature and in code, based on whether new basis vectors are built via what we denote as ``mixed channels" or ``split channels." We characterize their loss of orthogonality with an easily computable metric and prove that when [MATH] is symmetric positive definite, mixed channels have better orthogonality than split channels; however, numerical experiments demonstrate that straightforward predictions are not possible for indefinite or nonsymmetric matrices. We also provide a modular MATLAB toolbox, , that contains new versions of EKSMs with low-synchronization Gram-Schmidt backbones.
tldr: This paper analyzes stability and loss of orthogonality in extended Krylov subspace methods (EKSMs) for approximating matrix functions and solving Lyapunov/Sylvester equations.
motivation: EKSMs are attractive because they avoid pole selection while still achieving accurate Laurent approximations, but their inverse-including search space introduces implementation choices that can destabilize the algorithm in floating-point arithmetic.
method: The authors compare 'mixed channel' and 'split channel' basis construction variants, characterize loss of orthogonality via an easily computable metric, and prove that mixed channels are better for symmetric positive definite matrices, supported by numerical experiments on indefinite and nonsymmetric cases.
result: Mixed channels exhibit superior orthogonality to split channels for symmetric positive definite matrices, but no simple prediction holds for indefinite or nonsymmetric matrices; a modular MATLAB toolbox with low-synchronization Gram-Schmidt backbones is provided.
conclusion: The work gives practical guidance and tools for implementing stable EKSMs, though its contributions are confined to numerical linear algebra rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: From Detection To Decision: Calibration And Deferral For Prompt-Injection Detection
authors: Qianlong Lan, Anuj Kaul, Vinothini Pandurangan, Indranil Sanyal
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20907v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Prompt-injection defenses are commonly evaluated as binary detectors, although deployed LLM applications must make operational decisions about whether to allow, block, or escalate potentially malicious inputs. Recent probabilistic decision models aim to support such decisions through calibrated confidence estimates, but their reliability under distribution shift remains uncertain. We evaluate a native probabilistic decision model (Jev), two Llama Prompt Guard 2 classifiers (22M and 86M), and an LLM-based judge on 47,611 held-out examples spanning direct and indirect prompt injections, hard-benign inputs, obfuscation, and distribution shift. Using separate development and calibration splits, we assess detection performance, probability calibration, and allow-block-defer policies under a frozen evaluation protocol. The LLM judge achieves the highest overall discrimination (AUROC 0.897), followed by Jev (0.871), Prompt Guard 2 86M (0.757), and Prompt Guard 2 22M (0.714). However, Jev's native probabilities do not consistently outperform post-hoc calibrated classifier scores, and temperature scaling improves calibration without improving discrimination. At an empirical false-negative-rate target of 1%, all evaluated gate-reviewer systems require more than 91.8% escalation and incur substantial false-positive rates. These findings demonstrate that probabilistic outputs alone do not establish reliable security decisions under distribution shift. Effective LLM security systems must jointly evaluate detection, calibration, reviewer behavior, and operational decision policies.
tldr: The paper evaluates probabilistic calibration and allow-block-defer decision policies for prompt-injection detection under distribution shift, finding that calibrated outputs alone do not yield reliable security decisions.
motivation: Deployed LLM applications need operational decisions about malicious inputs, not just binary detection, and the reliability of calibrated confidence estimates under distribution shift is uncertain.
method: They compare Jev, two Llama Prompt Guard 2 classifiers, and an LLM judge on 47,611 held-out examples using separate development and calibration splits, assessing AUROC, probability calibration, and allow-block-defer policies under a frozen evaluation protocol.
result: The LLM judge achieves the highest AUROC (0.897), followed by Jev (0.871), Prompt Guard 2 86M (0.757), and Prompt Guard 2 22M (0.714); temperature scaling improves calibration but not discrimination, and at 1% FNR all systems require >91.8% escalation with substantial false positives.
conclusion: Probabilistic outputs alone do not establish reliable security decisions under distribution shift; effective LLM security must jointly evaluate detection, calibration, reviewer behavior, and operational decision policies.

title: What Survives Self-Evolution: Provenance Marks In Copied Agent Harnesses
authors: Jieyu Li, Jingya Li, Sheng Li, Xinpeng Zhang, Zhenxing Qian
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21458v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agent harnesses, the prompt and tool code around a base model, leak. Claude Code's 512,000 lines were mirrored within hours of a packaging error. A plagiarist can pass a leaked harness through a published self-evolver and ship the result as its own. We define this as a covert rewriting attack. No one targets a provenance mark, yet a large language model (LLM) proposer rewrites the file that carries it and a score keeps the better rewrites. We give the first measurement of marks under this attack, with three evolvers, five proposers and two environments. Published marks fail. KGW in the prompt survives GEPA's rewrites in 0 of 12 copies, AgentMark as released in 5 of 12. The proposer's habits decide survival, by two orders of magnitude across models, and selection protects a mark only when each decision sees enough games. We then build a mark for this attack. Its key is the order of near-tied entries of a table of where objects are found, built from public games, so deleting the table costs success, rewrites that keep its rows keep the order, and a customer reads the key from the agent's actions alone. On held-out games it is detected in 62 of 76 copies whose lineage rewrote its file. A scheme-aware plagiarist reshuffles the ties at no measurable cost, and a plagiarist who asks the proposer for more general code removes the key in 75-100% of rewrites.
tldr: The paper studies provenance marks in copied LLM agent harnesses under a covert rewriting attack and proposes a mark based on the order of near-tied table entries.
motivation: Leaked agent harnesses can be passed through self-evolvers and shipped as original work, so the authors aim to measure and improve provenance-mark survival under this realistic rewriting threat.
method: They define a covert rewriting attack, evaluate published marks using three evolvers, five proposers, and two environments, and then design a new mark keyed on the order of near-tied entries in a table of object locations built from public games.
result: Published marks largely fail, with survival depending heavily on the proposer; the proposed mark detects 62 of 76 held-out copies whose lineage rewrote its file, but scheme-aware plagiarists can reshuffle ties without measurable cost or remove the key in 75–100% of rewrites when requesting more general code.
conclusion: Provenance marking for self-evolving agent harnesses is fragile under adversarial rewriting, and the proposed scheme offers only partial robustness against determined plagiarists.

title: Superfast Spectral Compressed Sensing With Quadratic Convergence
authors: Xunmeng Wu, Jian-Feng Cai, Zongben Xu, Zai Yang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21068v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we study the spectral compressed sensing problem of recovering a spectrally sparse signal from linear compressive measurements. Exploiting the low-rank Hankel structure associated with the signal, we formulate a nonconvex fixed-rank optimization problem with a Hankel regularization. We propose a Superfast Iterative Hard Thresholding (SIHT) algorithm, where each iteration consists of a tangent-space least-squares update followed by a fixed-rank hard thresholding projection. SIHT is the first nonconvex algorithm with provable quadratic convergence for spectral compressed sensing. For random Gaussian measurements, it achieves exact recovery in the noiseless case and stable recovery in the noisy case with near-optimal sample complexity. To efficiently implement SIHT, we develop a parameterized conjugate gradient method for solving the least-squares subproblem, endowing SIHT with state-of-the-art computational and memory efficiency. Numerical experiments are provided to validate our results.
tldr: The paper proposes a Superfast Iterative Hard Thresholding (SIHT) algorithm for spectral compressed sensing that achieves provable quadratic convergence with near-optimal sample complexity.
motivation: Spectral compressed sensing of spectrally sparse signals is hampered by the computational cost of existing nonconvex methods and their typically slow (linear) convergence guarantees.
method: Exploiting the low-rank Hankel structure, the authors formulate a nonconvex fixed-rank optimization with Hankel regularization and solve it via tangent-space least-squares updates alternating with fixed-rank hard thresholding, with a parameterized conjugate gradient solver for the subproblem.
result: SIHT is the first nonconvex algorithm with provable quadratic convergence for spectral compressed sensing, achieving exact recovery in the noiseless case and stable recovery with near-optimal sample complexity under random Gaussian measurements, validated numerically.
conclusion: The work delivers a computationally and memory-efficient nonconvex algorithm with strong theoretical guarantees, advancing the classical signal-processing literature on spectral compressed sensing.

title: When Is A Better Llm Worth Paying For? Stochastic Optimization With Switching Mixed-Fidelity Oracles
authors: Tianjiao Li Swati Gupta
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21139v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used upstream of decision-making to clean data, detect label errors, and reconstruct missing values. Yet LLM-assisted data curation creates a new operational tradeoff: higher-fidelity models and richer prompts can be substantially more expensive, while the value of this additional fidelity depends on the downstream optimization accuracy. This raises the central question of this work: when should one pay for a better LLM, given a specific downstream task at hand? We study this question through stochastic optimization with mixed-fidelity first-order oracles, which can have systematic bias and state-dependent variance. We develop two cost-aware algorithmic frameworks that allow adaptive switching between stochastic oracles. With known bias, the first meta-algorithm applies a restarted, cost-aware policy that adaptively selects oracle fidelity across optimization stages. Its cumulative cost is no larger than that of the best fixed oracle in hindsight and can be substantially smaller. With unknown bias, we develop a budgeted certification scheme that uses occasional trusted-gradient evaluations to certify the optimization progress and eliminate unsuccessful oracle sources, and show an explicit tradeoff between certification cost and delayed detection of biased sources. We provide concrete realizations of these meta-algorithms by applying biased stochastic gradient extrapolation (SGE) and recursive regularization under state-dependent noise as subroutines. Synthetic and LLM-completion experiments illustrate the qualitative switching behavior predicted by the theory: the adaptive policy skips several expensive LLM oracles and substantially reduces cumulative cost relative to fixed high-fidelity alternatives while achieving comparable accuracy.
tldr: The paper develops cost-aware stochastic optimization algorithms that adaptively switch between mixed-fidelity gradient oracles (e.g., cheaper vs. more expensive LLMs) to reduce cumulative cost while preserving downstream accuracy.
motivation: LLM-assisted data curation forces practitioners to trade off model fidelity/prompt richness cost against downstream optimization accuracy, raising the question of when paying for a better LLM is worthwhile.
method: Two meta-algorithms are proposed: a restarted cost-aware policy for known bias that adaptively selects oracle fidelity across optimization stages, and a budgeted certification scheme using occasional trusted-gradient evaluations to detect and eliminate biased oracles when bias is unknown; both are instantiated via biased stochastic gradient extrapolation and recursive regularization.
result: The adaptive policies achieve cumulative cost no larger than the best fixed oracle in hindsight, and synthetic plus LLM-completion experiments show the policy skips several expensive LLM oracles and substantially lowers cumulative cost while matching fixed high-fidelity accuracy.
conclusion: Adaptive switching among mixed-fidelity stochastic oracles offers a principled way to decide when higher-fidelity LLMs are worth their cost, with theoretical guarantees and empirical validation.

title: Dual Representations And Proxy Characterization Of $h_2$ Norm For Partial Integral Equations
authors: Danilo Braghini, Tristan Thomas, Sachin Shivakumar, Javad M. Velni, Matthew M. Peet
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21355v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Duality and dual representations are essential tools for systems theory and controller synthesis. For any finite-dimensional causal linear time-invariant (CLTI) system, there exists a dual CLTI system with identical [MATH] and [MATH] norm. These relations are found by simply taking the adjoint of the transfer function. For nonlinear, time-varying or infinite-dimensional systems, however, such a transfer function may not exist or be difficult to obtain. For duality in the [MATH] norm, this obstacle is overcome by using the equivalent time-domain, induced [MATH]-norm characterization. For [MATH] norms there is no such equivalent characterization and hence proxy norms such as induced energy to peak and impulse to energy norms are used. These proxy norms bound the [MATH] norm in the CLTI case. However, neither of these [MATH] proxy norms equal the same [MATH] proxy of the canonical dual representation. In this paper, we overcome this by proposing a dual representation whose induced energy to peak proxy equals the impulse to energy proxy of the primal and vice-versa. This relation is developed in the context of Partial Integral Equation (PIE) representations. The result is then used to establish primal-dual operator inequalities for both proxy norms similar in form to the primal-dual LMIs used to characterize the [MATH] norm.
tldr: The paper develops dual representations for H2 norm proxy characterizations in partial integral equation systems, establishing primal-dual operator inequalities analogous to LMI conditions for the H2 norm.
motivation: Duality and dual representations are essential in systems and control theory, but for infinite-dimensional or nonlinear systems, H2 norm duality is hindered by the lack of equivalent time-domain characterizations and the mismatch between proxy norms under dualization.
method: The authors propose a dual representation for Partial Integral Equation (PIE) systems such that the induced energy-to-peak proxy of the dual equals the impulse-to-energy proxy of the primal, and vice versa, using operator-theoretic inequalities.
result: The construction yields primal-dual operator inequalities for both proxy norms, mirroring the form of primal-dual LMIs used for H2 norm characterization in finite-dimensional systems.
conclusion: This work provides a systematic duality framework for H2 proxy norms in PIE representations, potentially enabling controller synthesis for infinite-dimensional systems, but it is purely control-theoretic and unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Descending Everest With First-Order Oracles: Oracle Complexity Of Convex Optimization Under $(L_0,L_1)$-Smoothness
authors: Mikhail Rudomanov, Ivan Fomin, Alexander V. Gasnikov, Fedor S. Stonyakin
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21461v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For convex [MATH]-smooth functions, the curvature may grow together with the gradient norm. Therefore, even when [MATH], the gradient and the optimality gap at the starting point may be exponentially large in [MATH], and the bound [MATH], known for the accelerated method on functions with Lipschitz gradient, no longer describes the complexity of the problem. We determine the oracle complexity of this class for arbitrary deterministic first-order methods: for [MATH], the optimal number of oracle calls [MATH] satisfies [MATH]. The upper bound reads [MATH]: the method first passes through the large-gradient regime in [MATH] iterations with an inexact line search, and then the standard accelerated method with a constant stepsize takes over. The lower bound is obtained by means of chains and the orthogonal invariance principle on functions conjugate to strongly convex functions on a polytope. If the initial optimality gap is at most [MATH], the optimal bound becomes [MATH].
tldr: The paper determines the optimal oracle complexity for convex optimization under (L0,L1)-smoothness using deterministic first-order methods.
motivation: For convex functions with gradient-Lipschitz-like smoothness, standard accelerated complexity bounds fail when curvature grows with gradient norm, so a sharper complexity characterization is needed.
method: The authors design a two-phase method combining an inexact line search for the large-gradient regime with the standard accelerated method, and prove a lower bound using chains and orthogonal invariance on conjugate functions.
result: They show that for arbitrary deterministic first-order methods, the optimal number of oracle calls scales as O(L0/epsilon + sqrt(L1/epsilon)), matching upper and lower bounds, with a modified bound when the initial optimality gap is small.
conclusion: The work settles the oracle complexity of convex optimization under (L0,L1)-smoothness, extending optimal complexity results beyond classical Lipschitz-gradient assumptions.

title: Optimal First-Order Methods For A Class Of Structured H\"older-Smooth Problems
authors: Qi Deng Baiying Xin
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21595v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Convex optimization with H\"older-continuous gradients has attracted considerable attention as a framework bridging smooth and nonsmooth optimization. For this class, Nesterov's universal fast gradient method attains the optimal black-box complexity, and we study whether exploiting further problem structure can further improve this bound. In this paper, we study an important class of H\"older-smooth problems, namely regularized [MATH] regression with [MATH], whose loss has a [MATH]-H\"older-continuous gradient and for which the universal method requires [MATH] iterations. Exploiting the problem structure, we characterize a family of smooth approximations based on [MATH]-Huber smoothing and prove that, for any prescribed smoothness level, it minimizes the worst-case approximation error among smooth lower approximations of the scalar loss. Combined with accelerated proximal gradients, the smoothing approach attains an [MATH]-optimal solution in [MATH] matrix--vector products, which significantly improves the complexity guarantee for [MATH]. We show that this bound is optimal by providing a matching lower bound. Numerical experiments on synthetic and real data demonstrate the practical performance of the proposed methods.
tldr: The paper develops optimal first-order methods for a class of structured Hölder-smooth convex optimization problems by exploiting problem structure through Huber-type smoothing.
motivation: Hölder-smooth convex optimization bridges smooth and nonsmooth optimization, and the authors ask whether additional problem structure can beat the optimal black-box complexity of Nesterov's universal fast gradient method.
method: They study regularized regression with Hölder-continuous gradients, characterize a family of smooth approximations based on Huber smoothing that minimizes worst-case approximation error among smooth lower approximations, and combine this with accelerated proximal gradient methods.
result: The proposed approach achieves an optimal complexity in terms of matrix-vector products, improving upon the universal method's guarantee for a relevant parameter regime, with a matching lower bound and numerical experiments on synthetic and real data.
conclusion: The work shows that structured Hölder-smooth problems admit faster first-order methods than generic universal fast gradient methods, with optimality certified by lower bounds.

title: Thinking In Graphs: Neo4j-Backed Exploit-Chain Reasoning For Llm Penetration-Testing Agents
authors: Joas Antonio Dos Santos Barbosa
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20902v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM coding agents such as Claude Code and OpenAI Codex can drive penetration-testing tools, but they reason about an engagement as a flat list of findings in a context window. Attackers think in graphs: isolated low-severity exposures turn catastrophic once chained through credential capture, privilege escalation, and lateral movement. This gap feeds a common belief that AI agents cannot truly chain exploitation; we argue this describes the flat context window, not the model. We present ChainGraph, a pattern that externalizes exploit-chain reasoning into a Neo4j property graph wired to an off-the-shelf agent via the Model Context Protocol, no bespoke harness. Findings, attack steps, credentials, assets, and tamper-evident evidence receipts are typed nodes with pre/post-condition edges; JSON/Markdown holds documentary memory while Neo4j holds reasoning memory. We formalize five operator questions (next-step inference, entry-to-crown-jewel pathing, combined-severity promotion, evidence provenance, and chokepoint identification) as reusable Cypher and Graph Data Science queries, plus a chain-severity score distinct from per-finding local severity. On a synthetic multi-forest Active Directory engagement modeled on GOAD, in live Neo4j with GDS, three findings rated Medium in isolation become Critical once their path to the forest root is materialized, and betweenness centrality names the best chain break-points. Scoping each decision to a graph result rather than re-reading the engagement cut the reasoning payload by about 98% on a token proxy. We give a reproducible setup for Claude Code and Codex. Results are illustrative single-run measurements, not a benchmark.
tldr: ChainGraph externalizes exploit-chain reasoning for LLM penetration-testing agents into a Neo4j property graph accessed via the Model Context Protocol, enabling graph-based attack-path queries instead of flat context-window reasoning.
motivation: LLM coding agents can drive penetration-testing tools but reason over findings as a flat list, missing the chained exploitation (credential capture, privilege escalation, lateral movement) that attackers naturally think about in graph terms.
method: Findings, attack steps, credentials, assets, and tamper-evident receipts are modeled as typed nodes with pre/post-condition edges in Neo4j; five operator questions (next-step inference, pathing, severity promotion, provenance, chokepoints) are formalized as reusable Cypher and GDS queries and wired to off-the-shelf agents via MCP.
result: On a synthetic multi-forest Active Directory engagement modeled on GOAD, three individually Medium-rated findings become Critical once their path to the forest root is materialized, betweenness centrality identifies chain break-points, and scoping decisions to graph results cut reasoning payload by roughly 98% on a token proxy.
conclusion: Graph-structured reasoning memory appears to enable exploit-chain inference that flat context windows obscure, though the authors present illustrative single-run measurements rather than a benchmark.

title: FedSumUp: User-Auditable Privacy-Aware Representation Sharing For Resource-Constrained Federated Intelligence
authors: Jingwei Zhao, Tiantong Sun, Yuanyuan Song, Jinhuan Guo, Wei Zishuo, Shengyu Huang, Ziyuan Ren, Wei Chen, Xiaojin Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21194v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Existing federated data condensation methods face privacy risks, as uploaded synthetic data may preserve sensitive information and remain vulnerable to reconstruction attacks. Moreover, their generation often incurs considerable client-side computational overhead, limiting deployment on resource-constrained devices. To address these issues, we propose FedSumUp, which employs a learnable lossy compressor on clients to generate compact and visually interpretable representations. By controlling information capacity, FedSumUp reduces privacy leakage while allowing users to directly assess the privacy-utility tradeoff. We further introduce a dual-objective optimization mechanism to preserve task-relevant semantics while suppressing reconstruction risks. The compressor is trained on the server and only performs lightweight inference on clients. Since the server cannot access raw data, we develop a data-free closed-loop optimization strategy that optimizes the compressor by minimizing the discrepancy between original and twice-compressed representations after structure-preserving upsampling. Experiments on BloodMNIST, CIFAR-10, and ChestMNIST demonstrate reconstruction PSNR as low as 8.56 dB (with synthetic PSNR as low as 5.45 dB), client runtime reductions up to 96.5% (from 778s to 27s on ChestMNIST), and competitive classification accuracy (89.72% ChestMNIST, 82.24% BloodMNIST, 65.63% CIFAR-10), while remaining inherently robust to non-IID data distributions.
tldr: FedSumUp proposes a privacy-aware federated data condensation method using learnable lossy compressors to create compact, auditable representations with low client overhead.
motivation: Existing federated data condensation methods risk privacy leakage and have high client-side computational cost, limiting deployment on resource-constrained devices.
method: The method trains a learnable lossy compressor on the server, performs lightweight inference on clients, and uses data-free closed-loop optimization with a dual-objective mechanism to preserve semantics while suppressing reconstruction.
result: Experiments on BloodMNIST, CIFAR-10, and ChestMNIST show reconstruction PSNR as low as 8.56 dB, client runtime reductions up to 96.5%, and competitive classification accuracy while being robust to non-IID data.
conclusion: FedSumUp enables user-auditable privacy-utility tradeoffs and efficient federated intelligence on resource-constrained devices.

title: Model Checking HyperRecHML Is Decidable
authors: Elli Anastasiadi, Kim Guldstrand Larsen, Martin Zimmermann
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21379v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Temporal hyperlogics combine explicit quantification over traces with temporal requirements evaluated over the quantified traces. HyperRecHML is a temporal hyperlogic which allows for arbitrary mixing of trace quantification and the use of fixed points for expressing temporal requirements, which makes it very expressive in comparison to other first-order hyperlogics. HyperRecHML has already been successfully applied in runtime verification, but the decidability of its model checking problem remains open. We answer this question positively by providing two main contributions. Firstly, a normalization procedure that allows to reduce arbitrary HyperRecHML formulas to a normal form with restricted nesting of trace quantification and fixed points. Secondly, we provide an automata-based model checking algorithm for formulas of this normal form. The complexity of our algorithm is comparable to similar ones for other hyperlogics, despite the extra expressive power.
tldr: The paper proves that model checking for the temporal hyperlogic HyperRecHML is decidable by providing a normalization procedure and an automata-based algorithm.
motivation: HyperRecHML is expressive and useful for runtime verification, but its model checking decidability remained open.
method: The authors introduce a normalization that restricts nesting of trace quantifiers and fixed points, then give an automata-based model checking algorithm for normalized formulas.
result: They establish decidability of HyperRecHML model checking with complexity comparable to algorithms for similar, less expressive hyperlogics.
conclusion: The work resolves a key open problem in temporal hyperlogic verification, extending decidability to a more expressive logic without significant complexity blow-up.

title: Physics-informed Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (PIKANs) For Noise-robust Reconstruction Of Boiling Heat Flux From Infrared Measurements
authors: Siavash Khodakarami, Parimala Vardhan Vydyula, Aniruddha Bora, Justin A. Weibel, George Em Karniadakis
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20613v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recovering a noise-amplified inverse quantity from corrupted boundary data is a recurring problem in physics-informed learning for real-world applications. Specifically, small perturbations in the measured field are magnified through the spatial derivatives needed to reconstruct the target, and hence conventional discretization solvers turn them into large unphysical oscillations. We study this problem through the reconstruction of local time-resolved nucleate-boiling heat flux, which cannot be measured directly and must be inferred from infrared surface temperatures by solving an unsteady three-dimensional heat-conduction problem with sharp and rapidly evolving liquid-vapor interface gradients. We show that neither network architecture nor optimizer alone overcomes the spectral bias that smooths away these interface-scale features, and that the two must be addressed jointly. Our approach combines a Chebyshev physics-informed Kolmogorov-Arnold network (PIKAN) backbone, a quasi-second-order (SOAP) optimizer, and a temperature-annealed residual-based resampling scheme that concentrates collocation points at high-residual interface regions. Trained directly on experimental infrared measurements imposed as a boundary condition, the network resolves high-frequency bubble signatures and the high-flux distribution tail much better than a Fourier-feature PINN of equal size and training budget. In particular, it selectively filters measurement noise while preserving the physically meaningful high-frequency features, suppressing the spurious oscillations that contaminate finite-volume reconstructions and yielding more physically consistent heat-flux estimates from noisy experimental data.
tldr: A Chebyshev physics-informed Kolmogorov-Arnold Network with a quasi-second-order optimizer and residual resampling reconstructs boiling heat flux from noisy infrared temperature data.
motivation: Inverse reconstruction of local boiling heat flux from infrared measurements is ill-posed because small temperature perturbations are amplified by spatial derivatives, leading to unphysical oscillations in conventional solvers.
method: The authors combine a Chebyshev PIKAN backbone, a SOAP optimizer, and a temperature-annealed residual-based resampling scheme that concentrates collocation points near high-residual liquid-vapor interfaces.
result: Trained directly on experimental infrared boundary data, the model resolves high-frequency bubble signatures and the high-flux tail better than an equal-sized Fourier-feature PINN, while filtering measurement noise.
conclusion: Jointly addressing spectral bias through architecture and optimizer design enables more physically consistent heat-flux estimates from noisy experimental data.

title: pcNN-SN: A Physics-enhanced Predictor-corrector Neural Network Algorithm Coupled With The Discrete Ordinates Method For Neutron Transport Equations
authors: Cong Liu, Junxia Wei, Shuai Wang, Heng Yong
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20619v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Super-resolution machine learning methods hold promise for addressing the high computational costs associated with high-dimensional features in traditional transport simulations. This paper proposes a physics-enhanced neural network coupling algorithm for discrete ordinates (SN) transport calculations. Based on high- and low-accuracy data, we develop a predictor-corrector neural network (pcNN) to predict correction factors for coarse-grid solutions. Based on transport equations, local physical features containing subgrid-scale information are selected as network inputs. Dimensionless transformation of physical quantities reduces the input space dimensionality and narrows parameter distributions, facilitating network training. Physical constraints are incorporated into the network model, and the corrected solution retains its original conservation properties. pcNN and SN transport sweeps are internally coupled, and numerical solutions are corrected online. Numerical results demonstrate that this algorithm can effectively improve coarse-grid solutions to achieve a level of accuracy comparable to that of fine-grid results. The physics-based network design enables the model to demonstrate a certain degree of reusability under different computational conditions. Compared to mesh refinement, the pcNN-SN algorithm reduces the computation time for the three-dimensional test problem by more than 60%.
tldr: A physics-enhanced predictor-corrector neural network coupled with the discrete ordinates method accelerates neutron transport simulations while preserving conservation.
motivation: High-dimensional neutron transport simulations are computationally expensive, and super-resolution machine learning offers a way to reduce cost.
method: The authors develop a predictor-corrector neural network that predicts correction factors for coarse-grid SN solutions using local physical features and dimensionless inputs, incorporates physical constraints, and couples online with SN transport sweeps.
result: The pcNN-SN algorithm improves coarse-grid accuracy to near fine-grid levels, reduces computation time by over 60% for a 3D test problem, and shows some reusability under different conditions.
conclusion: Physics-enhanced machine learning can effectively accelerate neutron transport calculations, but the work falls outside the user's quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, and hybrid systems interests.

title: On The Assessment Of Domain Decomposition Approaches In Extended Physics-Informed Neural Networks For The Shock-Dominated Burgers Equation
authors: Juli\'an C. Restrepo Andr\'es F. Bola\~nos-Acosta
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20621v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) provide a mesh-free framework for solving partial differential equations but often struggle with sharp gradients and shock-dominated solutions. Extended Physics-Informed Neural Networks (XPINNs) address this challenge through domain decomposition; however, the effects of decomposition design, overlap, and local network capacity on solution accuracy remain insufficiently characterized. This work presents a systematic assessment of domain decomposition configurations for XPINNs applied to the one-dimensional viscous Burgers equation ([MATH]). We compare a standard PINN, a conventional XPINN, a shock-focused XPINN with increased network capacity in the shock-containing subdomain, and overlapping XPINNs with different overlap widths. All configurations are trained using a common protocol based on Adam, L-BFGS refinement, and ten Residual-based Adaptive Refinement (RAR) cycles. Performance is evaluated against a reference solution using global and shock-region relative [MATH] and [MATH] errors, maximum PDE residuals, and interface continuity errors. The results show that decomposition design strongly affects XPINN accuracy and shock resolution. Among the overlapping configurations, the smallest overlap provides the best accuracy, while larger overlaps degrade performance. The shock-focused XPINN achieves the lowest overall solution errors, indicating that increased local network capacity can provide greater benefit than increasing overlap alone. RAR produces the largest improvements during early refinement stages, followed by increasingly non-monotonic changes in accuracy. These findings highlight the importance of jointly considering decomposition, interface coupling, network capacity, and adaptive refinement for shock-dominated problems.
tldr: This paper systematically assesses domain decomposition configurations in extended physics-informed neural networks (XPINNs) for solving the one-dimensional viscous Burgers equation with shocks.
motivation: Physics-informed neural networks often struggle with sharp gradients and shock-dominated solutions, and XPINNs address this via domain decomposition, but the effects of decomposition design, overlap, and local network capacity are not well characterized.
method: The authors compare a standard PINN, a conventional XPINN, a shock-focused XPINN with increased capacity in the shock subdomain, and overlapping XPINNs with different overlap widths, all trained using Adam, L-BFGS refinement, and ten residual-based adaptive refinement cycles, and evaluate errors and residuals.
result: Decomposition design strongly affects accuracy; the smallest overlap performs best among overlapping configurations, and the shock-focused XPINN achieves the lowest overall solution errors, indicating that increased local capacity can outperform larger overlap.
conclusion: The findings highlight the importance of jointly considering decomposition, interface coupling, network capacity, and adaptive refinement for accurately solving shock-dominated problems with XPINNs.

title: Second-Order Homogenization Of Particulate Elastomeric Composites For Structural-Scale Damage Analysis
authors: Krishna Murthy Pabbu, Tarkes Dora Pallicity, Nelson Muthu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20624v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Damage prediction in particulate elastomeric composites is challenging due to the strong material heterogeneity, nearly incompressible behavior of the matrix, and the presence of localized stress concentrations arising from matrix-inclusion interactions. In the present work, a computational framework is developed for damage propagation analysis of particulate elastomeric composite structures. The effective constitutive response of the heterogeneous material is first determined using the second-order homogenization method. The resulting homogenized response is subsequently used to identify equivalent hyperelastic material parameters for structural simulations. A three-parameter isotropic damage model is incorporated to capture damage-induced softening. A mixed displacement-pressure finite element formulation, is used to alleviate volumetric locking associated with nearly incompressible property of elastomers. The proposed framework is validated through full-scale simulations and homogenized response involving composites with varying inclusion volume fractions. Numerical investigations demonstrate that the homogenized models is able to reproduce the global force-displacement response within 2% error and damage evolution characteristics of the heterogeneous composites while significantly reducing the computational cost.
tldr: The paper develops a computational framework for damage propagation analysis of particulate elastomeric composites using second-order homogenization and a mixed finite element formulation.
motivation: Damage prediction in particulate elastomeric composites is difficult due to material heterogeneity, near-incompressibility, and localized stress concentrations from matrix-inclusion interactions.
method: The authors use second-order homogenization to determine the effective constitutive response, fit equivalent hyperelastic parameters for structural simulations, and employ a three-parameter isotropic damage model with a mixed displacement-pressure finite element formulation to avoid volumetric locking.
result: The homogenized models reproduce global force-displacement response within 2% error and capture damage evolution characteristics while significantly reducing computational cost.
conclusion: The proposed framework provides an efficient and accurate approach for structural-scale damage analysis of particulate elastomeric composites.

title: BBun: An Unsteady Vortex-ring Panel Method For Interacting Lifting Bodies, Box Wings And Propellers
authors: Daniele Peri
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20629v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This report documents BBun (Blunt Body unsteady), a low-order code for the unsteady potential flow around one or more interacting three-dimensional bodies. The bodies are represented by vortex rings (piecewise-constant doublets) with a Neumann boundary condition; free vortex sheets are shed from the trailing edges and, optionally, from the tips, and convected in time, with an implicit unsteady Kutta condition. The report describes the choices that make the discretization consistent and convergent (a single desingularized kernel per wake line, a bordered factorization of the singular Neumann problem, interior velocity conditions for the nearly singular mode of ring-shaped bodies, the detection of the separation lines from the grid connectivity) and the extensions to several bodies, box wings, symmetric configurations (image method), non-lifting bodies, rigidly rotating bodies (propellers), the unsteady Bernoulli equation, a wake-body collision treatment and a strip-wise integral boundary layer. The verification and validation are reported in full: potential flow around a sphere, sensitivity and grid convergence, the two-dimensional limit, an independent vortex-lattice method, the NACA 0015 wing of McAlister and Takahashi (loads and chordwise pressures), the NACA 0012 profile drag, the biplane of Knight and Noyes, Prandtl's best wing system, Wagner's function and blade-element momentum theory for a propeller. A complete aircraft with counter-rotating tractor propellers illustrates the use of the code.
tldr: BBun is a low-order unsteady potential flow code using a vortex-ring panel method for interacting lifting bodies, box wings, and propellers, with full verification and validation.
motivation: The report documents a computational tool for unsteady aerodynamics of complex configurations involving multiple interacting bodies.
method: The method represents bodies by vortex rings with a Neumann boundary condition, sheds free vortex sheets from trailing edges and tips, convects them with an implicit unsteady Kutta condition, and includes extensions for multiple bodies, symmetric configurations, rotating bodies, and boundary layer coupling.
result: Verification and validation are presented for a sphere, grid convergence, 2D limit, vortex-lattice method, NACA 0015 and NACA 0012 wings, biplane, Prandtl's best wing system, Wagner's function, blade-element momentum theory, and a complete aircraft with counter-rotating propellers.
conclusion: The BBun code is a validated tool for unsteady potential flow analysis of interacting lifting surfaces, box wings, and propellers.

title: A Scalable Sharp-Interface Immersed Boundary Method For Moving Boundary Flow Simulation On Multi-GPU Systems
authors: Sushrut Kumar, Joshua Romero, Massimiliano Fatica, Jung-Hee Seo, Rajat Mittal
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21032v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sharp-interface immersed boundary methods provide a versatile framework for simulating flows with complex moving boundaries, but their irregular data structures, dynamic sparsity, and discontinuous pressure operators present significant challenges for efficient multi-GPU implementation. This work presents a fully GPU-native, multi-GPU acceleration of the sharp-interface immersed boundary solver, ViCar3D. The implementation combines a hybrid OpenACC/CUDA programming model with a matrix decomposition that isolates dynamically changing immersed-boundary operators, GPU-optimized geometric kernels, asynchronous dual-stream sparse matrix--vector execution, and a symmetric-memory-based sparse communication strategy. A GPU-oriented iterative solver employing a preconditioned stabilized bi-conjugate gradient (BiCGStab) method is developed to efficiently treat the pressure Poisson equation on highly stretched Cartesian grids. The resulting framework preserves the accuracy and versatility of the original solver while delivering substantial acceleration and scalability for simulations involving complex moving and deforming immersed boundaries, thereby extending the applicability of sharp-interface immersed boundary methods to extreme-scale computational fluid dynamics.
tldr: A fully GPU-native, multi-GPU implementation of a sharp-interface immersed boundary method for simulating moving boundary flows in computational fluid dynamics.
motivation: Sharp-interface immersed boundary methods are versatile for complex moving boundary flows but suffer from irregular data structures, dynamic sparsity, and discontinuous pressure operators that hinder efficient multi-GPU acceleration.
method: The authors combine hybrid OpenACC/CUDA programming with matrix decomposition that isolates dynamically changing immersed-boundary operators, GPU-optimized geometric kernels, asynchronous dual-stream sparse matrix-vector execution, symmetric-memory sparse communication, and a preconditioned BiCGStab solver for the pressure Poisson equation.
result: The framework preserves the accuracy and versatility of the original ViCar3D solver while achieving substantial acceleration and scalability for simulations with complex moving and deforming immersed boundaries.
conclusion: This work extends sharp-interface immersed boundary methods to extreme-scale computational fluid dynamics on multi-GPU systems, but it has no direct connection to quantum information theory, quantum thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Heterogeneous Hegselmann-Krause Dynamics Need Not Converge
authors: Behrouz Touri S. Rasoul Etesami
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20783v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give a six-agent counterexample to convergence of scalar heterogeneous Hegselmann--Krause dynamics.
tldr: The paper gives a six-agent counterexample showing that scalar heterogeneous Hegselmann-Krause opinion dynamics need not converge.
motivation: Convergence properties of bounded-confidence opinion dynamics are important for understanding consensus formation, and heterogeneous confidence bounds may alter known convergence guarantees.
method: The authors construct an explicit six-agent counterexample for scalar heterogeneous Hegselmann-Krause dynamics.
result: The example demonstrates that heterogeneous Hegselmann-Krause dynamics can fail to converge, unlike some homogeneous or previously studied cases.
conclusion: Convergence is not guaranteed in heterogeneous Hegselmann-Krause dynamics, so additional assumptions are needed for convergence results.

title: A Nonstandard Fractional Jacobi Pseudospectral Method For Weakly Regular Right-sided Caputo Terminal Problems
authors: Ibrahem G. Ameen, Magda Hammad, Mohsen Razzaghi, Mahmoud A. Zaky
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20829v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Right-sided fractional differential equations arising in terminal value problems present substantial analytical and numerical challenges due to their intrinsic nonlocal structure and the presence of weak algebraic-type singularities near the terminal point. These singular behaviors significantly degrade the performance of classical finite-difference, finite-element, and standard spectral methods, which typically rely on smoothness assumptions that break down in the fractional setting. In this work, we develop a comprehensive fractional pseudospectral framework specifically designed for nonlinear right-sided Caputo terminal value systems. The proposed method employs a versatile family of nonstandard fractional Jacobi basis functions whose endpoint-weighted structure naturally reflects the asymptotic behavior of right-sided fractional operators. This construction enables the accurate approximation of solutions with limited regularity near the terminal point, without requiring smoothing transformations or mesh grading. We establish the existence and uniqueness of the discrete numerical solution and derive rigorous convergence estimates that faithfully capture the inherent singularity structure of the problem. A series of numerical experiments validates the theoretical developments and demonstrates that the proposed approach delivers high-order accuracy and superior resolution of terminal-layer behavior compared with traditional spectral techniques. The resulting framework provides an efficient and reliable computational tool for challenging nonlinear fractional terminal value systems characterized by weak solution regularity.
tldr: Develops a nonstandard fractional Jacobi pseudospectral method for nonlinear right-sided Caputo terminal value problems with weak singularities near the terminal point.
motivation: Classical finite-difference, finite-element, and standard spectral methods degrade for right-sided fractional terminal value problems because of nonlocal structure and weak algebraic singularities that break smoothness assumptions.
method: Introduces a family of nonstandard fractional Jacobi basis functions with endpoint-weighted structure to approximate limited-regularity solutions without smoothing transformations or mesh grading, and establishes existence, uniqueness, and convergence estimates.
result: Numerical experiments show high-order accuracy and superior resolution of terminal-layer behavior compared with traditional spectral techniques.
conclusion: The framework provides an efficient and reliable computational tool for challenging nonlinear fractional terminal value systems with weak solution regularity.

title: Analog Rf Computing For Integrated Data And Ai Flows Over Wireless Networks
authors: Vincent W. S. Wong Wentao Yu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20841v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many resource-constrained edge devices require artificial intelligence (AI) services but are not powerful enough to store or execute neural networks (NNs). Analog radio frequency (RF) computing addresses this limitation by letting a base station (BS) multicast a waveform encoding NN weights to different clients. Each client then multiplies the received weight-encoded waveform with its locally generated input-encoded waveform through a passive mixer in its RF frontend, thereby realizing the matrix-vector multiplications (MVMs) needed for AI inference with an extremely low power and memory requirement. This can enable telecom operators to provide AI inference services to the edge devices connected to their networks. In practice, however, this multicast AI flow must share the spectrum, power, and spatial resources with other data flows. This paper considers a multi-user multiple-input multiple-output (MU-MIMO) downlink scenario and studies the resulting relative aggregate data rate reduction from integrating the multicast AI flow with the unicast data flows. We formulate a joint beamforming problem for the data and AI flows to maximize the aggregate data rate subject to computing accuracy, client energy, total power, and hardware-related constraints. We develop a weighted minimum mean-square error (WMMSE)-based algorithm to solve the problem. Numerical results based on 3rd Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) channels show that the relative aggregate data rate reduction from integrating an AI flow with data flows is below 5% in representative settings. This indicates that telecom operators can use analog RF computing to provide edge AI services while providing data communication services simultaneously.
tldr: This paper studies integrating a multicast analog RF computing (AI) flow with unicast data flows in a MU-MIMO downlink, formulating a joint beamforming problem to maximize aggregate data rate and solving it with a WMMSE-based algorithm.
motivation: Resource-constrained edge devices cannot store or execute neural networks, and analog RF computing via waveform multicast plus passive mixing enables low-power AI inference at the edge, but the AI flow must share spectrum, power, and spatial resources with conventional data flows.
method: A multi-user MIMO downlink scenario is modeled where the base station multicasts NN-weight-encoded waveforms and clients perform matrix-vector multiplications via passive mixers; a joint beamforming optimization subjects to computing accuracy, client energy, total power, and hardware constraints is solved using a WMMSE-based algorithm over 3GPP channels.
result: Numerical results based on 3GPP channels show the relative aggregate data rate reduction from integrating an AI flow with data flows is below 5% in representative settings.
conclusion: Telecom operators can use analog RF computing to provide edge AI inference services while simultaneously delivering data communication services with minimal rate loss.

title: Emergence Of Partially Hyperbolic Skew-products With Circle Fibers
authors: Mauricio Poletti Odylo Costa
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20946v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the statistical behavior of partially hyperbolic skew-products over Axiom A diffeomorphisms using emergence. Generically, these systems satisfy the Palis conjecture: they have a finite number of physical measures whose basins together have full volume. In particular, for Lebesgue almost every point, the empirical measures converge to one of finitely many physical measures. We study the non-generic case and prove that, even when the sequence of empirical measures may have uncountably many accumulation points, these systems have low emergence.
tldr: The paper studies statistical properties of partially hyperbolic skew-products with circle fibers over Axiom A diffeomorphisms, focusing on the emergence of physical measures.
motivation: The authors aim to understand the statistical behavior of these systems in both generic and non-generic cases, particularly regarding the convergence of empirical measures and the Palis conjecture.
method: They use the concept of emergence to analyze the number of accumulation points of empirical measures and the basins of physical measures.
result: Generically, these systems have finitely many physical measures whose basins cover full volume; non-generically, despite possibly uncountably many accumulation points, the systems exhibit low emergence.
conclusion: The work shows that partially hyperbolic skew-products with circle fibers have constrained statistical complexity, supporting low emergence even in non-generic settings.

title: On The Last-Iterate Convergence Of Clipped Gradient Methods
authors: Zijian Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21026v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In stochastic (strongly) convex optimization, establishing last-iterate convergence guarantees for first-order methods has recently garnered increasing attention, as this not only deepens the theoretical understanding of these algorithms but also aligns more closely with practice. Notably, people have demonstrated that one of the most famous, simple, and popular methods, Stochastic Gradient Descent ([MATH]), provably achieves last-iterate convergence. However, the existing results may have limited applicability, since they typically rely on strong conditions on the gradient noise (e.g., an exponentially decaying tail) rather than the more realistic heavy-tailed noise. Unfortunately, when faced with heavy-tailed noise, [MATH] is known to exhibit undesirable behavior or even fail to converge. To address the challenge of heavy-tailed noise, people have proposed [MATH], an algorithm that combines [MATH] with a simple mechanism, gradient clipping. Although [MATH] performs well in practice, its last-iterate convergence property remains highly underexplored. In this work, we prove the first optimal last-iterate rates in high probability for [MATH] under heavy-tailed noise, thereby closing a gap in the literature.
tldr: The paper proves optimal high-probability last-iterate convergence rates for clipped stochastic gradient methods under heavy-tailed gradient noise.
motivation: Last-iterate convergence guarantees for first-order methods are theoretically and practically important, but existing results for SGD rely on unrealistic light-tailed noise assumptions. Under heavy-tailed noise, SGD can fail to converge, motivating analysis of gradient clipping.
method: The authors analyze the clipped SGD (ClipSG) algorithm and derive high-probability last-iterate convergence rates in the stochastic (strongly) convex setting with heavy-tailed noise.
result: They establish the first optimal last-iterate convergence rates in high probability for clipped gradient methods under heavy-tailed noise, closing a gap in the optimization literature.
conclusion: Clipped gradient methods provably achieve optimal last-iterate convergence even under heavy-tailed noise, extending theoretical guarantees beyond the restrictive light-tailed regime.

title: Galerkin Finite Element Method For Time Fractional Diffusion-wave Equations With Constant Time Delay
authors: Xuan Li, Kaile Qiu, Chaobao Huang, Weiping Bu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21056v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper studies numerical methods for the time fractional diffusion-wave equations with the constant delay. Using a symmetric fractional-order reduction technique and introducing the auxiliary variable [MATH], we reformulate the original problem as an equivalent coupled system and for the first time carry out a rigorous regularity analysis of [MATH]. Based on the symmetric graded time mesh, the coupled problem is discretised by the [MATH] scheme in time and a standard finite element method in space, and the stability result of the developed fully discrete finite element scheme is established by means of a discrete fractional Gr\"onwall inequality. Furthermore, we derive a new comparison principle and reconstruct a new barrier function on each interval [MATH], [MATH] according to the properties of the symmetric graded mesh. Based on the new barrier function, we obtain new relevant properties, which lead to a novel and crucial stability property for the discrete fractional operator. Combining the obtained local truncation error in time gives a local error estimate for the fully discrete finite element scheme, which shows that our convergence result provides a unified framework that seamlessly encompasses both pointwise-in-time error estimates on uniform meshes and global-in-time error estimates on symmetrical graded meshes. Numerical experiments confirm the theoretical results.
tldr: The paper develops and analyzes a Galerkin finite element method for time fractional diffusion-wave equations with constant time delay, using symmetric fractional-order reduction and graded meshes.
motivation: Time fractional diffusion-wave equations with delay are important for modeling anomalous diffusion and viscoelasticity, but rigorous numerical analysis and stability results were lacking.
method: The authors reformulate the problem as a coupled system, discretize with a symmetric graded time mesh and finite element method in space, and establish stability using a new comparison principle and barrier function.
result: They prove stability and local error estimates for the fully discrete scheme, with a unified convergence framework covering both uniform and symmetric graded meshes, confirmed by numerical experiments.
conclusion: The proposed method provides a rigorous numerical framework for time fractional diffusion-wave equations with delay, with theoretical guarantees and practical applicability.

title: Conditional Limit Laws For Open Intermittent Dynamics
authors: Yaofeng Su Can Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21175v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We obtain conditional limit theorems for open intermittent Liverani-Saussol-Vaienti (LSV) maps.
