Unlike the results of closed systems (e.g. some uniformly expanding maps), we obtain a new limit distribution, which is different from the Gaussian law or the stable law, for both "regular" and singular observables.
tldr: The paper derives conditional limit laws for open intermittent Liverani-Saussol-Vaienti maps, yielding a new limit distribution for regular and singular observables.
motivation: To understand statistical properties of open intermittent dynamical systems, extending limit theorem results beyond closed uniformly expanding maps.
method: They analyze conditional limit theorems for open LSV maps and obtain a new limit distribution for both regular and singular observables.
result: A new non-Gaussian, non-stable limit distribution is found for both regular and singular observables in the open intermittent setting.
conclusion: The work advances dynamical systems and ergodic theory but has no direct connection to quantum information, information thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Observability As A Constraint Qualification For A Nonsmooth Bilevel PDE-constrained Problem
authors: Christian Clason, Alberto Dom\'inguez Corella, Jyrki Jauhiainen
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21377v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Motivated by experiment design for parameter identification in image reconstruction, we analyze a bilevel control problem involving sparse inversion at the lower level. Qualified optimality conditions in explicit multiplier form are shown to hold under either an observability condition for a coupled system or the Lebesgue nullity of a contact set induced by the lower-level adjoint variable. We prove that these conditions are independent of one another and that they cannot, in general, both be omitted. The approach is based on the characterization of local first-order geometric objects (tangent and normal cones) associated with a set of lifted constraints. Based on the resulting optimality conditions, we formulate a reduced gradient method and illustrate it through numerical experiments.
tldr: The paper derives qualified optimality conditions for a nonsmooth bilevel PDE-constrained optimization problem motivated by experiment design in image reconstruction, using observability conditions and nullity of a contact set as constraint qualifications.
motivation: Bilevel problems with sparse inversion at the lower level arise in optimal experiment design for parameter identification in image reconstruction, but standard constraint qualifications often fail in this nonsmooth setting.
method: The authors characterize local first-order geometric objects (tangent and normal cones) for a set of lifted constraints to obtain explicit multiplier-form optimality conditions, then propose a reduced gradient method validated by numerical experiments.
result: Qualified optimality conditions hold under either an observability condition for the coupled system or Lebesgue nullity of a contact set induced by the lower-level adjoint variable, and the two conditions are proven independent and not jointly omissible.
conclusion: The work provides a rigorous nonsmooth bilevel optimality framework with practical algorithmic consequences for PDE-constrained inverse problems.

title: An Alternating Minimization Algorithm For Federated Sparse Orthogonal Nonnegative Matrix Factorization
authors: Yanjiao Zhu, Xianchao Xiu, Yongyang Xiong, Wanquan Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21455v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we develop an alternating minimization algorithm for federated sparse orthogonal nonnegative matrix factorization (ONMF) with emphases on controlling client drift. To reduce communication frequency, clients perform multiple local updates between communication rounds, biasing updates toward their respective local objectives and giving rise to client drift, particularly under data heterogeneity. In federated sparse ONMF, global nonsmooth regularization further complicates drift control, as proximal mappings generally do not commute with averaging. To address these challenges, we develop an effective optimization algorithm that introduces variable splitting to decouple proximal operator evaluation from communication, allowing clients to handle joint sparsity regularization locally. In addition, the algorithm incorporates a correction term into the local gradients to adjust the update directions and mitigate client drift. We theoretically establish that the proposed algorithm achieves sublinear convergence to a bounded residual error under some mild conditions. Numerical experiments demonstrate favorable convergence behavior on a synthetic dataset and competitive clustering performance on real-world multi-view datasets.
tldr: The paper proposes an alternating minimization algorithm for federated sparse orthogonal nonnegative matrix factorization that controls client drift via variable splitting and gradient correction.
motivation: Federated sparse ONMF suffers from client drift due to multiple local updates and data heterogeneity, and nonsmooth regularization complicates drift control because proximal mappings do not commute with averaging.
method: The algorithm introduces variable splitting to decouple proximal operator evaluation from communication and adds a correction term to local gradients to mitigate client drift.
result: The authors prove sublinear convergence to a bounded residual error under mild conditions and show favorable convergence and competitive clustering performance on synthetic and multi-view datasets.
conclusion: The proposed federated optimization method effectively handles sparse ONMF with improved communication efficiency and drift control, though it lies outside quantum information research.

title: Algorithms For Computing Basins Of Attraction Associated With A Rational Self-map Of The Hopf Fibration Based On Lyapunov Exponents
authors: V. \'alvarez-Aparicio, J. M. Garc\'{\i}a-Calcines, L. J. Hern\'andez-Paricio, M. T. Rivas-Rodr\'{\i}guez
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21516v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The objective of this work is twofold. One, we develop a theory of iteration for complex rational functions so that the problems of overflow and indeterminacy caused by null, or almost null, denominators can be avoided when developing implementations. Second, we present easily implementable methods that allow the calculation of attracting cycles as well as the graphical representation of their basins of attraction. In order to deal with our first goal, we work with homogeneous complex coordinates, and we take the complex projective line as a model, which is expressed as a quotient of the 3-sphere through the Hopf fibration. An irreducible representation of a rational function can now be presented as a Hopf fibration endomorphism. As well as our second goal is concerned, we use Lyapunov functions and exponents to calculate the cycles associated with endomorphisms and to graphically represent the corresponding basins of attraction. We point out that our algorithms are based on the calculation of a finite set of non-negative real constants, and their calculation does not depend on the previous determination of the fixed points or attracting cycles.
tldr: This paper develops algorithms for computing basins of attraction of rational self-maps on the complex projective line using homogeneous coordinates, the Hopf fibration, and Lyapunov exponents.
motivation: The authors aim to avoid overflow and indeterminacy in numerical implementations when iterating complex rational functions with null or near-null denominators, and to provide easily implementable methods for visualizing attracting cycles and their basins.
method: They model the complex projective line as the quotient of the 3-sphere via the Hopf fibration, represent irreducible rational functions as Hopf fibration endomorphisms, and use Lyapunov functions and exponents to compute cycles and basins based on a finite set of non-negative real constants.
result: The proposed algorithms can calculate attracting cycles and graphically represent their basins of attraction without prior determination of fixed points or attracting cycles.
conclusion: The work offers a robust theoretical and practical framework for iterating complex rational functions, with applications in dynamical systems and numerical analysis.

title: A Hybrid High-Order Method For Variable-exponent Leray-Lions Problems With Convergence Under Minimal Regularity
authors: Romain Mottier Andr\'e Harnist
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21598v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider a homogeneous Dirichlet problem for nonlinear elliptic equations in divergence form with Leray--Lions fluxes of variable growth. The class includes the variable-exponent [MATH]-Laplacian and regularized Carreau--Yasuda-type laws. We propose and analyze a Hybrid High-Order (HHO) discretization on general polytopal meshes, a hybrid nonconforming method based on cell and face polynomial unknowns of arbitrary degree. We develop a variable-exponent polynomial and discrete functional toolkit centered on a mean-exponent norm equivalence, together with inverse, trace, Poincar\'e--Wirtinger, Sobolev--Poincar\'e, discrete Lebesgue embedding, interpolation, and compactness estimates adapted to HHO unknowns. We then establish well-posedness of the nonlinear discrete problem and convergence without assuming additional regularity of the exact solution beyond its natural energy space. The discrete potential converges strongly in every uniformly subcritical variable-exponent Lebesgue space, the reconstructed gradient converges strongly in the natural variable-exponent space, and the stabilization energy vanishes. Numerical experiments in two, three, and four space dimensions confirm convergence for singular solutions and for exponent fields ranging from close to [MATH] up to [MATH]. Quantitative a priori error estimates for the same method are derived in a companion paper.
tldr: The paper develops and analyzes a Hybrid High-Order discretization for nonlinear elliptic Leray-Lions problems with variable exponent growth on general polytopal meshes.
motivation: The goal is to provide a robust numerical method for variable-exponent Leray-Lions equations, including the variable-exponent p-Laplacian and Carreau-Yasuda-type laws, without requiring extra regularity of the exact solution.
method: The authors introduce a Hybrid High-Order method based on cell and face polynomial unknowns, along with a variable-exponent polynomial and discrete functional toolkit centered on mean-exponent norm equivalence, and derive inverse, trace, Poincare-Wirtinger, Sobolev-Poincare, embedding, interpolation, and compactness estimates.
result: They establish well-posedness of the nonlinear discrete problem and prove convergence under minimal regularity: the discrete potential converges strongly in uniformly subcritical variable-exponent Lebesgue spaces, the reconstructed gradient converges strongly in the natural variable-exponent space, and the stabilization energy vanishes.
conclusion: Numerical experiments in two, three, and four dimensions confirm convergence for singular solutions and for exponent fields ranging from close to 1 up to large values.

title: Empirical Evaluation Of Machine Learning For Cloud Cryptojacking Detection: Effects Of Preprocessing And Evaluation Protocols
authors: Nelly Elsayed Amitabh Chakravorty
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20658v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has been widely applied to cloud cryptojacking detection. Classical machine learning models remain among the most widely used approaches for cloud cryptojacking detection. This paper presents an empirical evaluation of six widely used classical machine learning models for AI-based cloud cryptojacking detection under different preprocessing and evaluation settings. Because no public cloud-native cryptojacking dataset is currently available, experiments were conducted using two publicly available proxy datasets, DS2OS and NSL-KDD. The evaluated models include Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, Gradient Boosting, Decision Tree, and K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN). Experimental results show that preprocessing choices and evaluation protocols have a measurable impact on model performance. On DS2OS, removing identifier-related features reduced the accuracy of most models to approximately 96%, while KNN achieved higher accuracy with lower attack recall. On NSL-KDD, models obtained 77 to 80\% accuracy on the official test set containing unseen attack types, compared with above 99.5% under a random train-test split. Attack-class precision, recall, and Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) further provide complementary insights into classifier performance beyond overall accuracy. The results provide an empirical comparison of commonly used classical machine learning models under consistent experimental settings and offer insights into how preprocessing, dataset selection, and evaluation methodology influence reported performance.
tldr: An empirical benchmark of six classical machine learning models for cloud cryptojacking detection, showing how preprocessing and evaluation protocols strongly affect reported performance.
motivation: Cloud cryptojacking—unauthorized cryptocurrency mining in cloud environments—is a growing security threat, and classical ML models are widely used for detection, yet results are often reported inconsistently across datasets and evaluation schemes.
method: The authors evaluate six classical ML models (Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, Gradient Boosting, Decision Tree, KNN) on two proxy datasets (DS2OS and NSL-KDD) under varying preprocessing choices and evaluation protocols, including random splits versus official test sets with unseen attack types.
result: Performance is highly sensitive to protocol: NSL-KDD accuracy drops from above 99.5% under random splits to 77–80% on the official test set, and on DS2OS removing identifier-related features reduces most models to roughly 96% accuracy, with KNN trading higher accuracy for lower attack recall.
conclusion: Preprocessing, dataset selection, and evaluation methodology materially influence reported cryptojacking-detection performance, so comparisons should rely on complementary metrics such as attack-class precision, recall, and MCC rather than accuracy alone.

title: Infuse: A Unified Surface Benchmark For Indirect Prompt Injection In Agentic Systems
authors: Thuy Dung Nguyen, Jingyi Guo, Rana Seda Dubauskas, Sreepriya Damuluru, Taylor T. Johnson, Kevin Leach
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20776v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM-based agents increasingly execute long-horizon, end-to-end workflows involving shell commands, code modification, dependency installation, and interaction with remote services. This growing autonomy expands their exposure to indirect prompt injection (IPI), where adversarial instructions embedded in external content are interpreted as legitimate task directives. Existing evaluations, however, often focus on isolated malicious strings, single-step tool calls, or narrowly scoped agent configurations. We introduce INFUSE, an end-to-end benchmark for evaluating IPI throughout the lifecycle of long-horizon agent workflows. INFUSE comprises 40 realistic tasks and a structured taxonomy of 56 attack scenarios spanning five threat categories. Attacks are injected through realistic interaction surfaces encountered during task execution, extending evaluation beyond attacks placed only in initial prompts or isolated tool interactions. We evaluate 19 LLMs from the GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama, Gemma, and Qwen families, producing 41,824 adversarial trajectories (26,220 without defenses) and 720 benign reference runs. Across the benchmark, mean attack success reaches 19.6% under LLM-based evaluation and 15.4% under heuristic verification, with per-model ASR-L ranging from 3.2% to 41.9%. Existing guard models provide limited protection, while prompt-level instructional hardening reduces mean attack success from 58.2% to 14.3%, revealing substantial but model-dependent security-utility trade-offs. Our code is available at [URL].
tldr: INFUSE is an end-to-end benchmark for evaluating indirect prompt injection (IPI) across the full lifecycle of long-horizon LLM agent workflows.
motivation: Increasingly autonomous LLM agents executing shell commands, code edits, and remote service interactions are exposed to adversarial instructions embedded in external content, yet existing evaluations focus on isolated malicious strings or single-step tool calls.
method: The benchmark comprises 40 realistic tasks and a taxonomy of 56 attack scenarios across five threat categories, with attacks injected through realistic interaction surfaces, and it evaluates 19 LLMs across six model families.
result: Mean attack success reaches 19.6% under LLM-based evaluation and 15.4% under heuristic verification, with per-model ASR-L ranging from 3.2% to 41.9%; guard models offer limited protection while prompt-level hardening reduces ASR from 58.2% to 14.3%.
conclusion: The work reveals substantial, model-dependent security-utility trade-offs and provides a unified surface benchmark for IPI in agentic systems.

title: Automating Observable Closure Analysis For Graph Transformation Models With MolFoundry
authors: Marcel Friedrichs, Addie Jordon, Juri Kol\v{c}\'{a}k, Daniel Merkle
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20821v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Graph transformations model changing systems, with applications in software, biology and chemistry, among others. We introduce MolFoundry, a graph transformation framework, and present a workflow for observable analysis that tracks the dynamics of local patterns through rule composition. Analysing rule compositions avoids the need to enumerate a potentially infinite state space. Building on rule-algebraic stochastic rewriting, MolFoundry's kernel composes rules with nested application conditions, including missing-edge constraints. Given rules, rates and query patterns, the algorithms iteratively identify auxiliary pattern counts and search for closure. Using exact counting identities supplied by graph-family backends, successful searches yield closed ordinary differential equations for average counts or, with justified individual jumps, finite event models describing joint changes and rates. We evaluate conditional composition and automated discovery of auxiliary observables against published calculations and independent rule application. Applications to aldol addition, copolymerization and chlorination show how the framework yields quantitative predictions directly from molecular graph rules.
tldr: MolFoundry automates observable closure analysis for graph transformation models by composing rules to derive ODEs or finite event models for pattern counts.
motivation: Graph transformation models of changing systems often require analyzing potentially infinite state spaces, which is computationally infeasible.
method: The framework uses rule-algebraic stochastic rewriting with nested application conditions, iteratively identifying auxiliary pattern counts and searching for closure using exact counting identities from graph-family backends.
result: Successful searches yield closed ordinary differential equations for average counts or finite event models, validated against published calculations and applied to aldol addition, copolymerization, and chlorination.
conclusion: MolFoundry provides a general workflow for quantitative predictions directly from molecular graph rules, avoiding state-space enumeration.

title: GhostLock: Learning-Assisted Blind Gps Signal Nullification Without Victim-Side Information
authors: Khalil Ahmad, Omar Ansari, Mohsin Kamal, Asif Iqbal, Muhammad Naveed Aman
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20831v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Global Positioning System (GPS) provides critical positioning, navigation, and timing (PNT) services for numerous safety- and mission-critical applications, making it an attractive target for physical-layer attacks. While GPS spoofing and jamming have been extensively studied, GPS Signal Nullification (GSN)-a physical-layer attack that suppresses authentic satellite signals through destructive interference prior to acquisition-remains largely unexplored. Existing wireless signal nullification techniques target conventional communication systems and typically require victim-side information, such as channel estimates or synchronization parameters, making them impractical for GPS. Furthermore, many GPS spoofing defenses assume authentic satellite signals remain available as trusted references, an assumption invalidated by GSN. To address this gap, we present GhostLock, a learning-assisted blind GSN framework requiring only an approximate target location estimate. GhostLock integrates a Blind Adaptive Filter (BAF) with a deep learning-based synchronization module to generate and align an anti-signal using only the attacker's locally received GPS signal, eliminating the need for victim-side observations. We implement GhostLock on a real-time software-defined radio (SDR) platform using GPS-SDR-SIM and GNU Radio. Experimental results demonstrate successful suppression of GPS signal acquisition, establishing the feasibility of blind GSN and motivating new detection and mitigation techniques for this emerging GPS threat model.
tldr: GhostLock introduces a learning-assisted blind GPS signal nullification attack that suppresses authentic satellite signals using only an approximate target location and the attacker's locally received signal.
motivation: GPS is critical for positioning, navigation, and timing, but GPS Signal Nullification (GSN) remains largely unexplored compared to spoofing and jamming, and existing nullification techniques require victim-side information.
method: The framework combines a Blind Adaptive Filter (BAF) with a deep learning-based synchronization module to generate and align an anti-signal, implemented on a real-time SDR platform using GPS-SDR-SIM and GNU Radio.
result: Experimental results demonstrate successful suppression of GPS signal acquisition without victim-side observations, establishing the feasibility of blind GSN.
conclusion: The work exposes a new physical-layer GPS threat model and motivates the development of detection and mitigation techniques against blind signal nullification.

title: Screwtape: Adversarial Transcript Editing For Monitor Red-Teaming
authors: Tyler Tracy Gosha Kozhevnikov
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20941v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present Screwtape, a pipeline that converts real agent transcripts into attacks that evade action-only monitors. An LLM attacker edits a transcript so that the agent causes a specified harm, such as leaking an API key or spawning an unmonitored agent. The edited actions are never executed, so we use an LLM verifier to reject attacks that are inconsistent with the original transcript or below a severity bar. The attacker revises the edit until the monitor no longer flags it. We applied Screwtape to 94 Claude Code and Codex transcripts from Redwood Research staff, optimizing against our own monitors. Across 252 runs, it produced 35 attacks that passed the verifier and evaded these monitors. Six of them, confirmed valid by human review, also evaded a held-out monitor provided by a frontier developer. We therefore demonstrate that a red-teamer without access to a developer's infrastructure can find confirmed failures of the developer's monitor. We expect to find more attacks when the pipeline runs inside the developer's infrastructure, with frontier attacker models that lack refusal safeguards and direct optimization against the production monitor. Developers can use these attacks to fix monitor blind spots, and evaluators can use them as counterexamples to safety claims about the monitor.
tldr: Screwtape is an adversarial transcript-editing pipeline that red-teams action-only LLM monitors by modifying real agent transcripts to evade detection while preserving plausible harmful actions.
motivation: Action-only monitors for LLM agents can miss harmful behavior, and developers need red-teaming methods to find monitor blind spots without access to production infrastructure.
method: An LLM attacker edits agent transcripts to induce a specified harm, while an LLM verifier rejects inconsistent or low-severity attacks; the attacker iterates until the monitor no longer flags the edited transcript.
result: Across 252 runs on 94 Claude Code and Codex transcripts, Screwtape produced 35 attacks that passed verification and evaded in-house monitors, with six human-confirmed attacks also evading a held-out frontier-developer monitor.
conclusion: External red-teamers can find confirmed monitor failures, and these adversarial transcripts can help developers harden monitors and challenge safety claims.

title: Page404: Breaking Gpu Isolation Through Hardware-assisted Page Migration
authors: Ravan Nazaraliyev, Yicheng Zhang, Nael Abu-Ghazaleh
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20962v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: NVIDIA's Grace Hopper (GH200) superchip represents a new generation of heterogeneous computing, tightly integrating a 72-core Arm-based CPU with a Hopper GPU on a single module via a high-bandwidth, cache-coherent interconnect. By eliminating the conventional PCIe bottleneck for CPU-GPU data movement, this design establishes a unified memory domain that scales to the capacities demanded by generative AI and high-performance computing (HPC) workloads. The architecture also introduces hardware-assisted page migration: driven by access counters, the system dynamically promotes frequently accessed pages from host CPU memory to GPU DRAM to improve memory locality. We study the security of this emerging architecture against new side- and covert-channel attacks targeting its page migration support. We analyze counter-driven migration across both the hardware mechanisms and the UVM driver's interrupt-handling pipeline, and identify two side-channel vulnerabilities: one rooted in the shared structure of access counters, and the other in the driver's response to migration interrupts. We further show that both channels are exploitable across Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) partitions, a feature intended to provide strong, hardware-enforced isolation between co-located tenants. Using proof-of-concept attacks, we build covert channels that reach roughly 8,500 bits per second through eviction-based signaling and 8,100 bits per second through migration-delay-based signaling across MIG instances. The interrupt-based channel also fingerprints inference workloads across distinct large language models (LLMs) and CPU SPEC2017 benchmarks, and estimates the prompt length processed during LLM inference with high accuracy. These results expose a security gap in hardware-managed heterogeneous memory systems and call into question the isolation guarantees of current MIG-enabled multi-tenant GPU deployments.
tldr: The paper identifies and exploits side-channel vulnerabilities in NVIDIA Grace Hopper's hardware-assisted page migration to break GPU isolation across MIG partitions.
motivation: Heterogeneous computing architectures with unified memory and hardware page migration introduce new security risks that may undermine isolation guarantees in multi-tenant GPU deployments.
method: The authors analyze access-counter-driven page migration and the UVM driver's interrupt pipeline, then build proof-of-concept covert channels and side-channel attacks across MIG instances.
result: They achieve covert channel bandwidths of ~8,500 bps via eviction signaling and ~8,100 bps via migration delay, and fingerprint LLM inference workloads and estimate prompt lengths with high accuracy.
conclusion: The findings expose a security gap in hardware-managed heterogeneous memory systems and challenge the isolation guarantees of current MIG-enabled multi-tenant GPU deployments.

title: Blind Watermarking Of Software Repositories Via Module Placement
authors: Khadija Mohamed, Khaled Fathy, Mamdouh Farouk, Mohamed M. Darwish
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21031v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Source-code watermarking supports provenance tracking by embedding a recoverable identifier in a software artifact. Many existing approaches encode this identifier in tokens or program syntax, exposing the watermark to transformations that modify the source text. We present PlaceMark, a blind watermarking system that encodes a payload in the placement of modules within a repository. Each eligible module is identified by its filename and top-level definition names. A secret key determines its ordered candidate destinations and its position in the reading order; the module's location within its candidate list determines the encoded symbol. Embedding relocates selected modules and updates their import references. Extraction uses the distributed repository, the key, and agreed decoding parameters, without an original copy or placement ledger. Capacity measurements on ten Python repositories yield nominal capacities of 249 to 2,166 bits in nine repositories, while one provides no placement channel. In 216 trials of the evaluated text transformations, the payload is recovered exactly. Relocation degrades recovery gradually on Django, Airflow and Salt, while on Pylint a path-based exclusion in our implementation lets relocation change carrier membership, and we measure it for an untargeted adversary and for one that concentrates its budget on the public carrier set. Changes to filenames or definition names alter the identity input and are measured separately. Exact recovery also depends on placement feasibility. The results characterize module placement as a carrier that can complement watermarks embedded in source text.
tldr: PlaceMark is a blind watermarking system that encodes a payload in the placement of modules within software repositories and extracts it without an original copy or placement ledger.
motivation: Existing source-code watermarking approaches embed identifiers in tokens or syntax, making them vulnerable to transformations that modify the source text, so a more transformation-resilient carrier is needed.
method: Each eligible module is identified by filename and top-level definition names; a secret key determines its ordered candidate destinations and reading position, and embedding relocates modules while updating import references. Extraction uses the distributed repository, the key, and agreed decoding parameters.
result: Capacity measurements on ten Python repositories yield nominal capacities of 249 to 2,166 bits in nine repositories, with exact payload recovery in 216 trials of evaluated text transformations; relocation degrades recovery gradually on some projects and depends on placement feasibility.
conclusion: Module placement can serve as a carrier that complements watermarks embedded in source text, though robustness varies with repository structure and adversary behavior.

title: Nomai: Scalable Federated Learning With Private Weights
authors: Yiyi Sun, Mushtari Sadia, Amrita Roy Chowdhury
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21059v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The twin goals of privacy-preserving federated learning (FL) -- harnessing distributed data while protecting the parties who contribute it -- demands three properties: model privacy, data privacy, and integrity. Achieving all three in a realistic deployment -- with a single coordinator and millions of users -- remains an open challenge that prior work has yet to fully resolve. We present NOMAI, the first scalable MPC-based FL system to provide all three guarantees simultaneously. NOMAI operates under an honest-majority assumption in the semi-honest model, with an extension to the malicious-with-abort setting. At its core, NOMAI combines a multi-committee MPC architecture with packed Shamir secret sharing, enabling SIMD-style secure computation that scales far beyond what monolithic n-party protocols can support. We further introduce ML-aware optimizations and new cryptographic primitives that substantially reduce per-user overhead. Our evaluation shows NOMAI is practically deployable at unprecedented scale: it reduces per-user computation to just <350 ms (semi-honest) and <700 ms (malicious) for per iteration of training MNIST, achieving three orders-of-magnitude improvements over prior work while seamlessly supporting populations of over 106 users. This demonstrates, for the first time, that MPC-based FL can meet the scale demands of real-world systems without compromising on privacy or integrity.
tldr: Nomai is a scalable secure multi-party computation based federated learning system that provides model privacy, data privacy, and integrity for millions of users.
motivation: Privacy-preserving federated learning requires simultaneously achieving model privacy, data privacy, and integrity at realistic scales, which prior work has not fully resolved.
method: The paper introduces a multi-committee MPC architecture with packed Shamir secret sharing for SIMD-style secure computation, along with ML-aware optimizations and new cryptographic primitives.
result: Nomai reduces per-user computation to under 350 ms (semi-honest) and under 700 ms (malicious) per MNIST training iteration, achieving three orders-of-magnitude improvement and supporting over 10^6 users.
conclusion: The work demonstrates that MPC-based federated learning can meet real-world scale demands without sacrificing privacy or integrity.

title: Approve What, Exactly? Effect Binding And Trusted Rendering For Agent Step-Up Authorization
authors: Sai Varun Kodathala, Prashanth Pollishetty, Jaylen Cargill
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21063v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI agents now pause for approval before they send money, delete files or email outsiders, and that approval is usually treated as a second factor. We argue it is one only when compromising the agent cannot produce it and when it names exactly what it approves, and we test both conditions. We define twelve attacks on the approval path, including decoy recipients, amount cancellation, card padding, label spoofing, enrollment squatting and threshold splitting, and run them against the Agent Payments Protocol (AP2), the Microsoft action-bound approval design and Model Context Protocol (MCP) elicitation. An audit of ten agent runtimes finds no third-party verifiable approval record, no flood limits where measurable, and post-approval argument changes in four of eight runtimes with measurable binding. As a reference defense we build ASU (Agent Step-Up), a gateway that renders the approval card from a canonical effect descriptor, has a passkey on the phone of the user sign its digest, and executes only the stored call. Tamarin proves its binding, single-use and key-level non-repudiation properties under three stated hypotheses (53 lemmas). Across 27,108 scripted trials and 609 AgentDojo attack pairs, ASU stops substitution, replay and grant stretching, and the trusted card cuts forged-narration attack success from 0.54 to 0.03. With 15 current language models as automated approvers, the trusted card raises the attack catch rate from 0.30 to 0.98, at the cost of refusing 16 percent of harmless near misses, mostly due to a placeholder artifact in our stimuli. A second device adds nothing measurable over a trusted on-host confirmation in these experiments, flooding still succeeds 0.45 to 0.60 of the time against a modeled approver, and approval cannot stop effects that policy already allows. Code, data and proofs: [URL].
tldr: The paper analyzes and improves security for AI-agent step-up authorization by binding approvals to canonical effects and using trusted rendering with passkeys, but it is outside quantum information research.
motivation: AI agents increasingly pause for human approval before sensitive actions, yet approval is often treated as a second factor without verifying what exactly is being approved or whether the agent can forge it.
method: The authors define twelve approval-path attacks, audit ten agent runtimes and protocols including AP2 and MCP elicitation, and build ASU, a gateway that renders approvals from a canonical effect descriptor, signs its digest with a phone passkey, and executes only the stored call.
result: ASU proves binding, single-use and non-repudiation properties in Tamarin under three hypotheses, stops substitution, replay and grant stretching across 27,108 scripted trials and 609 AgentDojo pairs, and raises automated-approver attack catch rate from 0.30 to 0.98.
conclusion: Trusted effect binding can substantially improve agent step-up authorization security, although flooding attacks remain effective and a second device offered no measurable benefit in these experiments.

title: Metric Dimension Is NP-complete On Graphs Of Treewidth Two
authors: Tristan Benoit
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21133v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The metric dimension of a connected graph is the least number of vertices whose distance vectors distinguish all vertices. We show that deciding whether the metric dimension of a graph is at most a given integer is NP-complete on graphs of treewidth at most two. As the problem is polynomial on trees, the graphs of treewidth one, this settles the treewidth threshold of its hardness, which was known to lie between two and twenty-four. The reduction is from satisfiability of formulas in which every literal occurs at most twice. To such a formula with [MATH] clauses and [MATH] variables it associates a graph [MATH] of treewidth at most two with [MATH] vertices, whose metric dimension is [MATH] if the formula is satisfiable and [MATH] otherwise.
tldr: The paper proves that computing the metric dimension of a graph is NP-complete even for graphs of treewidth at most two, pinning down the exact treewidth threshold for hardness.
motivation: The metric dimension problem was known to be polynomial on trees (treewidth one) and hard somewhere between treewidth two and twenty-four, leaving the true hardness threshold unresolved.
method: A reduction from satisfiability of formulas where each literal occurs at most twice constructs, from a formula with M clauses and N variables, a treewidth-2 graph whose metric dimension distinguishes satisfiable from unsatisfiable instances.
result: Deciding whether a graph's metric dimension is at most a given integer is NP-complete on graphs of treewidth at most two, settling the threshold at treewidth two.
conclusion: Graphs of treewidth two are the precise boundary between tractable and NP-hard metric dimension computation.

title: Stronger Judges Do Not See More: Deployment-Integrity Blindness In Llm Evaluation
authors: Jianchang Su, Dawei Xiang, Yifan Zhang, Wei Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21135v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM-agent evaluation reports behavioral scores but leaves the identity of the deployed runtime stack unreported. A tampered deployment that preserves evaluated outputs passes every output-only evaluator. We introduce DIB-Bench, a benchmark that measures this deployment-integrity blindness across 7,560 scored examples, six tamper types, and an evaluator ladder from regex scorers through LLM judges to GPT-5-nano. Stronger evaluators accept more tampered outputs: mean acceptance rises from 88.6% (rule-based) to 94.1% (GPT-5-nano), and a trigger-conditional tamper invisible on the evaluation suite produces 48-100% harmful outputs, rising with model capability. A PAC-style bound shows that tampers with zero output shift are undetectable from outputs at any sample size; a manifest-hash identity channel detects them with zero samples. Behavioral fingerprinting identifies the model component above chance (76.7%) but covers one of six stack components. We also propose a graded deployment-identity descriptor for evaluation reports.
tldr: The paper introduces DIB-Bench, a benchmark showing that LLM-agent evaluators are blind to deployment-stack tampering that preserves evaluated outputs, with stronger judges accepting more tampered outputs.
motivation: Behavioral evaluation of LLM agents reports scores without recording the runtime stack identity, so a tampered deployment that preserves outputs evades every output-only evaluator.
method: A benchmark of 7,560 scored examples spanning six tamper types and an evaluator ladder (regex scorers to LLM judges to GPT-5-nano), combined with a PAC-style bound and a manifest-hash identity channel.
result: Mean tamper acceptance rises from 88.6% (rule-based) to 94.1% (GPT-5-nano), trigger-conditional tampers yield 48-100% harmful outputs, and zero-output-shift tampers are provably undetectable from outputs at any sample size.
conclusion: Output-only evaluation cannot certify deployment integrity; the authors recommend a manifest-hash identity channel and a graded deployment-identity descriptor for evaluation reports.

title: ExecWeave: Cross-Layer Execution Provenance For Observable Agentic Software
authors: Meng Chang Chen Guo-Wei Wong
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21146v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agentic software invokes tools, launches processes, accesses files, and communicates with local or remote services. Application traces describe logical operations, whereas operating-system telemetry records machine activity without necessarily identifying the responsible agent action. Relating these evidence planes is a reconstruction problem: a plausible but unsupported association can assign an effect to the wrong principal. We present ExecWeave, a local-first system that materializes provider semantics and independently observed runtime events into a typed execution graph. The implementation retains separate source artifacts, distinguishes logical occurrences from repeated evidence, and records attribution, inference, and causal-status metadata. An optional command-to-process correlator emits a non-causal inferred bridge only when its bounded search yields one compatible observed process; uniqueness within this observed candidate set is not a guarantee of causal correctness. OS-observed file and network effects acquire a semantic tool or agent principal only through an observed process plus a justified command-to-process association; session-correlated file-system events do not by themselves provide that principal. Source code is available at [URL].
tldr: ExecWeave is a local-first provenance system that correlates OS telemetry with application traces into a typed execution graph for agentic software.
motivation: Agentic software spans tools, processes, files, and network services, so relating application-level logical actions to OS-observed machine events is difficult and prone to misattribution.
method: The system materializes provider semantics and runtime events into a typed graph with attribution, inference, and causal-status metadata, optionally using a bounded command-to-process correlator that emits inferred bridges only when unique within observed candidates.
result: It provides a cross-layer execution provenance reconstruction approach that separates logical occurrences from repeated evidence and explicitly marks non-causal inferred associations.
conclusion: ExecWeave improves observability and auditability for agentic software, but its contribution is in systems provenance and not quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Clean Data Can Still Carry Backdoors: Support-Persistent Backdoors For Model Reuse
authors: Junhoo Lee, Baekseung Kim, Seungyeon Kim, Nojun Kwak
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21208v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Traditional backdoor attacks inject artificial trigger patterns into training data, causing models to misclassify triggered inputs while maintaining normal behavior on clean samples. Since these artificial triggers are absent in clean datasets, standard knowledge distillation (KD) typically eliminates them, leading to the common belief that KD serves as an effective purification defense. In this paper, we propose DAR (Discover-and-Relabel), a support-persistent backdoor method that retains its behavior even after clean-data distillation. DAR identifies naturally abundant patterns in low-dimensional feature subspaces using subspace clustering and applies label-only poisoning to samples that inherently satisfy the discovered rule. At test time, the backdoor is activated by locally modifying the corresponding subspace of the target images. By instantiating spatial and frequency operators, DAR achieves attack accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art backdoor attacks in ImageNet classification and CLIP-based prompt tuning. Notably, DAR keeps attack success above 96% after clean KD and remains defense-resistant in practice. Project page: [URL].
tldr: The paper proposes DAR, a support-persistent backdoor attack that survives clean-data knowledge distillation by exploiting naturally abundant patterns in low-dimensional feature subspaces and using label-only poisoning.
motivation: Traditional backdoor attacks rely on artificial triggers absent from clean data, so knowledge distillation (KD) is widely believed to purify them. This work challenges that assumption by showing clean data itself can carry persistent backdoors.
method: DAR uses subspace clustering to identify naturally occurring patterns in feature subspaces, poisons only labels of samples that inherently satisfy the discovered rule, and activates the backdoor at test time by locally modifying the target image's corresponding subspace via spatial or frequency operators.
result: DAR achieves attack accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art backdoor attacks on ImageNet classification and CLIP-based prompt tuning, maintains over 96% attack success after clean KD, and remains defense-resistant in practice.
conclusion: Clean-data distillation is not a reliable defense against backdoors, and support-persistent attacks pose a serious threat to model reuse and sharing.

title: Trigger Value Selection In Clean-Label Malware Backdoors: An Effectiveness-Detectability Analysis
authors: Tri Budi Sabdo Utomo, Kazushi Okamoto, Koki Karube, Kei Harada, Atsushi Shibata
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21269v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Clean-label backdoor poisoning is a threat to machine learning-based malware classifiers because poisoned samples can be inserted into training data without changing their labels. Previous explanation-guided attacks mainly focus on selecting important trigger features, but the values assigned to these features can also affect the attack behavior. In this paper, we study trigger value selection as an independent design factor in clean-label backdoor attacks against feature-based malware classifiers. We evaluate several value-selection strategies on EMBER 2018 and a Win64 PE subset of EMBER 2024 using LightGBM classifiers. We compare rare-value, SHAP-based, frequency-bounded, co-occurrence-aware, and quantile-based selectors under random and distribution-based malware-similar benign sampling. The results show that aggressive selectors such as MinPopulation and CountAbsSHAP can achieve high attack success rate, especially under distribution-based sampling, but they are also easier to detect by sanitization methods such as Isolation Forest. In contrast, selectors such as CorrCountAbsSHAP and Quantile95 can reduce poison recall while keeping useful attack effectiveness. These findings show that trigger value selection is not merely an implementation detail, but an important design choice that shapes the effectiveness and detectability profile of clean-label malware backdoor attacks.
tldr: This paper studies how trigger value selection affects the effectiveness and detectability of clean-label backdoor attacks on feature-based malware classifiers.
motivation: Clean-label backdoor poisoning poses a threat to machine learning-based malware classifiers, and prior work has mainly focused on selecting important trigger features rather than the values assigned to them.
method: The authors evaluate rare-value, SHAP-based, frequency-bounded, co-occurrence-aware, and quantile-based value-selection strategies on EMBER 2018 and a Win64 PE subset of EMBER 2024 using LightGBM classifiers under random and distribution-based benign sampling.
result: Aggressive selectors such as MinPopulation and CountAbsSHAP achieve high attack success rates, especially under distribution-based sampling, but are more easily detected by sanitization methods like Isolation Forest, while CorrCountAbsSHAP and Quantile95 reduce poison recall with useful attack effectiveness.
conclusion: Trigger value selection is an important design choice in clean-label malware backdoor attacks, shaping both effectiveness and detectability.

title: When Rotation Bounds Nothing: Streaming Image Classifiers To Field Nodes Under Physical Capture
authors: Ran Dubin Daniel Gilkarov
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21276v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Field nodes run image classifiers locally, exposing a first-class asset, the trained model, to theft. Trusted-execution enclaves, collaborative-inference splits, and encrypted storage assume the device owner is the adversary from deployment. Here the operator owns the node, and an adversary seizing it reads only what cold-boot capture finds resident. One answer stores nothing: a chunkable multi-exit model streams into volatile memory, rotating to bound residency. We characterise the capture envelope on real LTE traces across two victims of one architecture, against passive and adaptive adversaries. Neither survives a capable adversary; recovery cost alone differs. Against a from-scratch victim the uncaptured stages must be learned: the adaptive adversary gains most at shallow seizures, ends the CIFAR-10 envelope at every rotation, and stays rotation-bounded on CIFAR100, from 42.6% of usable seizures at 5 s to 86.8% at 30 s. Against the same architecture sliced from a public pretrained backbone, the adversary downloads those stages, recovering at least 90% of maximum accuracy at all depths, taking usable CIFAR-100 seizures from 0.0% to 97.3% at 5 s, given the victim's full labelled training set. Delivery-side secrecy raises a seizure's price; a public copy of the withheld stages erases it.
tldr: The paper studies streaming multi-exit image classifiers to field nodes to limit model theft from cold-boot memory captures, showing that rotation bounds exposure only against weaker adversaries and fails against adaptive recovery.
motivation: Field nodes expose trained models to physical seizure, and existing defenses often assume the device owner is trustworthy, which is not the case when the operator owns the node.
method: The authors characterize capture envelopes on real LTE traces using a chunkable multi-exit model streamed into volatile memory with rotation, testing passive and adaptive adversaries against two victims of the same architecture.
result: Neither victim survives a capable adversary; against a from-scratch victim the adaptive adversary remains rotation-bounded on CIFAR-100 (42.6% to 86.8% usable seizures from 5s to 30s), while against a pretrained-backbone victim recovery reaches at least 90% maximum accuracy at all depths.
conclusion: Rotation-based residency bounds are insufficient when an adversary can supplement seizure data with public pretrained components, and delivery-side secrecy only raises the price until a public copy of withheld stages erases the advantage.

title: Combining Llm And Dynamic Analysis For Universal Testing Of Static Application Security Testing Tools
authors: Huaien Zhang, Yu Pei, Hao Chen, Shin Hwei Tan
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21309v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Static application security testing (SAST) tools help detect potential software vulnerabilities, but they themselves contain faults undermining reliability and usability. Automated testing can address these issues, yet current techniques suffer from limited program transformation diversity and lack mechanisms to verify generated variants, leading to reduced fault detection and high manual effort. We present LLM4SAST, the first universal framework detecting faults in SAST tools using large language models and dynamic feedback. Our key insight is leveraging LLMs to understand and transform code in diverse programming languages. We design novel metamorphic relations with transformations to guide variant generation, using an LLM to produce multi-language variants that satisfy these relations. To reduce erroneous variants and identify unique faults, we propose two heuristics: dynamic-feedback-driven selection and program-differencing-based clustering. For each metamorphic relation, a report-centric test oracle detects variants that fail tests and identifies underlying faults by differentially analyzing SAST reports of the seed program and its variants. LLM4SAST identified 66 unique faults across six SAST tools, with 32 confirmed or fixed after being reported to developers, demonstrating effectiveness. The proposed heuristics eliminate 47.8% of false positives, and LLM4SAST detects 3.4 times more faults while requiring only 39.8% of the variants compared to existing approaches.
tldr: LLM4SAST is a framework that combines large language models with dynamic analysis to test static application security testing (SAST) tools for faults.
motivation: SAST tools themselves contain faults that undermine reliability, and existing automated testing approaches suffer from limited program transformation diversity and lack mechanisms to verify generated variants.
method: The framework uses LLMs to generate multi-language code variants guided by novel metamorphic relations, then applies dynamic-feedback-driven selection and program-differencing-based clustering to reduce false positives, with a report-centric oracle to detect faults.
result: LLM4SAST identified 66 unique faults across six SAST tools, with 32 confirmed or fixed by developers, eliminated 47.8% of false positives, and detected 3.4 times more faults using only 39.8% of the variants compared to existing approaches.
conclusion: LLM4SAST provides an effective universal framework for automated fault detection in SAST tools, significantly improving fault detection while reducing manual effort and false positives.

title: Learning Warm Starts For The Simplex Method From Measured Solver Cost
authors: Felix Parker, Danielle A. Ripsman, Emmett Springer, Kimia Ghobadi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20892v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Learned warm starts for the simplex method build starting bases using predictions of which variables will be basic at optimality. Prior work has shown that starting bases predicted by graph neural networks can sharply reduce iteration counts, but the time saved may fall well short of the iterations saved. On 25 classes of linear programs (LPs), we find that a strong supervised basis predictor removes two thirds of the dual simplex's iterations but only a third of its time. Two effects explain the gap: the iterations removed by a good start tend to be cheap, and closeness to an optimal basis does not rank starts by cost. We prove that two starts with equal overlap with an optimal basis and equal pivot counts can differ in linear-algebra work by a factor that grows with the square root of the number of rows. Empirically, across the starts of one LP, the pivot count explains 71% of the variance of log solve time, while the CPU instruction count explains 98.5%. We introduce CostStart, which uses supervised prediction for the basis and trains a small policy on measured instruction counts to choose, per LP, how many predicted columns to use, which algorithm and pricing rule to run, and whether to warm-start at all. On unseen LPs of the training classes, including LPs four times the training size, CostStart roughly halves the solve time relative to the solver's default start and is 1.4 to 2.2 times as fast as two published methods retrained on the same data.
tldr: The paper introduces CostStart, a learning-based warm-start method for the dual simplex method that uses measured CPU instruction counts to select predicted basic variables, algorithm, and pricing rule, roughly halving LP solve times.
motivation: Graph-neural-network predicted warm starts reduce simplex iteration counts but often fail to reduce wall-clock time, since removed iterations tend to be cheap and basis overlap does not rank starts by actual cost.
method: The authors analyze why iteration savings overstate time savings, prove that equal-overlap, equal-pivot starts can differ in linear-algebra work by a factor growing like the square root of the row count, and train a small policy on measured instruction counts to choose how many predicted columns to use and which algorithm/pricing rule to run.
result: Across 25 LP classes, a strong supervised basis predictor removes two thirds of dual simplex iterations but only a third of the time; pivot counts explain 71% of log solve-time variance while instruction counts explain 98.5%, and CostStart roughly halves solve time versus the default start and is 1.4-2.2x faster than two published methods.
conclusion: Cost-accurate, instruction-level measurement rather than iteration-based proxies is essential for turning learned warm starts into real speedups in LP solving.

title: A Geometric Criterion For The Dimension Of Morgan-Scott Spline Spaces $S_{2r}^r(\Delta_{\mathrm{MS}})$
authors: Xinyu Wu, Yi Zheng, Jiansong Deng
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21192v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish a geometric dimension criterion for spline spaces on nondegenerate standard Morgan-Scott triangulations with four distinct edge directions at each interior vertex. For every integer [MATH], concurrence of the three auxiliary lines joining corresponding interior and boundary vertices implies that [MATH] exceeds the Schumaker lower bound by one. The proof constructs a quadratic form through the six dual spoke points and uses its [MATH]th power to define a nonzero functional annihilating the image of the smoothing-cofactor map. Diener's upper bound then gives the dimension formula. We also give a matrix representation of this functional and an explicit example in the quadratic case. Combined with the known necessary conditions and the negative-branch exclusion of Deng, Feng, and Kozak, the result yields a necessary and sufficient concurrence criterion for [MATH].
tldr: The paper establishes a geometric dimension criterion for bivariate spline spaces on standard Morgan-Scott triangulations using a quadratic form built from dual spoke points.
motivation: Determining the dimension of spline spaces on triangulations is a fundamental problem in approximation theory, and Morgan-Scott triangulations are a key test case for the Schumaker lower bound.
method: The authors construct a quadratic form through six dual spoke points, use its r-th power to define a nonzero linear functional annihilating the image of the smoothing-cofactor map, and apply Diener's upper bound to obtain the dimension formula.
result: For nondegenerate standard Morgan-Scott triangulations with four distinct edge directions at each interior vertex, the concurrence of three auxiliary lines is necessary and sufficient for the spline space dimension to exceed the Schumaker lower bound by one.
conclusion: Combined with prior necessary conditions and Deng-Feng-Kozak negative-branch exclusion, the work yields a complete geometric concurrence criterion for the dimension of S_{2r}^r(Δ_MS).

title: Degree Growth Of Rational Maps With Laurent Property
authors: Melih Emin Can
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21627v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Algebraic entropy measures the exponential growth of the degrees of iterates of rational self-maps. It is introduced by Bellon and Viallet in . We study degree growth for rational maps arising from recurrences with the Laurent property, with particular emphasis on Gale--Robinson recurrences. We develop a direct method for determining the degree growth from the recurrence relation itself, reducing the problem to the study of associated max-linear, or tropical recurrences. We first obtain a closed formula for the degrees of iterates for a broad class of homogeneous quadratic Laurent recurrences. We then apply this result to the two-term Gale--Robinson family and derive an explicit quadratic growth formula with a periodic correction term. For three-term Gale--Robinson recurrences, we express the algebraic entropy in terms of the associated tropical growth rate sequence. Based on explicit computations, we formulate a conjecture for the general three-term family predicting quadratic growth with a periodic correction. We prove the conjecture for the infinite family with parameters [MATH], [MATH], and [MATH].
tldr: The paper studies degree growth and algebraic entropy for rational maps arising from Laurent recurrences, especially Gale-Robinson recurrences, using tropical/max-linear methods.
motivation: Algebraic entropy measures exponential complexity growth of iterated rational maps, and recurrences with the Laurent property provide a rich class for which growth behavior is not fully understood.
method: The authors develop a direct method reducing degree-growth questions to associated max-linear or tropical recurrences, and derive closed formulas for homogeneous quadratic Laurent recurrences and Gale-Robinson families.
result: They obtain explicit quadratic growth formulas with periodic corrections for two-term Gale-Robinson recurrences, express algebraic entropy via tropical growth rates for three-term cases, and conjecture then prove a general three-term formula for an infinite parameter family.
conclusion: The work advances the theory of algebraic entropy in integrable-like recurrence systems, but it is a pure mathematics contribution unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Accord: Schelling-Point Arbitration As A Composable Solana Primitive
authors: Fabian Schuh
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20666v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accord is an arbitration oracle on Solana. Any Solana program can create an application specific court (i.e. subaccord) and file disputes. A random jury of a specialized, stake-weighted juror pool reviews encrypted evidence and votes under commit--reveal. Jurors that vote with the final ruling earn fees and slashed stake. Jurors that vote against it lose stake. Appeals grow the panel stepwise from 3 to 31 jurors, which raises both the cost of maintaining a captured verdict and, under certain conditions, the probability of a correct majority. Each pool defines its own collateral mint and its own fee mint, so the economics can fit the application. This paper elaborates the mechanism, the incentive model, the residual trust assumptions, and the differences to the established court on EVM, Kleros. We further discuss implementation details that are Solana specific.
tldr: Accord is a Schelling-point arbitration oracle implemented as a composable Solana primitive, where stake-weighted jurors resolve disputes via commit-reveal voting and escalating appeals.
motivation: Existing decentralized arbitration systems like Kleros are built on EVM chains, and the authors aim to provide an application-specific, economically tunable dispute-resolution mechanism native to Solana.
method: The paper specifies a mechanism design in which Solana programs create subaccords, disputes are judged by randomly selected stake-weighted jurors voting under commit-reveal, with appeals expanding panels stepwise from 3 to 31 jurors and each pool defining its own collateral and fee mints.
result: The analysis details the incentive model, shows that escalating appeals raise the cost of capturing a verdict and under certain conditions raise the probability of a correct majority, and articulates residual trust assumptions and differences from Kleros.
conclusion: Accord offers a composable, Solana-specific arbitration primitive with tunable economics, though it remains outside the quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, and hybrid systems scope of interest.

title: Care-sd: Explainable Reasoning Architecture For Local Slm Self-Disclosure Analysis In Textual Data
authors: Aisvarya Adeseye, Adeyemi Adeseye, Mohammad Tahir, Jouni Isoaho
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21151v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cybersecurity interviews uncover critical security experiences, behaviors, and privacy concerns often not fully captured by conventional technical assessments. Consequently, identifying genuine self-disclosures is challenging because statements are context-dependent, categories overlap, and automated interpretations may introduce unsupported claims. Locally deployed Small Language Models (SLMs) protect sensitive participant data by keeping processing within controlled environments, but their limited reasoning capabilities make simple prompting insufficient for context-aware and factually reliable analysis. This study developed CARE-SD (Context-Adaptive Reasoning and Explanation for Self-Disclosure), a novel four-module architecture integrating context-adaptive processing, hierarchical disclosure reasoning, explanation-consistency verification, and cross-batch reconciliation. We evaluated three local SLMs, including Llama 1B, Qwen 1.5B, and Llama 3B, using 82 independently annotated cybersecurity interviews across five organizational sectors. Comparisons included conventional classifiers, three prompting strategies, larger 8B--32B models, and architectural ablations. Two independent reviewers assessed disclosure labels, factual claims, and explanation correctness. CARE-SD improved the accuracy and evidence reliability of SLMs, increasing Llama 3B Macro-F1 from 0.80 to 0.88 while reducing unsupported claims by 60\%. Remarkably, the 3B model matched the 20B reference model in category Macro-F1, demonstrating the effectiveness of the architecture without requiring a larger model.
tldr: CARE-SD is a four-module architecture that improves local small language models' accuracy and evidence reliability when identifying self-disclosures in cybersecurity interview transcripts.
motivation: Cybersecurity interviews reveal sensitive security behaviors and privacy concerns that conventional technical assessments miss, but automated detection of genuine self-disclosure is hard due to context dependence and overlapping categories. Locally deployed SLMs protect participant privacy yet lack the reasoning capability for reliable context-aware analysis.
method: The authors built CARE-SD, combining context-adaptive processing, hierarchical disclosure reasoning, explanation-consistency verification, and cross-batch reconciliation, and evaluated three local SLMs (Llama 1B, Qwen 1.5B, Llama 3B) on 82 annotated cybersecurity interviews against conventional classifiers, prompting strategies, larger 8B–32B models, and ablations.
result: CARE-SD raised Llama 3B's Macro-F1 from 0.80 to 0.88 while cutting unsupported claims by 60%, and the 3B model matched a 20B reference model in category Macro-F1.
conclusion: A structured reasoning-and-explanation architecture can substantially improve the factual reliability and accuracy of small local language models for sensitive qualitative text analysis without requiring larger models.

title: A Coupled Fluid Naghdi Shell Windkessel Model For Pulmonary Artery Banding: Partitioned Numerical Scheme And Parameter Estimation
authors: Yifan Wang, Josip Tambaca, Suncica Canic
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20966v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a 3D fluid structure interaction model for blood flow through deformable vessels with localized constrictions, motivated by pulmonary artery banding in neonates with congenital heart disease. The model couples incompressible Navier Stokes equations in an Arbitrary Lagrangian Eulerian framework with a Naghdi shell model for the arterial wall and a three element Windkessel model for downstream circulation. The shell describes a 3D cylindrical vessel wall with variable radius and is defined on a 2D reference domain. Its low regularity formulation retains membrane, bending, and transverse shear deformation while requiring only first derivatives of the reference midsurface, accommodating piecewise smooth geometries with discontinuous surface slopes. We derive the coupled variational formulation and develop a non-iterative partitioned scheme with a Robin-type interface condition incorporating arterial wall inertia. For a linearized fixed domain problem, we establish a discrete energy estimate under suitable assumptions. A unscented Kalman filter estimates proximal and distal resistances and compliance from inlet-pressure observations. Numerical experiments demonstrate consistent pressure wave propagation and wall deformation under spatial and temporal refinement. Comparisons of the standard Naghdi shell and a modified, predominantly radial shell model reveal how structural deformation mechanisms affect wave speed and displacement. An idealized pulmonary artery banding example demonstrates the coupled fluid shell Windkessel model with parameter estimation. The framework enables investigation of the hemodynamic and mechanical effects of localized constrictions and their dependence on downstream vascular properties.
tldr: A 3D fluid-structure interaction model couples Navier-Stokes, a Naghdi shell, and a Windkessel model to simulate pulmonary artery banding, with a partitioned numerical scheme and unscented Kalman filter parameter estimation.
motivation: Pulmonary artery banding in neonates with congenital heart disease requires understanding hemodynamic effects of localized constrictions, motivating a computational model that captures blood flow, vessel deformation, and downstream circulation.
method: The authors derive a coupled variational formulation combining incompressible Navier-Stokes in an ALE framework, a low-regularity Naghdi shell for the arterial wall, and a three-element Windkessel model, then develop a non-iterative partitioned scheme with a Robin-type interface condition and use an unscented Kalman filter to estimate resistances and compliance.
result: Numerical experiments show consistent pressure wave propagation and wall deformation under refinement, comparisons between standard and radial shell models reveal deformation effects on wave speed and displacement, and an idealized banding example demonstrates the coupled model with parameter estimation.
conclusion: The framework enables investigation of hemodynamic and mechanical effects of localized constrictions and their dependence on downstream vascular properties, providing a computational tool for studying pulmonary artery banding.

title: The Best Ulam Constant Of The N-th Order Linear Differential Operator With Constant Coefficients
authors: Jawad Boutarfass, Iz-Iddine El-Fassi, Lahcen Oukhtite
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21122v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let [MATH] be a Banach space over the field [MATH], and let [MATH] be the [MATH]-th order linear differential operator defined by [MATH], where [MATH] are fixed scalars and [MATH] is a fixed positive integer. It is well known that [MATH] is Ulam stable if and only if its characteristic equation has no roots on the imaginary axis. In this paper, we determine the best Ulam constant of [MATH] under this condition, for an arbitrary order [MATH] and without any restriction on the multiplicities of the roots of the characteristic equation. This improves and completes several known Ulam stability results for this operator and provides the best estimate possible for the error between approximate and exact solutions of the equation [MATH], where [MATH]. Moreover, as an auxiliary result, we give an explicit formula for the general solution of this equation.
tldr: The paper determines the best Ulam constant for an n-th order linear differential operator with constant coefficients, assuming the characteristic equation has no roots on the imaginary axis.
motivation: Ulam stability of differential operators is a classical functional-analysis problem, and finding the optimal (best) stability constant provides the sharpest error bound for approximate solutions.
method: The authors analyze the characteristic equation of the constant-coefficient operator, handle arbitrary root multiplicities, and derive an explicit formula for the general solution to identify the best Ulam constant.
result: They obtain the best Ulam constant for any order n without restrictions on root multiplicities, improving and completing earlier Ulam stability results for this operator.
conclusion: The work sharpens the theory of Ulam stability for linear differential operators and gives the optimal error estimate between approximate and exact solutions.

title: Hybrid DeepXAI Fusion Network For Interpretable Big Data Analytics And Secure Cloud Decision-Making Systems
authors: B. Nancharaiah, Ramakrishna Kolikipogu, J. Sulthan Alikhan, Lakshmana Phaneendra Maguluri, Elangovan Muniyandy, D. Baburao
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20661v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Big data analytics supports modern intelligent systems, but model complexity and limited transparency can undermine interpretability, trust, and security in decision-making. This paper presents the Hybrid DeepXAI Fusion Network, a deep learning framework that integrates temporal, relational, and contextual features with explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) mechanisms. The architecture combines one-dimensional convolutional neural networks (1D-CNNs) for temporal feature extraction, Transformer encoders for contextual modeling, and graph neural networks (GNNs) for inter-feature dependency analysis. An attention-based fusion mechanism integrates these representations. Class Activation Mapping (CAM) and an explanation loss are incorporated to improve interpretability and explanation consistency. The framework is designed for deployment in a federated cloud architecture, using homomorphic encryption and blockchain-based auditing to support data privacy and accountability. Experimental evaluations across healthcare, finance, and energy datasets report 98.42% accuracy, 97.9% precision, 98.1% recall, and a 98.0% F1-score, outperforming the evaluated CNN-LSTM, Transformer-only, and XGBoost baselines. Under projected gradient descent (PGD) adversarial perturbations, the model reportedly retains accuracy above 91.5%. Scalability experiments report throughput of 80,000 messages per second with latency below 200 milliseconds. These results suggest that the proposed framework has potential for interpretable and secure cloud-based decision-support systems.
tldr: A deep learning framework combining 1D-CNNs, Transformers, GNNs, and XAI mechanisms for interpretable big data analytics in secure cloud decision-making.
motivation: Big data analytics suffers from model complexity, limited transparency, and security concerns in decision-making.
method: The Hybrid DeepXAI Fusion Network integrates temporal, relational, and contextual features via 1D-CNNs, Transformer encoders, and GNNs, fused with attention, and incorporates CAM and explanation loss for interpretability; it uses federated cloud architecture with homomorphic encryption and blockchain auditing.
result: It reports 98.42% accuracy, 97.9% precision, 98.1% recall, 98.0% F1-score across healthcare, finance, and energy datasets, and retains above 91.5% accuracy under PGD adversarial perturbations.
conclusion: The framework shows potential for interpretable and secure cloud-based decision-support systems, though it is not related to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Audio-Based Condition Monitoring For Agricultural Machinery: Stakeholder Needs, Adoption Barriers, And Mvp Requirements
authors: Tashfain Ahmed, Mohammadali Saffary, Kehinde Elelu, Duc Hung Luong, Joshua Siegel
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21293v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Failures of agricultural machinery are costly when breakdowns occur during narrow work windows and are discovered too late for planned service. Audio-based condition monitoring offers a low-cost retrofit sensing path because operators already treat abnormal sound as an informal diagnostic cue. Whether such systems are adopted, however, depends on how well they fit farm workflows, repair constraints, and stakeholder decision-making. This paper reports a stakeholder discovery study of audio-based condition monitoring for agricultural machinery. We synthesize semi-structured interviews with farm operators, dairy operators, dealership and service personnel, manufacturers, integrators, and domain experts, together with a short survey. Across sources, downtime avoidance emerged as the dominant value driver, and failures were most commonly recognized through unusual noise and loss of functionality. Survey responses further indicate a gap in maintenance visibility and low penetration of predictive tools. These findings narrow the opportunity from generic ``AI diagnosis'' to low-friction early warning and evidence generation for maintenance planning. Modern tractors appear to be a weaker initial wedge because many are already instrumented and supported by mature service programs. Implements, attachments, hidden rotating components, small-to-medium operations, and continuous-use settings such as dairy present clearer need because failures in these contexts are harder to perceive, sensing coverage is lower, and downtime consequences are higher. We translate these findings into requirements for a minimum viable product (MVP) that prioritizes maintenance actionability over full automation: commodity audio capture, contextual annotation, asset-specific baselines, persistent-deviation detection, temporally stable alerts, and evidence artifacts that support operator inspection and dealer triage.
tldr: A stakeholder discovery study identifies needs, adoption barriers, and MVP requirements for audio-based condition monitoring of agricultural machinery.
motivation: Agricultural machinery failures during narrow work windows are costly, and audio-based retrofit sensing may provide low-cost early warning, but adoption depends on fitting farm workflows and stakeholder decision-making.
method: The authors conducted semi-structured interviews with farm and dairy operators, dealership and service personnel, manufacturers, integrators, and domain experts, supplemented by a short survey.
result: Downtime avoidance emerged as the dominant value driver, with failures often recognized through unusual noise; survey responses revealed low predictive-tool penetration and a maintenance visibility gap, suggesting tractors are a weaker initial wedge than implements and continuous-use settings like dairy.
conclusion: The findings translate into MVP requirements prioritizing low-friction early warning and evidence generation over full automation, including commodity audio capture, contextual annotation, asset-specific baselines, persistent-deviation detection, stable alerts, and maintenance-planning artifacts.

title: Evaluating And Improving Static Application Security Testing Tools For Rust
authors: Huaien Zhang, Zhengjie Zhao, Yu Pei, Tian Dong, Minxue Pan, Shin Hwei Tan, Hao Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21373v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rust has become a popular systems programming language in recent years because of its strong guarantees on memory and concurrency safety. Many types of system software have been re-implemented in Rust. However, Rust programs can still suffer from common memory and concurrency vulnerabilities due to unsafe code and misunderstandings of its complex mechanisms. To mitigate such vulnerabilities, developers often rely on static application security testing (SAST) tools. However, the effectiveness of existing Rust SAST tools on real-world vulnerabilities remains underexplored.
