In this paper, we first conduct an empirical evaluation of mainstream Rust SAST tools using security vulnerabilities identified in real-world Rust applications. We systematically assess their effectiveness, uncover common weaknesses, and analyze the root causes behind them. Motivated by the study, we propose TRUST, a large language model (LLM)-assisted automated testing framework. TRUST automatically analyzes the official Rust reference to derive and implement semantics-preserving transformations. It leverages these transformations to generate mutant programs for evaluating Rust SAST tools and uncovering potential faults within them. Overall, TRUST has revealed 46 faults across six popular SAST tools, 17 of which have been confirmed. In addition, our study yields ten empirical findings and four practical lessons that provide actionable guidance for developing more effective, robust, and maintainable Rust SAST tools.
tldr: This paper empirically evaluates Rust static application security testing (SAST) tools and proposes TRUST, an LLM-assisted framework that generates semantics-preserving mutants to uncover faults in those tools.
motivation: Rust's safety guarantees do not eliminate memory and concurrency vulnerabilities from unsafe code and complex language mechanisms, so developers rely on SAST tools whose real-world effectiveness is underexplored.
method: The authors first conduct an empirical evaluation of mainstream Rust SAST tools using real-world vulnerabilities; then they build TRUST, which uses an LLM to analyze the Rust reference and derive semantics-preserving transformations for generating mutant programs that test SAST tools.
result: TRUST revealed 46 faults across six popular Rust SAST tools, 17 of which were confirmed, and the study produced ten empirical findings and four practical lessons for improving Rust SAST tools.
conclusion: The work provides actionable guidance for developing more effective, robust, and maintainable Rust SAST tools, highlighting the utility of LLM-assisted mutation testing for security tool evaluation.

title: AeroProp-X: An Open-Source, Self-Verifying Method-of-Characteristics Toolkit For Edge-Capable Rocket Nozzle Design And Aerothermodynamic Analysis
authors: Aryuemaan Kumar Chowdhury
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20612v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The design of supersonic rocket nozzles by the Method of Characteristics is a mature discipline, yet the software that implements it is frequently either proprietary, heavyweight, or opaque, which limits reproducibility and classroom and field use. This paper presents AeroProp-X, an open-source, dependency-light toolkit that synthesizes shock-free minimum-length nozzle contours and evaluates their ideal aerothermodynamic performance entirely on commodity hardware without graphics acceleration or network access. The central contribution is methodological rather than physical: the planar characteristics solver is made self-verifying by exploiting an exact gas-dynamic invariant, namely that the computed exit wall height ratio must equal the isentropic area ratio at the design Mach number, so that every generated contour reports its own discretization error automatically. We describe the governing theory, the layered software architecture, and the synthesis algorithm, and we validate the implementation against analytic compressible-flow tables and against the expansion ratios of historical flight engines. The solver reproduces tabulated gas-dynamic quantities to table precision and converges to the exact area ratio with relative error below three parts in ten thousand, while remaining small enough to run interactively on an embedded-class processor. We argue that built-in verifiability, dependency minimalism, and explicit scoping of the ideal-flow assumptions together make the tool well suited to education, preliminary design, and reproducible research.
tldr: AeroProp-X is an open-source, self-verifying Method-of-Characteristics toolkit for designing and analyzing supersonic rocket nozzles on commodity or edge hardware.
motivation: Existing Method-of-Characteristics software for rocket nozzle design is often proprietary, heavyweight, or opaque, limiting reproducibility and practical use in education and field settings.
method: The toolkit synthesizes shock-free minimum-length nozzle contours using a planar Method-of-Characteristics solver and makes the solver self-verifying by checking that the computed exit wall height ratio matches the isentropic area ratio at the design Mach number.
result: The implementation reproduces analytic compressible-flow tables to table precision and converges to the exact area ratio with relative error below three parts in ten thousand while remaining lightweight enough for embedded-class processors.
conclusion: Built-in verifiability, dependency minimalism, and explicit ideal-flow assumptions make AeroProp-X well suited for education, preliminary design, and reproducible research in rocket nozzle aerothermodynamics.

title: Rat-ec: Introducing A New Open-Source 3d Volume-Integral Eddy-Current Module
authors: Daniel Mayr, Jeroen van Nugteren, Julien Dular, Mariusz Wozniak, Jasmin Smajic, Juerg Leuthold
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21315v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present RAT-EC, an open-source volume-integral eddy-current module for unstructured meshes, driven in the time domain by coils of arbitrary winding geometry. It is the first openly available code of this kind and part of the open-source RAT suite. Because only the conductor is meshed, neither the surrounding air nor an artificial outer boundary has to be modelled, which simplifies model preparation and brings problems with thin gaps and intricate air regions within reach of standard hardware. The formulation combines a semi-analytical evaluation of the singular and near-singular inductance terms, a multi-level fast multipole method that accelerates both the far-field inductance action and the coil field, topology-aware constraints for multiply connected conductors, and a matrix-free, GPU-accelerated time integration. The implementation is verified against closed-form solutions for a conducting sphere and a conducting ring, and is validated on the TEAM-7 benchmark. At 50 Hz, RAT-EC reproduces the measured field as accurately as finite-element solutions. At 200 Hz, it agrees with a converged finite-element model, but both deviate from published measurements, which suggests that this benchmark point should be re-examined. RAT-EC provides an open platform for volume-integral eddy-current simulation and method development.
tldr: RAT-EC is an open-source volume-integral eddy-current simulation module for unstructured meshes, using semi-analytical inductance evaluation, fast multipole acceleration, and GPU-accelerated time integration.
motivation: Eddy-current simulations often require meshing air regions and artificial boundaries, which complicates model setup and limits problems with thin gaps or intricate geometries on standard hardware.
method: The module employs a volume-integral formulation that meshes only conductors, combined with semi-analytical singular/near-singular inductance terms, a multi-level fast multipole method, topology-aware constraints, and matrix-free GPU time integration.
result: It is verified against closed-form solutions for a conducting sphere and ring and validated on TEAM-7; at 50 Hz it matches measurements as accurately as finite-element solutions, while at 200 Hz both methods deviate from published measurements.
conclusion: RAT-EC provides an open platform for volume-integral eddy-current simulation and method development, suggesting that the 200 Hz TEAM-7 benchmark point should be re-examined.

title: Two Sample Sizes In Test-Time Llm Ensembling: Buffered Erm And Minimax Theory
authors: Arash A. Amini Zhi Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21363v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Test-time scaling can improve the performance of large language models by generating multiple answers to a question and aggregating them. Weighted ensembles extend this idea by drawing answers from several models, with the weights determining how often each model is used. Learning these weights from a training dataset involves two sample sizes: [MATH] labeled questions and [MATH] generations per model and question. We study their interplay through the clean risk, the population error of the ensemble's infinite-generation voting rule. Under a margin condition with exponent [MATH], we show that empirical risk minimization (ERM) with a calibrated margin buffer achieves excess risk of order [MATH], up to logarithmic factors, for fixed numbers of models and candidate answers. To investigate the optimality of this dependence on [MATH] and [MATH], we analyze a simplified submodel with two models and two possible answers per question. We characterize its minimax excess risk up to constants by a Hellinger modulus for a binomial-mixture experiment. Polynomial approximation and spectral analysis reveal three regimes. When questions are relatively scarce, the [MATH] term governs learning and the general buffered ERM is optimal. In an intermediate regime, pooling generation counts across questions improves upon estimating each answer distribution separately, with only logarithmic gains from additional questions. With sufficiently many questions, the minimax excess risk reaches an [MATH] identification floor that persists even with infinitely many questions. The submodel's lower bounds also apply to general ensembles, matching the buffered-ERM upper bound up to logarithmic factors when questions are scarce and in parts of the intermediate regime. Questions remain about the transitions between regimes and the construction of matching pooled estimators for general ensembles.
tldr: This paper studies the interplay between two sample sizes—labeled questions and generations per model per question—in test-time LLM ensemble learning, with buffered ERM upper bounds and minimax lower bounds.
motivation: Test-time scaling via weighted LLM ensembles can improve performance, but the statistical roles of the number of labeled questions and the number of generations per model are not well understood.
method: The authors analyze clean risk under a margin condition, propose calibrated buffered ERM, and derive minimax excess risk for a simplified two-model two-answer submodel using Hellinger modulus, polynomial approximation, and spectral analysis.
result: Three regimes emerge: sample-size-limited learning where ERM is optimal, an intermediate regime where pooling generation counts helps, and an identification-floor regime even with infinitely many questions.
conclusion: The submodel lower bounds extend to general ensembles and match buffered-ERM upper bounds in several regimes, while transitions between regimes and matching pooled estimators remain open.

title: Poisoning The Neighborhood: A Topology-Aware Topic-Level Attack On Large-Scale HNSW-based Rag Systems
authors: Yufei Chen, Yao Wang, Haibin Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21464v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) mitigates hallucinations and knowledge staleness in large language models using external knowledge. However, ingestion from public and third-party sources exposes RAG systems to poisoning attacks. Existing attacks are designed and evaluated under exact retrieval, where poisoned documents participate in global ranking. Deployment-scale systems instead rely on approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) indexes such as hierarchical navigable small world (HNSW), where limited search budgets, graph-search reachability, and local benign-document competition invalidate this assumption and degrade existing attacks. We present a topology-aware topic-level poisoning attack against large-scale HNSW-RAG that generalizes to unseen topic queries. We organize poisoned documents into a Hub-Satellite structure: Satellites provide competitive entry points across semantic regions, while Hubs strengthen local cohesion and facilitate cascading retrieval. For generation, we propose an entity-claim promotion attack combining evidence anchoring and entity-claim coupling to promote the target entity via a target claim across different query regions. On 2M-document Wikipedia, our attack maintains over 72% retrieval success and reaches 31.29% attack success, substantially outperforming baselines; domain-specific experiments further support its effectiveness. Structural analyses show that the Hub-Satellite topology forms in HNSW, indicating that graph structure contributes to improved poisoned-document retrieval. Existing poisoning defenses cannot mitigate the attack, exposing graph-structural risks in HNSW-RAG systems.
tldr: A topology-aware topic-level poisoning attack against large-scale HNSW-based RAG systems that exploits graph structure to improve poisoned document retrieval and generation.
motivation: RAG systems are vulnerable to poisoning via public data ingestion, but existing attacks assume exact retrieval and fail under approximate nearest-neighbor indexes like HNSW used in deployment-scale systems.
method: The attack organizes poisoned documents into a Hub-Satellite structure to provide competitive entry points and local cohesion, and uses an entity-claim promotion attack combining evidence anchoring and entity-claim coupling for generation.
result: On a 2M-document Wikipedia dataset, the attack maintains over 72% retrieval success and 31.29% attack success, outperforming baselines, and existing poisoning defenses cannot mitigate it.
conclusion: The work exposes graph-structural risks in HNSW-RAG systems, showing that topology-aware poisoning can generalize to unseen topic queries and bypass current defenses.

title: Stationarity Equations For Fractional Affine Area Measures: Ellipsoid Rigidity And Polytopal Solutions
authors: Dong Qiu Xingyu Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21024v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Xi and Zhao established a first variation formula for affine inequalities involving radial mean bodies, and asked two geometric questions about the resulting stationarity equation: whether the bodies already known to satisfy it are the only ones, and whether its smooth solutions are exactly the ellipsoids. We answer both. Every strictly convex solution of the equation with [MATH], [MATH] is an ellipsoid, which answers the second question affirmatively while replacing smoothness and everywhere positive Gauss curvature by strict convexity. Every full-dimensional facet-transitive polytope satisfies the equation, and so does the polar of every vertex-transitive polytope with respect to its volume centroid; the rhombic dodecahedron, the thirteen Catalan solids and the bipyramids over regular polygons other than the octahedron provide infinitely many affinely inequivalent solutions that are not affine images of regular polytopes or balls, so the answer to the first question is negative. The rigidity proof compares overlap integrals along a continuous Steiner path: stationarity forces an increase of order [MATH], whereas a nonaffine chord midpoint function forces an increase of order [MATH]. For negative parameters the required comparison rests on a minimization formula over bounded measurable auxiliary sets.
tldr: The paper solves two geometric questions about stationarity equations for fractional affine area measures, proving ellipsoid rigidity for strictly convex solutions and constructing polytopal solutions.
motivation: Xi and Zhao established a first variation formula for affine inequalities and asked whether known bodies are the only solutions and whether smooth solutions are exactly ellipsoids.
method: The authors use a continuous Steiner path and compare overlap integrals, with a minimization formula over bounded measurable auxiliary sets for negative parameters.
result: Every strictly convex solution with certain conditions is an ellipsoid, while many facet-transitive polytopes and polar vertex-transitive polytopes provide infinitely many non-ellipsoidal solutions.
conclusion: The second question is answered affirmatively and the first negatively, revealing rich families of affinely inequivalent polytopal solutions.

title: Kernel-Based Heterogeneous Mean Field Games On A Continuum Type Space
authors: Luebo Xia Guangchen Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21423v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper studies a class of heterogeneous mean field games on a continuum type space, in which interactions are generated by a Hilbert-Schmidt kernel operator acting on the type-indexed mean state profile. The control set is allowed to be a general closed convex subset of a Euclidean space, and the optimal feedback is characterized through the unique maximizer of the Hamiltonian. For a prescribed mean-field path, the stochastic maximum principle leads to a family of fully coupled forward-backward stochastic differential equations (FBSDEs) indexed by the agent type. Under Lipschitz conditions and a monotonicity assumption on the reduced coefficients, the frozen FBSDE is globally well posed. We then formulate the consistency problem as a fixed-point problem for the kernel mean-field path. When the operator norm of the interaction kernel is sufficiently small, the resulting map has an invariant ball and is continuous and compact, so that Schauder's theorem yields existence of a mean field Nash equilibrium. Uniqueness follows under an aggregate monotonicity condition adapted to the kernel coupling. A linear-quadratic example illustrates how finite-rank interactions and heterogeneous risk preferences produce coupled collective modes, and yields a spectral smallness condition for existence and an explicit sufficient condition for uniqueness.
tldr: The paper studies heterogeneous mean field games on a continuum type space with Hilbert-Schmidt kernel interactions, proving existence and uniqueness of mean field Nash equilibria via fully coupled FBSDEs and Schauder's fixed-point theorem.
motivation: Mean field games with heterogeneous agents and continuum type spaces are relevant to economics and finance, but the paper does not address quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
method: The authors use the stochastic maximum principle to derive a family of fully coupled forward-backward stochastic differential equations indexed by agent type, then formulate a fixed-point problem for the kernel mean-field path and apply Schauder's theorem.
result: Existence of a mean field Nash equilibrium is obtained when the interaction kernel's operator norm is sufficiently small, and uniqueness follows under an aggregate monotonicity condition; a linear-quadratic example illustrates coupled collective modes and spectral conditions.
conclusion: This is a theoretical contribution to mean field game theory and stochastic control, with no direct relevance to the user's quantum information, quantum thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems research directions.

title: Forensic Analysis Of The HackRF One With PortaPack Mayhem Firmware
authors: D\"uzg\"un K\"u\c{c}\"uk
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20647v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Software-defined radios (SDRs) have become an inexpensive, portable platform for replay attacks, location spoofing and jamming. The HackRF One can operate stand-alone when fitted with a PortaPack interface board running the open-source Mayhem firmware. No peer-reviewed study has addressed the forensic analysis of this device family. This work establishes, at source-code level, where forensically relevant data reside on the microSD card of a device running Mayhem v2.0.1, in which format, when they are written and how they should be interpreted. The methodology is applied to an SD card image that the author acquired from their own device after four months of real use, and every inference is drawn from the image alone. The workflow covers timestamp rules that depend on the real-time clock (RTC) battery state, traces of on-device trimming and text editing, cluster-level recovery of deleted in-phase/quadrature (IQ) captures, and decoding of recorded signals cross-checked with an independent decoder. In the example image, the final part of a deleted IQ capture and a trimmed-away capture segment are recovered, and six captures are attributed to a single rolling-code on-off keying (OOK) transmitter sharing one 32-bit identifier. The study provides practitioners with an artifact catalogue, interpretation rules and acquisition recommendations.
tldr: A forensic analysis of the HackRF One SDR with PortaPack Mayhem firmware, detailing where and how forensically relevant data are stored on its microSD card.
motivation: Software-defined radios like HackRF One with Mayhem firmware are increasingly used for replay attacks, spoofing, and jamming, but no peer-reviewed forensic study of this device family existed.
method: Source-code-level inspection of Mayhem v2.0.1 was combined with forensic analysis of an SD card image from a device used for four months, covering timestamp rules, deleted file recovery, IQ capture recovery, and signal decoding.
result: The study recovered a deleted IQ capture and a trimmed capture segment, attributed six captures to a single rolling-code OOK transmitter, and produced an artifact catalogue and interpretation rules.
conclusion: The work provides practitioners with forensic acquisition and interpretation guidance for HackRF One/PortaPack Mayhem devices, though it is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: The Noise Cost Of Reservoir Locality In Broadband Quantum Amplifier Chains
authors: Chengxi Li, Hao Zhu, Tie-Fu Zhang, Lin Zhuang, Wanzi Sun, Wuming Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20654v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Directional quantum amplifiers enable weak-signal readout while protecting the source, but reservoir noise limits sensitivity. Finite-band suppression must reconcile frequency-dependent responses with fixed local couplings and finite rates. We construct adjacent-site loss channels attaining the known single-frequency minimum under local compatibility conditions, as an uncapped benchmark. For specified uniform and dimerized chains, we compare fixed reservoirs at matched drift, ports, high-gain band and complete gain/loss rate caps. At the representative cap [MATH] and halfwidth [MATH], nearest-neighbor arithmetic band average noise exceeds the unrestricted optimum by more than [MATH] quanta in the uniform chain for every finite [MATH]. Boundary-response bounds give necessary rates and targets requiring range two. At [MATH], finite-auxiliary calculations retain a noise advantage under matched total coupling budgets; response bounds quantify noise-resolution tolerances. These theoretical results guide reservoir design and noise calibration for a proposed cryogenic microwave array with a [MATH] kHz design band.

title: Surviving Readout Errors And Incomplete Postselection In Monitored Quantum Circuits
authors: Murtaza Ali Mir, Teemu Ojanen, Ali G. Moghaddam
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20712v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study how readout errors affect dynamics in monitored quantum circuits. Such errors make postselection effectively incomplete, conditioning trajectories on imperfect rather than true records. Focusing on U(1)-symmetric circuits, we find that the charge-sharpening transition survives at a finite error rate, with the sharp phase's vanishing fluctuations replaced by a finite steady-state plateau. The charge fluctuations show a shallow minimum near the ideal transition point as a function of measurement rate, signaling the competition between measurement-induced purification and noise-induced mixing. By decomposing the fluctuations into quantum and classical contributions, we show the minimum marks where incomplete postselection still retains enough trajectory memory to attenuate noise-induced mixing, leaving a detectable signature of the transition even in a noisy setting. Mid-circuit measurements are far harder to mitigate against readout errors than standard end-of-circuit ones, because the errors corrupt the postselection itself; the decomposition therefore offers a minimal mitigation framework and a route to locate the transition directly from experimental data. Our results show that charge sharpening survives readout errors in a quantitative and experimentally accessible way.

title: Standard And Bipolar Rectification In Tilted Periodically-Driven Quantum Systems
authors: Juan Jos\'e Mendoza-Arenas Joaqu\'in Pe\~{n}uela-Parra
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20765v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Developing mechanisms to control transport in correlated quantum systems is essential for advancing quantum circuit technologies. In this work, we establish a rectification mechanism for both particle and energy flow in a fermionic system coupled to external baths, in the presence of a tilted potential modulated locally by a time-periodic drive. The drive generates particle and energy currents even in the absence of chemical or thermal bias between the baths. These drive-induced currents are enhanced at resonant frequencies at which avoided crossings occur in the Floquet quasienergy spectrum, reflecting the role of the Floquet states as intermediate channels for transport. Once a bias between the baths is introduced, the drive-induced current contribution can reinforce, compete with, or even cancel the bias-induced contribution. These effects enable rectification in the non-interacting regime, which we quantify via the rectification coefficient [MATH]. This coefficient measures the asymmetry between transport up the tilt (forward bias) and down the tilt (reverse bias). In addition to standard rectification, where transport is reduced under reverse bias, we identify a regime of bipolar rectification, in which the current flows only up the tilt regardless of the bias polarity. At the boundary between standard and bipolar regimes, the system achieves perfect rectification, corresponding to complete suppression of the reverse-bias current. In the presence of interactions between particles, the parameter region that supports bipolar rectification is enlarged and [MATH] can be enhanced by many orders of magnitude. Our results establish a rectification mechanism for particle and energy transport that can be experimentally realized in condensed matter and cold atom systems.

title: Monoprop: Scaling Pauli And Majorana Propagation Via Anticommutation Indices
authors: Aaron Miller
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21000v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce monoprop, an open-source, massively parallel operator-propagation framework for fermion and qubit bases. For [MATH] qubits or modes, existing codes represent each of the [MATH] tracked operator terms (Pauli strings or products of Majorana operators) as a [MATH]-bit string, testing each for anticommutation with the gate at [MATH] cost per gate. Here, we introduce the anticommutation index which rapidly looks up the terms anticommuting with a gate. A local gate changes only the terms that touch its sites, and when terms are truncated to act on few sites, only a fraction [MATH] touch any given qubit or mode, and we use this to prove the time per gate scales as [MATH]. This counterintuitive result tells us that for a fixed number of terms, increasing the number of sites can make things faster. We demonstrate this numerically, and show monoprop scales almost ideally to 8192 cores, tracking [MATH] terms. Beyond propagation, we present memory-efficient surrogate graphs, which record one propagation and replay it at new angles, for fast energy re-estimation and parameter gradients, and an efficient method for finding energy-minimising gates and optimal angles for simulating adaptive quantum-chemistry circuits.

title: Restarted Fixed-Point Acceleration Of Proximal Admm For Capped-$\ell_1$ Penalized Optimization
authors: Hongyuan Tao, Fan Wu, Wei Bian
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21444v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider box-constrained optimization with a convex, Lipschitz continuous loss function that may be nonsmooth and a capped-[MATH] penalty. Exploiting the convex branch representation of the capped-[MATH] penalty, we construct an associated nonexpansive fixed-point mapping for each branch and, based on these mappings, propose a restarted accelerated proximal alternating direction method of multipliers (RA-pADMM). The resulting algorithm consists of a preliminary branch identification phase and a subsequent accelerated phase based on either the Halpern or fast Krasnosel'ski--Mann iteration, together with a sufficient decrease restart mechanism. We prove that the preliminary phase terminates after finitely many iterations and that only finitely many branch updates are accepted during the subsequent phase. The primal iterates and proximal outputs converge to a common lifted stationary point, which is also a [MATH]-strong local minimizer of the corresponding cardinality penalized problem. Moreover, the Halpern and fast Krasnosel'ski--Mann variants achieve nonergodic [MATH] and asymptotic [MATH] convergence rates, respectively, for both the objective value gap and the Karush--Kuhn--Tucker residual associated with the final branch. Numerical experiments on sparse recovery and real data classification problems demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed RA-pADMM algorithm.
tldr: The paper proposes a restarted accelerated proximal ADMM algorithm for box-constrained optimization with a capped-l1 penalty, with convergence guarantees and numerical experiments on sparse recovery and classification.
motivation: The capped-l1 penalty is useful for sparse optimization but leads to nonconvex and nonsmooth problems that require specialized algorithms with strong convergence properties.
method: The authors use a convex branch representation of the capped-l1 penalty to build nonexpansive fixed-point mappings, then design a restarted accelerated proximal ADMM combining branch identification with Halpern or fast Krasnosel'skii--Mann iterations and a sufficient decrease restart.
result: They prove finite termination of the preliminary phase, finitely many accepted branch updates, convergence to a lifted stationary point that is also a local minimizer, and establish nonergodic O(1/k) and asymptotic O(1/k^2) rates for the Halpern and fast Krasnosel'skii--Mann variants, supported by numerical experiments.
conclusion: The proposed RA-pADMM is effective for sparse recovery and real data classification, but the work is entirely in optimization and machine learning and has no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Density Of Repelling Periodic Points For Cubic Rational Maps
authors: Nha Xuan Truong
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21559v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove the repelling-density conjecture for cubic rational maps over [MATH]: for every prime [MATH], the classical Julia set is the closure of the classical repelling periodic points. By B\'ezivin's theorem, it suffices to prove that a nonempty classical Julia set contains a classical repelling periodic point. The case [MATH] follows from known results for tame maps, so we treat residue characteristics two and three. We argue by contraposition, assuming that the map has no classical repelling periodic points. Maps with potential good reduction already have empty classical Julia set. Otherwise, we conjugate the map to an explicit normalized form and analyze its coefficients. In each case, we obtain coefficient restrictions and establish a uniform bound on the spherical derivatives of all iterates. This bound implies equicontinuity on the classical projective line and hence emptiness of the classical Julia set.
tldr: The paper proves the repelling-density conjecture for cubic rational maps over p-adic fields, showing the Julia set equals the closure of repelling periodic points.
motivation: To resolve a conjecture in arithmetic dynamics for cubic rational maps in residue characteristics two and three, extending known results for tame maps.
method: Uses contraposition: assuming no classical repelling periodic points, the map is conjugated to a normalized form and coefficient restrictions yield a uniform bound on spherical derivatives, implying equicontinuity and emptiness of the Julia set.
result: For every prime, the classical Julia set of a cubic rational map is the closure of its classical repelling periodic points, with the cases p=2 and p=3 handled explicitly.
conclusion: The repelling-density conjecture holds for cubic rational maps over p-adic fields, advancing the understanding of p-adic dynamics and Julia sets.

title: A Priori Error Estimates For A Hybrid High-Order Method On Variable-exponent Leray-Lions Problems
authors: Romain Mottier Andr\'e Harnist
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21611v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We derive a priori error estimates for the Hybrid High-Order (HHO) discretization of variable-exponent Leray--Lions problems introduced in a companion convergence study. HHO methods belong to the family of hybrid nonconforming methods, based on cell and face polynomial unknowns of arbitrary degree. Under additional broken regularity of the exact solution and its flux, we establish a localized error estimate that retains the individual element sizes and a global estimate whose rate distinguishes the purely subquadratic, mixed subquadratic--superquadratic, and purely superquadratic regimes. In the subquadratic range, we also derive a regime-dependent refinement that compares the local approximation scale with the local non-degeneracy scale and recovers the optimal polynomial order when that scale is resolved by the mesh. The analysis relies on variable-exponent approximation properties of polynomial projectors, mean-exponent tools for discrete polynomial spaces, and weighted monotonicity estimates. The framework also covers regularized and mildly non-symmetric anisotropic Carreau--Yasuda-type fluxes. Numerical experiments on Cartesian and Voronoi meshes support the predicted rates and show that the regularity assumption on the flux cannot be dispensed with.
tldr: The paper derives a priori error estimates for a Hybrid High-Order discretization of variable-exponent Leray-Lions problems.
motivation: To establish error estimates for HHO methods applied to nonlinear problems with variable exponents.
method: The analysis uses variable-exponent approximation properties of polynomial projectors, mean-exponent tools, and weighted monotonicity estimates.
result: Localized and global error estimates are obtained, distinguishing subquadratic, mixed, and superquadratic regimes, with regime-dependent refinement for subquadratic cases.
conclusion: Numerical experiments confirm the predicted rates and show the necessity of the flux regularity assumption.

title: Matoi: Selective Revalidation Of Consequence Evidence For Agent Authorization
authors: Zexun Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.21394v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Matoi separates reusable consequence evidence from current execution authority and durable occurrence history. Its finite query-aware contract covers branches, ordered collections and negative lookups. A consumer reuses only its own checked evidence whose observations remain valid; signed requests, live grants, quota and uncertain outcomes remain separate obligations. Conditional correctness arguments distinguish locally serialized claims from nontransactional remote effects. Two studies strengthen cost attribution and domain evaluation. A 1,440-cell matched-wire study repeats 144 authored inputs. With compact input bytes identical, reuse reduces complete lifecycle cost by 3.49 percent in JS and 1.79 percent in Python. Combined representation/reuse reductions against full proof are 10.87 and 16.53 percent; five of twelve family intervals for the matched comparison cross one in each language. A prospectively frozen AgentDojo Banking mapping covers 5/16 user plans and 7/9 attack plans. Both governed strategies preserve five exact benign transfers and refuse 35 reused attack-plan/policy crosses. Pre-satisfied utility predicates are reported separately from completed work. These are original scripted synthetic tools, not autonomous agents or a real bank. Earlier studies retain cheaper protected-cache alternatives, policy-compatible phishing, provider duplication and post-claim revocation. Separate JS/Python consumers establish finite-profile interoperability within the same project; durable recovery rechecks evidence and retains uncertain reservations. The results support a bounded, auditable reuse and execution contract, not a new general incremental algorithm, arbitrary-tool closure, atomic third-party commitment or production superiority.
tldr: Matoi proposes a bounded, auditable contract for selectively revalidating reusable consequence evidence in agent authorization while separating execution authority and occurrence history.
motivation: Agent authorization systems need to reuse previously checked evidence safely without conflating it with current permissions, grants, quotas, or uncertain outcomes.
method: The paper defines a finite query-aware contract covering branches, ordered collections, and negative lookups, and supports it with conditional correctness arguments plus two empirical studies in JavaScript and Python and an AgentDojo Banking mapping.
result: Reuse reduces complete lifecycle cost by 3.49% in JS and 1.79% in Python, with combined representation/reuse reductions of 10.87% and 16.53%; the AgentDojo mapping preserves five benign transfers and refuses 35 reused attack-plan/policy crosses.
conclusion: The results support a bounded, auditable reuse and execution contract, not a new general incremental algorithm, arbitrary-tool closure, atomic third-party commitment, or production superiority.
